It checks whether you can look at a small organization like Kalmia, say what it owns, say what could hurt it, and explain why one problem deserves attention before another. After the chapters come the practice parts:

  • Part A reviews every lesson of the five classes (22 lessons, plus a one-page map of Topics 1 and 2): the terms, the numbers, the Kalmia facts and the traps that cost marks.
  • Part B gives you 10 case studies, on Kalmia Coffee Roasters and on a real Canadian ransomware case, each with its most likely answers.
  • Part C holds 45 multiple-choice questions (MCQs): one correct answer each.
  • Part D holds 35 multiple-select questions (MSQs). The number in round brackets next to each one tells you how many answers are correct.
  • Part E holds 20 short essay questions, each with a model answer and a marking guide.
  • Parts F, G and H give you the answer key, the abbreviations and the official sources.

Every question shows the chapter and sub-chapter it covers (📍), a hint (💡), the answer (✅) and a short explanation of why that answer is right (📝). Try the question before you look at the answer. Reading answers you never attempted feels like studying, but very little of it stays.

⚠️ Topic 4 is on the mid-term too. Class 6 (Friday, November 6: network architecture, obsolete software and how to read a vulnerability scan report) belongs to the exam. This package covers Classes 1 to 5 in depth. Keep your Class 6 hand-out next to it and review it the same way: big ideas first, then the exam traps, then practice.

Whatever we do not finish in class, you finish at home. Every answer and every explanation is in the package, so nothing depends on having been there at minute 2:41.

Multiple-choice (MCQ). Read the stem twice. Try to answer in your head before you look at the options, then find the option that matches what you thought. Watch the small words: NOT, first, best, most likely. When two options both look right, one of them usually answers a different question from the one asked.

Multiple-select (MSQ). The number in round brackets is a gift: it tells you exactly how many boxes to tick. Treat each option as a separate true-or-false statement about the stem. Do not tick a fourth option "just in case" when the question asks for three.

Short essay. Find the verb first. Define wants a precise meaning. Explain wants a cause and its effect. Compare wants both sides, point by point. Justify wants a reason you could defend in front of Nadia Roy. Apply wants Kalmia, by name. A strong answer makes three moves: the idea in course vocabulary, the reason behind it, and a concrete Kalmia example. Eight to fifteen lines is plenty. Marks go to precision, not to length.

Calculations. Write the formula, the scale you used and the result, then the action that goes with it. For example: score = likelihood × impact = 4 × 4 = 16, which falls in Kalmia's High band (10–16), so a treatment plan is due within 30 days. A correct number with no reasoning earns fewer marks than you would expect.

The six words of Class 1 form one chain. Learn them in this order and a surprising number of questions answer themselves.

Word What it means At Kalmia
Asset Anything of value that needs protection: information and whatever stores, processes or carries it NAS-01 and its shares, the POS (point of sale) tablets of Café Plateau, the web shop
Threat A potential cause of an unwanted event, described by its source (who or what) and its event (what happens) A ransomware group sends a phishing e-mail and steals a password
Vulnerability A weakness in an asset, a procedure or a control that a threat can exploit One NAS-01 administrator password shared by four people, no MFA (multi-factor authentication)
Risk The possibility that a threat exploits a vulnerability and harms an asset, rated by likelihood × impact Ransomware on NAS-01: likelihood 4 × impact 4 = 16, High
Impact The size of the harm in business terms if the event happens About three days without wholesale preparation, roughly $28,500 of sales
Control A measure that lowers the likelihood, the impact or both Individual administrator accounts with MFA, an offline backup tested every month

A

Part A — Comprehensive content review

One section per class and one sub-section per lesson. For each lesson, read the big idea, make sure you could explain every line of "What you must know" to a classmate without notes, and pay close attention to the exam traps: they are the mistakes beginners make most often.

Class 1 gave you the toolbox for the whole term: the job, six precise words, three security properties, a ten-step process with Kalmia's 5 × 5 matrix, two frameworks and the company you analyze in every lab. Nearly every mid-term question leans on this chapter. If you can explain each section below to a classmate without notes, Monday evening will feel shorter.

The big idea. The course trains one job, competency EZ02 (risk and threat analysis), and covers all of it: list what an organization owns, find out who or what could hurt it, judge how probable and how damaging each problem would be, and recommend measures. You do it on one fictional company, Kalmia, and every lab is one chapter of the same report, the Integrative Project.

What you must know

  • Public information sources can be read by anyone: newsletters, security advisories such as those of the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/encheck), CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) records (🔗 https://www.cve.org/check), MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) (🔗 https://attack.mitre.org/check), frameworks. Private sources are the organization's confidential documents: asset inventory, penetration-test, compliance, incident and monitoring reports, policies.
  • Scope is the boundary of the analysis: which sites, systems, data and people are assessed, which are not, and why. The scope statement (objective, scope, dependencies, stakeholders, deliverables) is page one of the project and step 1 of every risk analysis.
  • Three scope questions: Does Kalmia own or control it? Does it store, process or transmit Kalmia's information? Would its failure stop sales or production? No Kalmia information: out of scope (the espresso machines). Owned, controlled or configured by Kalmia: in scope (NAS-01, the cafés, the web shop, Kalmia's cloud accounts). Not controlled but able to stop sales: dependency, recorded but not assessed (the payment processor, the providers' data centres). Anything else: confirm with the owner (staff phones used for e-mail).
  • Status: labs are graded one by one; the assembled report and optional presentation (November 26) are formative (feedback, no mark), not summative (certifies learning, counts toward the grade).
  • Rule of this course (Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice v2.0 (🔗 https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlcheck), section 7.3): study threat information; never interact with live malicious infrastructure or its operators.
Lab What it produces What it needs first
Lab 1 Asset inventory and infrastructure map The scope statement
Lab 2 Threat catalogue The asset list of Lab 1
Lab 3 Risk register and prioritization The threats of Lab 2
Lab 4 Risk treatment and prevention plan The register of Lab 3

🧭 At Kalmia: Nadia Roy never asked for a "risk analysis". She asked: "What could stop us from selling coffee next week, and what would it cost us?" Your first job is to turn that into a one-page scope that everyone signs before work starts, with Nadia Roy as risk owner and Karim Haddad, Sophie Tremblay, Lucas Martin and the MSP (managed service provider) as stakeholders.

⚠️ Exam trap: "Hosted elsewhere" does not mean "out of scope". The web shop sits on a rented server, but Kalmia administers it, so it belongs in Lab 1. Out of scope is kept for items with no Kalmia information at all.

📌 Remember: Four labs, one company, one report, and the scope decides what goes into Lab 1.

The big idea. "Our risk is hackers", "that old server is a threat": in an analysis, loose talk like this leads to wrong decisions, because each of the six words names something measured and treated differently. The definitions follow the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/glossarycheck), NIST SP (Special Publication) 800-30 (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/30/r1/finalcheck) and the ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27000 vocabulary (🔗 https://www.iso.orgcheck).

What you must know

  • Asset: anything of value that needs protection: information and whatever stores, processes or carries it. Primary assets (business processes, information) matter for their own sake; supporting assets (hardware, software, networks, people, sites) are what they rely on. Each has an asset owner (accountable, not necessarily the user), a location and a value.
  • Threat: a potential cause of an unwanted event that can harm an asset. The threat source is who or what, adversarial (criminal group, dishonest employee) or not (error, equipment failure, power outage, flood); the threat event is what happens (phishing e-mail, encryption, mistaken deletion). Threats exist even when you have no weakness for them to use; you control your exposure, rarely the source.
  • Vulnerability: a technical, procedural, human or physical weakness in an asset, a procedure or a control that a threat can exploit. A predisposing condition eases exploitation without being a defect itself, like a flat network. To exploit is to use a vulnerability to cause harm; the code doing it is also an exploit.
  • Risk: the possibility that a threat exploits a vulnerability and harms an asset, measured by likelihood (how probable the harmful event is) and impact: score = likelihood (1–5) × impact (1–5), from 1 to 25. Remove the asset, the threat or the vulnerability and the risk falls. Inherent risk is counted before controls; residual risk is what remains after them.
  • Impact: the size of the harm if the event happens, in business terms: operations, money, legal duties (a declaration to the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec) (🔗 https://www.cai.gouv.qc.ca/englishcheck), PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) (🔗 https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/check) for cards), reputation, health and safety. "High" alone is useless; days, dollars and obligations are not. Impact and likelihood are independent.
  • Control: a measure that lowers likelihood, impact or both. By nature: administrative (policies, procedures, training), technical (MFA (multi-factor authentication), encryption, backups, logging), physical (locks, badges, cameras). By function: preventive (stops the event), detective (reveals it), corrective (limits the damage, restores); Topic 6 adds deterrent, compensating and directive. Record existing controls before rating.
  • Risk statement: one sentence linking vulnerability, threat, asset and impact, the unit of every register; no product names, no solutions.
Because [vulnerability], [threat source] could [threat event] [asset],
which would [impact in business terms].
Term Kalmia example
Primary / supporting asset Loyalty list of 18,500 members, 60 roast profiles / NAS-01
Threat source / threat event A ransomware group / a phishing e-mail, then encryption
Vulnerability One NAS-01 administrator password shared by four people, no MFA
Impact About three days without wholesale preparation (about $28,500 of sales)
Risk R1: likelihood 4 × impact 4 = 16
Control MFA (preventive), refund-report review (detective), offline backup (corrective)

🧭 At Kalmia: NAS-01's existing control is a nightly backup to a USB (Universal Serial Bus) disk permanently plugged into it. It is a real corrective control, and ransomware would encrypt it along with the data. A control can exist and still fail you: record it, then judge it.

⚠️ Exam trap: A sentence that holds only one of the six words is not a risk. "We have no MFA" is a vulnerability; "a ransomware group" is a threat source. A risk needs a threat, a vulnerability, an asset and an impact in the same sentence.

📌 Remember: Threat = who or what could harm you; vulnerability = your own weakness; risk = likelihood × impact when they meet on an asset.

The big idea. "Impact" always means impact on one or more of three properties of information, the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad (some authors write AIC (availability, integrity, confidentiality) to avoid confusion with a certain American agency). ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27000 (🔗 https://www.iso.orgcheck) defines information security as preserving them, and EZ02 asks you to evaluate the effects on each. Name the property from what happened to the information, never from the kind of attack.

What you must know

  • Confidentiality: information is disclosed only to authorized persons, processes or devices; violated by unauthorized disclosure. Controls: least privilege (only the access the job needs), MFA (multi-factor authentication), encryption (TLS (Transport Layer Security) on the web), offboarding on the last day.
  • Québec: a confidentiality incident (unauthorized access to, use or disclosure of personal information, its loss, or any other breach of its protection) goes into a register under the private-sector law modernized by Law 25 (🔗 https://www.legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca/en/document/cs/p-39.1check); with a risk of serious injury, the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec) (🔗 https://www.cai.gouv.qc.ca/englishcheck) and the persons concerned are notified.
  • Integrity: accurate, complete, changed only by authorized means, including authenticity (it comes from its claimed source) and non-repudiation (the author cannot credibly deny the action); violated by unauthorized modification or destruction, malicious or accidental. Controls: second-person approval, hashing, digital signatures, logs, version history, backups.
  • Availability: timely, reliable access for authorized users when they need it; violated by disruption (outage, destruction, denial of service). Controls: tested offline backups, redundancy, patching, a UPS (uninterruptible power supply), the BCP (Business Continuity Plan) and DRP (Disaster Recovery Plan) of Topic 6. The RTO (recovery time objective) is how fast a system must be back; the RPO (recovery point objective) is how much recent data may be lost.
  • Rating: three questions per asset (disclosed? altered? unavailable?), each rated on the FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 199 (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/199/finalcheck) scale: Low = limited adverse effect, Moderate = serious, High = severe or catastrophic. The high-water mark makes the category the highest of the three, never an average.
  • Trade-offs: MFA on every login protects confidentiality but slows access. The asset owner decides which property matters most; the analyst records it.
Kalmia asset Confidentiality Integrity Availability Category
Loyalty member list (18,500 people) High Moderate Low High
Roast profiles (60 recipes) Moderate High Moderate High
Web shop and checkout page Moderate High High High
POS (point of sale) service, 9 terminals Moderate Moderate High High
Digital menu boards Low Moderate Low Moderate
Guest Wi-Fi Low Low Low Low

🧭 At Kalmia: INC-02 (June 9): a look-alike e-mail got the importer's bank details changed in Sage 50, and an $18,400 payment was stopped only by Karim Haddad's call-back. Integrity, High. INC-03 (August 22): the cloud POS service refused cards in all three cafés from 08:05 to 10:20, about $1,000 lost. Availability, Moderate. INC-04 (September 18, found October 2): a former shift supervisor exported the 18,500 member records. Confidentiality, High, and a confidentiality incident that Nadia Roy must record and assess; the analyst names the obligation, she decides.

⚠️ Exam trap: The fake "new banking details" e-mail smells like phishing, so students write "confidentiality". Ask what happened to the information: supplier data was changed without authorization. That is integrity; the $18,400 is the impact, not the property.

📌 Remember: Disclosed means confidentiality, altered means integrity, unusable means availability; the category is the highest of the three.

The big idea. A risk analysis is a repeatable procedure that identifies, estimates and evaluates risks: two analysts with the same facts should land close together. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-30 Rev. 1 (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/30/r1/finalcheck) runs a risk assessment in four phases: prepare, conduct, communicate, maintain. ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27005:2022 (🔗 https://www.iso.org/standard/80585.htmlcheck) runs risk management as context, identification, analysis, evaluation and treatment, with communication and monitoring throughout. The course merges them into ten steps.

What you must know

  • Prepare and identify. (1) Context: purpose (the owner's question), scope, assumptions, risk criteria (scales, matrix, thresholds, fixed before any rating) and the risk owner, who has the authority to accept or treat a risk (Class 1). (2) Assets, with owner, location, value and CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) rating (Lab 1). (3) Threats, adversarial or not, from public sources such as the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/encheck), CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) and MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) (Lab 2). (4) Vulnerabilities and existing controls (Topic 4).
  • Analyze. (5) Likelihood: the source's capability and intent, exposure, incident history, existing controls. (6) Impact: the CIA ratings and the business consequences. (7) Score = likelihood × impact, then read the level.
  • Evaluate, treat, communicate. (8) Risk evaluation: compare with the criteria and rank the risk register (statement, likelihood, impact, score, level, owner, treatment); ties go to the higher impact (Lab 3). (9) Treat: reduce (controls), transfer (insurance, contract), avoid (stop the activity) or accept (keep it knowingly); the risk owner accepts the residual risk in writing (Lab 4). (10) Report in business language and review at every change, at least once a year.
  • Kalmia's criteria were sized for about $6.8 million of revenue and approved by Nadia Roy before the analysis.
  • Only fourteen scores exist: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 16, 20, 25. Hence no band for 17 to 19.
  • Ordinal labels: 16 is worse than 8, but not twice the money. Money values need the quantitative ALE (annualized loss expectancy) = SLE (single loss expectancy) × ARO (annualized rate of occurrence), in Topic 5; ours is semi-quantitative.
Rating Likelihood: the event is expected… Impact: the consequence would be…
1 Rare: not in the next three years Negligible: under $1,000; no customer notices
2 Unlikely: once in two to three years Minor: $1,000 to $10,000; one site disrupted for less than four hours
3 Possible: about once a year Moderate: $10,000 to $50,000; operations disrupted up to one day; a few customers affected
4 Likely: several times a year Major: $50,000 to $250,000; several days of disruption; a declaration to the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec) (🔗 https://www.cai.gouv.qc.ca/englishcheck)
5 Almost certain: monthly or more, or already happening Severe: over $250,000; widespread exposure of personal information; survival of the business at stake
Score Level Kalmia's rule
1–4 Low Accept and monitor; review once a year
5–9 Medium Treat within the quarter, or accept with a written justification by the risk owner
10–16 High Treatment plan within 30 days; reported to the President
20–25 Critical Immediate action within 7 days; the President decides personally 
R1  4 x 4 = 16  High    Ransomware encrypts NAS-01 and its backup
R2  3 x 5 = 15  High    Skimming script on the web shop checkout
R4  3 x 4 = 12  High    Former employee exports the loyalty list
R3  4 x 3 = 12  High    Fake bank-details e-mail diverts a payment
R5  2 x 4 = 8   Medium  ROAST-PC compromised, production stops
R6  3 x 2 = 6   Medium  Cloud POS outage in a weekend rush
R7  2 x 1 = 2   Low     Guest Wi-Fi abused for illegal downloads

🧭 At Kalmia: R1 is the worked example. Likelihood 4: weekly phishing, a shared administrator password, no MFA (multi-factor authentication). Impact 4: about three days without wholesale preparation (about $28,500), recovery costs, HR (human resources) files possibly exposed. The score, 16, is High: a plan within 30 days. MFA, individual administrator accounts, a monthly-tested offline backup and endpoint protection bring the residual risk to about 2 × 2 = 4, Low, which Nadia Roy can accept.

⚠️ Exam trap: The tie-break applies only to equal scores. R2 has the highest impact (5), yet R1 ranks first because 16 beats 15; R4 passes R3 only because both score 12 and R4 has the higher impact (4 against 3). And multiply: 3 × 5 = 15, never 3 + 5 = 8.

📌 Remember: Criteria first, then score = likelihood × impact: Low 1–4, Medium 5–9, High 10–16, Critical 20–25.

The big idea. Two documents, two questions. ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27005 (🔗 https://www.iso.org/standard/80585.htmlcheck) answers "how do we run the risk management process?": the method. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 (🔗 https://www.nist.gov/cyberframeworkcheck) answers "which outcomes does our cybersecurity program achieve, and which should it achieve?": a map of outcomes and a shared language with management. NIST publishes mappings (informative references) between them. The labs follow the method; the project report uses the map.

What you must know

  • Framework versus standard: a framework is a published, structured set of outcomes, practices or steps that makes cybersecurity comparable; a standard is approved by consensus in a recognized body, either certifiable (ISO/IEC 27001 (🔗 https://www.iso.org/standard/27001check)) or guidance (27005). The CSF is voluntary guidance.
  • Publishers: NIST (🔗 https://www.nist.govcheck), a non-regulatory United States federal agency, publishes the CSF and the SP (Special Publication) 800 series. ISO (🔗 https://www.iso.orgcheck) and the IEC (🔗 https://iec.ch/homepagecheck) write the 27000 family in their joint committee JTC (Joint Technical Committee) 1/SC (Subcommittee) 27: 27000 vocabulary, 27001 ISMS (information security management system) requirements, 27002 controls, 27005 risk management.
  • CSF 2.0 (February 26, 2024): outcomes, not methods, for every size and sector. Six Functions: GOVERN (GV), IDENTIFY (ID), PROTECT (PR), DETECT (DE), RESPOND (RS), RECOVER (RC). GOVERN is new and sits in the centre because it informs the other five; all six run at the same time.
  • Core: 6 Functions, 22 Categories, 106 Subcategories. ID.AM (Asset Management) holds ID.AM-01 and ID.AM-02, the hardware and software inventories of Lab 1; ID.RA (Risk Assessment) holds ID.RA-04, the impacts and likelihoods of Lab 3; GV.RM (Risk Management Strategy) belongs to GOVERN.
  • Profiles and Tiers: the Current Profile (outcomes achieved now, and how well) against the Target Profile (outcomes chosen and prioritized); the gap becomes the action plan. Tiers describe the rigour of risk governance and management: 1 Partial, 2 Risk Informed, 3 Repeatable, 4 Adaptive.
  • ISO/IEC 27005:2022 (4th edition, October 2022): guidance for any organization, supporting an ISMS built on ISO/IEC 27001 and adapting ISO 31000 (🔗 https://www.iso.org/iso-31000-risk-management.htmlcheck).
  • Five activities: context establishment (scope, risk and acceptance criteria); risk identification, event-based (from risk sources and scenarios) or asset-based (from assets, threats, vulnerabilities); risk analysis (qualitative, semi-quantitative or quantitative); risk evaluation (compare, prioritize); risk treatment (controls checked against ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A, residual risk accepted by the risk owners). Communication and consultation, and monitoring and review, run throughout; the process is iterative. In ISO vocabulary, risk assessment = identification + analysis + evaluation.
Function Outcome (paraphrased) Kalmia example
GOVERN (GV) Strategy, expectations and policy are set and monitored Nadia Roy approves the risk criteria
IDENTIFY (ID) Current risks are understood The Lab 1 inventory, the Lab 3 register
PROTECT (PR) Safeguards manage the risks MFA (multi-factor authentication), patching, training
DETECT (DE) Possible attacks are found and analyzed Someone reads the POS (point of sale) refund report
RESPOND (RS) Action is taken on a detected incident A written procedure for a ransom note
RECOVER (RC) Affected operations are restored NAS-01 restored from a tested offline backup

🧭 At Kalmia: On a 0–4 scale made up for a first look (0 = nothing in place, 4 = measured and improved regularly), the interview gives GOVERN 1, IDENTIFY 1, PROTECT 2, DETECT 1, RESPOND 1, RECOVER 1. Nadia Roy's targets for the end of 2027: 3 everywhere, except DETECT at 2. The largest gaps (2 points) are GOVERN, IDENTIFY, RESPOND and RECOVER, the usual pattern when a small company buys security products first and organizes the work later, or never. On the ISO/IEC 27005 side, Labs 1 to 4 walk the process in order, from context to treatment.

⚠️ Exam trap: That 0–4 score is a course convention, not a CSF Tier. And the CSF is not certifiable; ISO/IEC 27001 is.

📌 Remember: ISO/IEC 27005 is how you run the process; CSF 2.0 is which outcomes you reach, with GOVERN in the centre.

The big idea. Kalmia's facts should come to you as easily as your own address. Torréfaction Kalmia inc. (Kalmia Coffee Roasters Inc.) is fictional, people, systems and incidents included. You meet it through an interview whose method lasts all term: ask, record, then verify.

What you must know

  • Business: founded in 2014; roastery and head office in Saint-Laurent (Montréal); cafés in Plateau-Mont-Royal, Old Montréal and Laval; 46 employees (8 roastery, 7 office, 31 cafés). About $6.8 million of revenue: cafés 40%, wholesale to some 140 restaurants and grocers 35%, web shop 25%, with a third of online revenue in November and December.
  • People: Nadia Roy, President and CEO (chief executive officer), risk owner and, as the highest authority, person in charge of personal information under Québec's private-sector law (🔗 https://www.legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca/en/document/cs/p-39.1check); Karim Haddad, operations (approves payments over $5,000); Sophie Tremblay, finance and HR (human resources); Lucas Martin, half-time IT (information technology) coordinator with no security training. Outside: an MSP (managed service provider), a web developer, a host, SaaS (software as a service) providers for the POS (point of sale), loyalty and payroll, and the payment processor, a dependency.
  • Systems: one flat roastery LAN (local area network), 192.168.10.0/24, where every device reaches every other, behind firewall FW-HQ; café routers with staff and guest Wi-Fi. 15 computers (two sales laptops and ROAST-PC on Windows 10), 9 POS tablets with 9 card readers, 7 cameras. Web shop: WordPress, WooCommerce, 23 plugins on a VPS (virtual private server).
  • Data: 18,500 loyalty members, about 2,300 online subscribers, employee files with SIN (Social Insurance Number) and bank details. No card numbers: the processor and the POS provider keep them. Key business information: 60 roast profiles, wholesale contracts, the daily order plan.
  • Priorities: never miss a wholesale delivery (availability); protect customers' information (confidentiality); a working web shop in November and December (availability, checkout integrity); the roast profiles as recipe book (confidentiality, integrity). Constraints: one part-time IT person, about $8,000 of budget, no holiday downtime, nothing that slows the café counter.
  • First interview: ten questions to Lucas Martin gave about 25 asset rows in six types and nine warning signs, possible risk factors to verify with evidence in Topic 4 before they enter the register. Lab 1 adds an Nmap (Network Mapper) (🔗 https://nmap.org/check) scan of the lab replica.
  • End of support: the date after which a vendor stops free security updates (Windows 10: October 14, 2025). Case rule: never search for, contact or test a real company with a similar name, and scan only the lab replica.

🧭 At Kalmia: The starter list numbers equipment and services A-01 to A-24 and information D-01 to D-07, each with an owner and a location. A-08, NAS-01, belongs to Lucas Martin while its data belongs to Sophie Tremblay and Karim Haddad; D-04, the roast profiles, belongs to Karim Haddad and lives on ROAST-PC and NAS-01. The starter network sketch shows the four sites, the Internet and the cloud services, warning signs outlined.

⚠️ Exam trap: "No card numbers stored" does not mean "no card risk": the checkout page can still be tampered with, which is why R2 exists. And a warning sign is not a vulnerability until Topic 4 confirms it.

📌 Remember: 46 people, 4 sites, $6.8 million, 18,500 members, 60 roast profiles, nine warning signs, one risk owner: Nadia Roy.

Class 2 asked what Kalmia owns, who can administer each piece, and which pieces matter most. On Monday, expect register rows, licence counts, labels, tiers and scanner output to interpret. Study the four lessons as one workflow: the exam and Lab 1 treat them that way.

The big idea. Every risk needs an asset, so the analysis starts with what the organization owns. Count the computers, read the register, scan the network: three different numbers, and the devices in the gaps are the ones nobody patches. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 (🔗 https://www.nist.gov/cyberframeworkcheck) opens its Identify Function with ID.AM-01 (hardware inventories), and the CIS (Center for Internet Security) Controls v8.1 (🔗 https://www.cisecurity.org/controls/v8-1check) put this inventory first, as Control 1.

What you must know

  • Hardware asset: any device, physical or virtual, that holds, handles or carries the organization's information, or that runs equipment the business relies on. CIS Safeguard 1.1 names four families (end-user devices, network devices, non-computing or IoT (Internet of Things) devices, servers) and includes virtual, remote and cloud devices, plus regularly connected devices the company does not own, such as an employee's phone on the staff Wi-Fi.
  • OT (operational technology): devices that control physical equipment, like ROAST-PC. A scan or a restart can stop production.
  • Six required fields (Safeguard 1.1): network address if static, hardware address, machine name, owner, department, approved to connect. Kalmia adds the asset tag (permanent, never reused), make, model, serial, custodian, OS (operating system) or firmware, life-cycle status and date last seen.
  • MAC (Media Access Control) address: 48 bits, the first 24 being the OUI (Organizationally Unique Identifier) that names the manufacturer in the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) registry (🔗 https://standards.ieee.org/products-programs/regauth/oui/check). It stays with the device, so it is the matching key; the IP (Internet Protocol) address may change with each DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) lease. Randomized phone addresses have no manufacturer prefix.
  • Four sources: records (what was bought), physical verification (switched-off devices, the backup disk), network records (DHCP log, firewall ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) table, switch MAC table; Safeguard 1.4 wants DHCP logs reviewed weekly) and discovery tools (active scanning 1.3, passive listening 1.5, agents and MDM (mobile device management)).
  • Reconciliation: comparing what is recorded with what was found, giving four states (table); Kalmia calls a device missing after 30 days unseen. Safeguard 1.2: every week, unauthorized devices are removed, denied remote connection or quarantined; legitimate ones are approved and registered.
  • Life cycle (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/using-information-technology-asset-management-itam-enhance-cyber-security-itsm10004check)): planning, procurement and acquisition, deployment (tag, owner and secure configuration first), operation and maintenance, retirement and disposal (storage sanitized per NIST SP (Special Publication) 800-88 Rev. 2 (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/88/r2/finalcheck), September 2025).
  • Permission: the right, granted to one identity, to do one particular thing to one particular resource: physical access, local administration, remote administration (web page, SSH (Secure Shell), remote desktop) or ordinary use.
  • Three rules: least privilege (only the rights needed, only as long as needed); accountability (each action traced to one person, impossible with a shared account); factory credentials changed before service. Mirai showed why in 2016, seizing hundreds of thousands of cameras and video recorders with about sixty factory logins over Telnet (alert TA16-288A (Mirai and other botnets), now on the site of CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2016/10/14/heightened-ddos-threat-posed-mirai-and-other-botnetscheck)). For each device, list its administrator accounts and the people who hold their passwords, note whether MFA (multi-factor authentication) is on, and record any outside company's access with its end date.
State Meaning Next action
Matched Recorded and seen recently Update "last seen"
Missing Recorded, not seen for more than 30 days Ask the owner: travelling, lost, stolen, broken?
Unknown (rogue) Seen, never recorded Find who connected it; approve and register, or remove, deny remote connection, quarantine
Not network-visible No network interface (a USB (Universal Serial Bus) disk) Check it physically
Level Kalmia's permission rules
HIGH Factory or empty password; administrator account shared by several people; outside company with no end date
MEDIUM Only an outside company can administer; daily account with administrator rights; personal account; contractor holding physical access
LOW Factory account name kept, password changed; standard login shared by a team

🧭 At Kalmia: Lucas Martin's register (25 head-office devices) against 60 days of FW-HQ sightings: 23 matched, 1 missing (SALES-LT2, unseen for 42 days), 1 not network-visible (BKP-USB-01), 4 unknown (a Raspberry Pi, a TP-Link extender, two phones). Of 21 permission findings, 7 were HIGH, including shared administrator accounts on NAS-01 and ROAST-PC, the roaster vendor's open-ended remote access and factory passwords on two cameras. The Raspberry Pi was the vendor's undeclared data logger, which still needs an owner, a formal approval and password rules like any other device.

⚠️ Exam trap: Missing and unknown are mirror images, and someone swaps them every term. Missing: recorded, but not seen for more than 30 days. Unknown: seen, but never recorded, and not automatically hostile.

📌 Remember: A device that is not in the register has no owner, no patch schedule and no protection.

The big idea. The hardware register proves that PC-FIN-01 exists, not what runs on it, and most attacks go through software. Hence ID.AM-02 (software, services and systems) in NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 (🔗 https://www.nist.gov/cyberframeworkcheck), and CIS (Center for Internet Security) Control 2 (🔗 https://www.cisecurity.org/controls/inventory-and-control-of-software-assetscheck): only authorized software installed and running. Log4Shell, CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) entry CVE-2021-44228, made the point in December 2021: the guidance of CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/news/apache-log4j-vulnerability-guidancecheck) began by finding which programs contained Log4j.

What you must know

  • Five kinds: operating systems and firmware, applications, extensions and plugins (23 on the web shop), cloud services or SaaS (software as a service) with accounts and contracts but nothing installed (loyalty, POS (point of sale), payroll; CSF ID.AM-04 (supplier services)), and components and scripts. An SBOM (software bill of materials) lists the components inside one product; CISA's SBOM page (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/topics/information-communications-technology-supply-chain-security/sbomcheck) gives its elements.
  • The record (Safeguard 2.1): title, publisher, install or first-use date, business purpose; where applicable, URL (Uniform Resource Locator, the address of a web page), app store, version, deployment mechanism, decommission date and licence count. Review it at least twice a year, and add computer, authorized and supported.
  • End of support: the publisher stops security updates. Safeguard 2.2 authorizes only supported software, unless a documented exception names the mitigating controls and the residual risk management accepts, with a monthly review.
  • Windows 10: Microsoft (🔗 https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/end-of-supportcheck) ended support on October 14, 2025. ESU (Extended Security Updates) (🔗 https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/whats-new/extended-security-updatescheck): up to three years, one at a time, version 22H2 only, USD (United States dollars) 61 per device in year one, doubling yearly. Kalmia bought none.
  • Licence: the Copyright Act (🔗 https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/C-42/section-2.htmlcheck) protects a program as a literary work, so you buy a licence, usually through an EULA (end-user licence agreement). Overuse is a legal and financial risk; cracked copies add malware and no updates, and the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice (🔗 https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlcheck), section 6.6, bans them in labs.
  • Compliance: use never exceeds purchase, counted with the right metric (table). Open source costs nothing but carries obligations, mostly on modification or redistribution: permissive licences (MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology), Apache-2.0) or copyleft ones (modified versions keep the same terms). SPDX (Software Package Data Exchange) (🔗 https://spdx.org/licenses/check) provides short identifiers.
  • Software permissions: administrator rights on daily accounts let anyone install anything, and installs in a user profile bypass IT (information technology). A LocalSystem service has full control of the computer: fine for an approved updater, a finding for unapproved software. Inventory the grants cloud apps receive when someone clicks "Accept", and reclaim named licences from former employees. Allowlisting (Safeguard 2.5) lets only approved software run: App Control for Business or AppLocker.
  • Collecting: three registry Uninstall keys (64-bit, 32-bit, current user) plus the OS (operating system) through CIM (Common Information Model). Never the WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) class Win32_Product, which checks and may repair every package. Linux: dpkg-query -W or rpm -qa; at scale, automated tools (Safeguard 2.4).
Licence metric What is counted At Kalmia
Per user Distinct people Microsoft 365 (12), Sage 50 (2), Acrobat Pro (2)
Per device Distinct computers RoastMaster Pro (1, ROAST-PC)
Concurrent Simultaneous users None
Subscription / perpetual Renewed, or bought once Microsoft 365 and Sage 50 are subscriptions
OEM (original equipment manufacturer) Tied to the computer it came with Windows on the Dell computers
Freeware Free; terms may limit use Chrome, Acrobat Reader
Open source Use, study, change, share under a published licence 7-Zip, Firefox

🧭 At Kalmia: Six lab computers, 28 items, a ten-product register. Three unauthorized products: RoastLink Remote 2.1.7 on ROAST-PC as a LocalSystem service, PDF (Portable Document Format) Super Converter 3.0.2 in Sophie Tremblay's profile with a LocalSystem updater, WinRAR 7.01 on two computers. Two unsupported computers, ROAST-PC and SALES-LT1, unpatched for 374 days on October 23, 2026. Acrobat Pro is over-deployed, 3 users for 2 licences. Microsoft 365's 5 of 12 is only a sample; the admin centre holds the real count.

⚠️ Exam trap: "It still boots" does not mean "it is supported": ROAST-PC starts every morning and has had no security update since October 14, 2025. Same family of mistake: counting a per-user licence in computers, or a per-device licence in people.

📌 Remember: For every program, ask: may we run it, is it still patched, and with whose rights does it run?

The big idea. An inventory lists what exists; priorities say what matters. With about forty assets, a half-time IT (information technology) coordinator and about $8,000 for security this year, Kalmia must choose. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 (🔗 https://www.nist.gov/cyberframeworkcheck) asks for it in ID.AM-05 (prioritization by classification, criticality, resources and mission impact), and ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27001:2022 (🔗 https://www.iso.org/standard/27001check) in Annex A controls 5.9 (inventory with owners), 5.12 (classification) and 5.13 (labelling).

What you must know

  • Classification: a sensitivity level set by the harm of disclosure or modification. The label names it and brings handling rules: who reads, where it is stored, how it is sent, how it is destroyed (table).
  • Rules: the label follows the information into every copy; a system takes the highest label it holds, so the web shop, with 2,300 subscribers' names and addresses, is Confidential. Minimums: SIN (Social Insurance Number), bank or health data mean Restricted; other personal information and trade secrets mean Confidential. Owners may go higher, never lower.
  • Québec's private-sector act (🔗 https://www.legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca/en/document/cs/P-39.1check): section 10 asks for measures reasonable for the sensitivity, purpose, quantity, distribution and medium of personal information; section 3.1 puts the highest authority (Nadia Roy) in charge of protecting it unless delegated in writing, title and contact published online. The CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec) (🔗 https://www.cai.gouv.qc.ca/check) oversees it.
  • Government of Canada (🔗 https://www.canada.ca/en/public-services-procurement/services/industrial-security/security-requirements-contracting/safeguarding-equipment-sites-assets-information/levels-security.htmlcheck): Protected A, B, C (injury, serious injury, extremely grave injury) and Confidential, Secret, Top Secret (national interest).
  • FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 199 (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/199/finalcheck): impact is low (limited adverse effect), moderate (serious) or high (severe or catastrophic) for each of C, I and A. The security category lists the three; the overall level is the highest, the high-water mark of FIPS 200 (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/200/finalcheck). NIST SP (Special Publication) 800-60 (🔗 https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-60v1r1.pdfcheck) maps information types to categories.
  • Owner and custodian: the owner, an accountable manager, decides the label, approves access and proposes risk treatment; the custodian handles permissions, backups and updates. Business roles own information, IT usually guards it, and the IT coordinator owns infrastructure devices. Nadia Roy, the risk owner, accepts residual risk.
  • RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed): R does the work, A answers for it (one person only), C is consulted, I is informed. For the HR (human resources) share of NAS-01: Sophie Tremblay is A for label and access, Lucas Martin A for permissions and backups, InfoNord R for backups, Nadia Roy A for the residual risk.
  • Criticality: dependence, measured by a BIA (business impact analysis). MTD (maximum tolerable downtime): the longest acceptable outage. RTO (recovery time objective): time to restore, never above the MTD. RPO (recovery point objective): maximum data loss in time, which sets backup frequency. Record the worst season: the web shop is Tier 2 in July, Tier 1 in November–December.
  • Two axes, one rule: label against tier gives four quadrants (protect confidentiality, keep running, protect and keep running, standard care). Nadia Roy's priority rule sorts by category, then tier, then label, then shortest MTD, and feeds Labs 3 and 4.
SC web shop = {(confidentiality, Moderate), (integrity, High), (availability, High)}
overall level = max(C, I, A) = High
Label Harm if disclosed Kalmia examples and handling
Public None Menu, product pages; free once approved
Internal Minor; staff only Procedures, daily order plan; staff accounts only
Confidential Significant Customer data, contracts, financial records, roast profiles; named groups, encrypted outside
Restricted Severe, legal, hard to repair Employees' SINs and bank details, administrator passwords; named people, MFA (multi-factor authentication), quarterly review
Tier MTD Kalmia examples
Tier 1 — critical 4 h or less POS (point of sale) service 2 h, daily order plan 4 h, web shop in November–December
Tier 2 — high Over 4 h, up to 24 h ROAST-PC 8 h, roast profiles 24 h
Tier 3 — medium Over 24 h, up to 72 h Financial records, employee files (next pay run)

🧭 At Kalmia: Nadia Roy's workshop raised five of ten labels (web shop, ROAST-PC, roast profiles, employee files, camera recordings), and eight assets reached High, so tier and label did the sorting: rank 1 is the web shop (Moderate, High, High; Tier 1), rank 10 the marketing photos. D-01, the loyalty records of 18,500 people, is rated C = High yet stays Confidential: the kind of data sets the label, the size of the possible damage sets the rating.

⚠️ Exam trap: The high-water mark takes the maximum, never the average. And keep the axes apart: a label answers "how bad if it leaks?", a tier answers "how long can we live without it?". The daily order plan is only Internal, yet Tier 1.

📌 Remember: Label for secrecy, tier for urgency, category for the worst of C, I and A, and one named owner for each asset.

The big idea. Tonight's lists become one workbook, and the network gets its say: the Lab 1 template holds one line per asset, and Nmap (Network Mapper) (🔗 https://nmap.org/check) shows which addresses answer, with which services. The legal rule comes first. Only the lab replica 192.168.10.0/24, only during the exercise, only with the signed authorization.

What you must know

  • Template: Read me, Hardware, Software, Licence check, Permissions, Classification, Scan, Scan log, Changes, Lists. Drop-downs keep one vocabulary, and tool columns stay apart from people columns: a scanner never knows the owner or the tier.
  • Nmap: free and open source, published in 1997 by Gordon Lyon, with Zenmap as a graphical front end and Ndiff to compare one scan with the next. An active scanner (it probes, then reads the answers) is what CIS (Center for Internet Security) Safeguard 1.3 (🔗 https://www.cisecurity.org/controls/inventory-and-control-of-enterprise-assetscheck) calls active discovery. It is also a dual-use tool.
  • The law: scanning without authorization may be an offence under section 342.1 of the Criminal Code (🔗 https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/c-46/section-342.1.htmlcheck). For the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice (🔗 https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlcheck), section 7.6, a scan is "an intrusive act, not an observation": logged, alarming, able to crash a fragile device. The Nmap Project's legal advice (🔗 https://nmap.org/book/legal-issues.htmlcheck): written permission, the tightest target; -sV can crash weak applications.
  • Annex D authorization: owner and authority, exact range, exclusions, permitted activities, dates, emergency contact. Tonight: 192.168.10.0/24 until November 5, 2026, minus .20 (ROAST-PC, discovery only, as the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/using-information-technology-asset-management-itam-enhance-cyber-security-itsm10004check) urges caution with operational technology) and .200 (the scanner). Never your home, workplace or college network, not even a ping sweep; results stay confidential (section 7.5).
  • Step 1, -sn: host discovery, no port scan. Default probes: ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) echo, TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) SYN (synchronize, the TCP flag that opens a connection) to 443, TCP ACK (acknowledgement, the TCP flag that confirms received data) to 80, ICMP timestamp. On local Ethernet, ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) replaces them and returns MAC (Media Access Control) addresses and manufacturers. -n skips DNS (Domain Name System), -oX writes XML (Extensible Markup Language). Without sudo: TCP connections on 80 and 443, and no MAC. CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) /24 = 256 addresses (.0 to .255); 25 answered.
  • Step 2: a port (0 to 65535, per TCP or UDP (User Datagram Protocol)) identifies one service. -sV finds service and version, -O guesses the OS (operating system) with an accuracy (administrator rights), --top-ports 100 replaces the default 1,000, -iL reads targets, --exclude removes forbidden ones, -T3 is the default timing. Know 22 SSH (Secure Shell), 23 Telnet, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), 139/445 SMB (Server Message Block), 443 HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure), 554 RTSP (Real Time Streaming Protocol), 631 IPP (Internet Printing Protocol), 9100 printing, 3389 RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol), and 5000 for NAS-01's web administration.
  • Step 3: XML is the format for programs (-oA writes all formats). The converter matches hosts by MAC as known, new or scanner; ROAST-PC is "discovery only"; silent recorded devices are listed, but not up is not missing.
  • Step 4 and limits: scan log (date, range, authorization), keep the XML, repeat (Safeguard 1.3: daily for Implementation Groups 2 and 3) and compare with Ndiff. A scan misses what is off, firewalled, out of range or in the cloud, and its OS guess is a probability: one source of four, never the inventory.
sudo nmap -sn -n -T3 -oX discovery.xml 192.168.10.0/24
sudo nmap -sV -O -T3 --top-ports 100 --exclude 192.168.10.20,192.168.10.200 -iL live.txt -oX services.xml
Port state Meaning
open A service accepts connections: attack surface
closed The host answered; nothing listens there
filtered Probes are dropped by a firewall; no verdict possible
unfiltered Reachable, open or closed unknown (ACK scan only)
open|filtered Cannot tell open from filtered (UDP, some scans)
closed|filtered Cannot tell closed from filtered (idle scan only)

🧭 At Kalmia: Friday, 19:05: discovery took under 3 seconds (25 hosts up), and service detection on 23 hosts took 97 seconds. Of 41 open ports, 17 were exposed services: Telnet on SW-HQ and two cameras, unencrypted administration pages, file sharing on two workstations, remote desktop on PC-IT-01. Add three new devices, six computers fully filtered, THERMO-HQ all closed, and three silent laptops that are away, not lost.

⚠️ Exam trap: Closed, filtered and not up are three different answers. Closed: the host replied, nothing listens. Filtered: a firewall swallowed the probe. Not up: nothing answered discovery. A computer with every port filtered is still up, since it answered ARP.

📌 Remember: No signed authorization, no packet; and a scan is one source of the inventory, never the inventory itself.

Class 3 closed Topic 2 with three questions no list can answer: what Kalmia cannot afford to lose and for how long, how its networks fit together, and who can reach which information. On the mid-term, expect to calculate recovery objectives, place items on the right network view and work out effective access from a few permission entries.

The big idea. Class 2 listed what Kalmia owns. Nadia Roy wants something else: what must keep working, and how long each activity can stop before the harm turns serious. No scanner answers that; the process owners do, through a BIA (business impact analysis), and their answers become a few numbers per process.

What you must know

  • Required by EZ02 (criterion 1.3); NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 (🔗 https://www.nist.gov/cyberframeworkcheck) in GV.OC-04 and GV.OC-05 (Govern function, Organizational Context category) and ID.AM-04 and ID.AM-07 (Identify function, Asset Management category: supplier services, data); CIS (Center for Internet Security) Safeguard 3.2 (🔗 https://cas.docs.cisecurity.org/en/latest/source/Controls3/check), a data inventory reviewed at least yearly.
  • A business process delivers a result to a customer or the company; it is critical when stopping it does serious harm. Critical data is information such a process needs to run, or whose leak or tampering would do serious harm; record its owner, label and location in its three states (at rest, in transit, in use). A critical service is any IT (information technology) or supplier service the process relies on, often off-site and invisible to scans: find it through interviews and contracts.
  • Three steps in NIST SP (Special Publication) 800-34 Rev. 1 (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/34/r1/upd1/finalcheck): determine the processes and their recovery criticality; identify the resource requirements; identify the recovery priorities. ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 22301 (🔗 https://www.iso.org/publication/PUB100442.htmlcheck) makes it a core continuity activity.
  • Kalmia's scale: financial, reputation, legal and operational impact, from 1 (negligible) to 5 (critical), rated at 1, 2, 4, 8, 24 and 72 hours and one week. The MTD (maximum tolerable downtime) is the shortest duration at which at least one category hits 3 (serious).
  • The numbers. MTD: the longest total outage the owner can accept (ISO 22301 calls it the MTPD (maximum tolerable period of disruption)). RTO (recovery time objective): the time allowed to bring back the systems and data. WRT (work recovery time): the time then needed to check data, key in paper transactions and restart. MTD = RTO + WRT, so the RTO is always shorter than the MTD. RPO (recovery point objective): the maximum age of the last good copy, a limit on data loss that is not part of the MTD. Tiers: MTD up to 4 h, Tier 1; up to 24 h, Tier 2; up to 72 h, Tier 3; longer, Tier 4.
  • Café sales (P-01): reputation reaches 3 at 2 hours, so MTD 2 h; managers need 0.5 h to re-enter paper sales, so RTO 1.5 h; RPO 1 h; Tier 1.
  • A recovery gap: a resource with no redundancy takes longer to restore than the RTO allows. A data gap: a resource is backed up less often than the RPO demands. Unknown supplier restore time: read the contract or ask. A SPOF (single point of failure) is a component with no alternative whose failure alone halts a process; a shared one halts several.
  • Backups must survive the incident: a copy left plugged into its system falls to the same ransomware. Record frequency, restore time, offline copy and tested restore (an untested time is an estimate). NIST IR (Interagency or Internal Report) 8286D (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/ir/8286/d/finalcheck) extends the BIA to confidentiality and integrity.
  • Rogers, July 8, 2022. During a planned upgrade, staff removed a routing filter from the distribution routers, and one router pushed more than 900,000 routes into core routers that normally receive about 10,000; the core routers stopped. Because wireless and wireline share one core network, mobile, Internet and home phone service failed for more than 12 million customers, 9-1-1 calls included, for about 26 hours (2024 independent report of the CRTC (Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission) (🔗 https://crtc.gc.ca/eng/publications/reports/xona2024.htmcheck)). Interac Debit and Interac e-Transfer went down across Canada; Interac (🔗 https://www.interac.ca/en/content/news/interac-statement-on-rogers-outage/check) wrote that its redundant networks should not have been so vulnerable to the Rogers maintenance, then added a secondary network carrier and a third link (June 2023).
Process (owner) MTD (h) WRT (h) RTO (h) RPO (h) Tier
P-01 Café sales, three cafés (Karim Haddad) 2 0.5 1.5 1 1
P-02 Web shop orders and subscriptions (Nadia Roy) 4 1 3 1 1
P-03 Wholesale order preparation and delivery (Karim Haddad) 4 1 3 4 1
P-04 Roasting production (Karim Haddad) 8 2 6 24 2
P-05 Supplier payments and accounting (Sophie Tremblay) 72 8 64 24 3
