P-07 Loyalty program (Nadia Roy) 168 4 164 24 4
P-08 Video surveillance of the premises (Karim Haddad) 168 2 166 24 4

🧭 At Kalmia: Lucas Martin found 8 recovery gaps (POS (point of sale) cloud service, 2.25 h against an RTO of 1.5 h; Internet lines, 24 h), 3 data gaps, 2 suppliers to ask, 2 backups that stay online (BKP-USB-01 never leaves NAS-01) and 9 single points of failure, 3 shared: NAS-01 (4 processes), the head office Internet line (3), the POS cloud service (2).

⚠️ Exam trap: The RTO is the MTD minus the WRT, never plus. And a recovery gap compares a restore time with the RTO, while a data gap compares a copy interval with the RPO.

📌 Remember: Owners give the ratings, the risk owner sets the threshold, the analyst applies both and shows the consequences.

The big idea. An inventory says what exists, not how devices connect or where information leaves the company. The physical view shows where things are and how they are cabled; the logical view shows how information moves, and every trust boundary crossing on it is a place to look for findings.

What you must know

  • Required by EZ02 (criterion 1.4); NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 (🔗 https://www.nist.gov/cyberframeworkcheck) in ID.AM-03 (Identify function, Asset Management category: network communication and data flows); CIS (Center for Internet Security) Safeguard 12.4 (🔗 https://cas.docs.cisecurity.org/en/latest/source/Controls12/check): diagrams reviewed yearly or after a significant change; 12.2: segmentation, least privilege, availability; 3.12: keep sensitive data off less sensitive assets.
  • Zone: devices with the same protection needs and rules. Trust boundary: the line between zones of different trust (Internet and internal network, office and roasting equipment, supplier and company). Every crossing must pass a control: firewall rule, authentication, encryption, approval with an end date. An uncontrolled crossing is a finding.
  • Segmentation divides a network into zones and controls the traffic between them; a flat network is one zone where every device reaches every other. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/top-10-security-actions-no-5-segment-and-separate-information-itsm10092check) asks for it in ITSM.10.092 (a publication of its management series): group systems by sensitivity and function, then control what passes between the groups.
  • Target, 2013. The U.S. Senate Committee on Commerce report of March 26, 2014 (🔗 https://www.commerce.senate.gov/services/files/24d3c229-4f2f-405d-b8db-a3a67f183883%5Ccheck) says attackers first stole the credentials of Fazio Mechanical Services, an HVAC (heating, ventilation and air conditioning) contractor, with malware-laden e-mails, used them on an external supplier portal not fully cut off from Target's network, then worked their way to the systems holding customer data. They took about 40 million payment card accounts and personal information on up to 70 million customers. The report's verdict: Target had failed to properly isolate its most sensitive network assets.
  • A trustworthy diagram: one diagram, one view; the inventory's hostnames and asset tags (a mismatch is a reconciliation error); a title block (title, site, version, date, author, data source, Confidential) and a legend; public IP (Internet Protocol) addresses from the RFC (Request for Comments, the numbered documents that define Internet standards) 5737 (🔗 https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc5737/check) blocks 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24 and 203.0.113.0/24; checked against the switch port list, DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) leases and a walk-through, then dated. Tool: diagrams.net (draw.io) (🔗 https://app.diagrams.net/check).
  • Map checks: FLAT-ZONE (OT (operational technology), cameras, IoT (Internet of Things) or personal devices beside workstations, servers or POS (point of sale)), DECISION-NEEDED and TRUST-BOUNDARY with no end date are HIGH; UNTAGGED, IP-OUTSIDE, STATIC-IN-DHCP, DUPLICATE-IP and UNKNOWN flows are MEDIUM; NO-LINK is LOW.
Aspect Physical view Logical view
Shows Rooms, racks and positions in rack units (U, 44.45 mm), cables with switch port and wall jack, Wi-Fi access points, provider entry point Subnets in CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) notation, routers and firewalls, zones, external services, flows with protocol, port, direction, purpose
OSI (Open Systems Interconnection, the seven-layer reference model of networking) layer Layer 1, physical Layer 3, network
Used to Find and isolate a device, plan repairs, check physical security See boundary crossings, unknown flows, missing zones

🧭 At Kalmia: In the head office server closet, rack R1 holds SW-HQ at U2, FW-HQ at U3 and NAS-01 on a shelf at U4 beside its backup disk; the provider's fibre terminal is on the wall. Jack D-12 serves ROAST-PC; D-20 to D-23 feed the four cameras by PoE (Power over Ethernet). All 28 head office devices share 192.168.10.0/24 (254 usable hosts) with no internal rule: FLAT-ZONE, HIGH. The Plateau café isolates its guest Wi-Fi (192.168.21.0/24) from staff (192.168.20.0/24), yet a camera and the menu screen still share the staff zone with the POS tablets.

⚠️ Exam trap: If you can touch it (jack, port, rack position, cable), it goes on the physical view; an address, zone, flow or rule goes on the logical one. A firewall appears on both.

📌 Remember: A network diagram is only as good as the date of its last verification.

The big idea. Class 2 recorded who administers each device. Now: who can read, modify or erase each body of information, and through which permission? The permissions map is a grid of identities (rows), resources (columns) and effective access (cells); compared with each job's needs, it exposes too much access, too little, and accounts that should be gone.

What you must know

  • Required by the course's first learning outcome (represent all information assets and their associated permissions) and NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 (🔗 https://www.nist.gov/cyberframeworkcheck) PR.AA-05 (Protect function, Identity Management, Authentication and Access Control category): permissions defined, managed, enforced and reviewed, with least privilege and separation of duties.
  • Accounts. An account represents an identity in one system: named (one person), shared (entrepot, roastery, admin) or service (scanner, used by PRN-HQ-1). A group receives a permission once for all its members.
  • ACL (access control list): the list on each folder. Each line is an ACE (access control entry): trustee (account or group), permission (Read, Modify, Full Control), allow or deny, explicit or inherited. Get-Acl and icacls read it; Get-SmbShareAccess reads the share's own permissions.
  • Effective access: pool every entry naming the account, any of its groups, or Everyone. Allows add up, an explicit Deny beats an Allow, and across the network Windows checks both the share and the NTFS (New Technology File System, the Windows file system) permissions: the stricter wins. Kalmia's export holds only Allows, so the highest level granted wins.
  • Need to know and least privilege. The role matrix, agreed with the data owners (Sophie Tremblay: Finance, HR (human resources), Scans; Karim Haddad: Production, Surveillance; Camille Bouchard: Marketing), sets each job's access per resource. Need to know grants access only when the job requires it; least privilege grants the lowest level that does the job. CIS (Center for Internet Security) Safeguard 3.3 (🔗 https://cas.docs.cisecurity.org/en/latest/source/Controls3/check) requires it, and section 20 of Québec's Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector (🔗 https://www.legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca/en/document/cs/P-39.1check) lets employees access personal information only when their duties need it.
  • RBAC (role-based access control) gives permissions to groups by role: a mover changes group, a review reads one line per role (CIS Safeguard 6.8, yearly). SoD (separation of duties) splits critical functions so nobody can commit a fraud alone and hide it (NIST glossary (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/separation_of_dutycheck)). In INC-02, an $18,400 transfer to a fraudulent account was stopped only because Karim Haddad phoned the importer.
  • JML (joiner, mover, leaver). CIS Safeguard 6.1 (🔗 https://cas.docs.cisecurity.org/en/latest/source/Controls6/check) grants access at hiring or role change; 6.2 disables accounts immediately upon termination; 5.1 validates the account inventory quarterly; 5.3 disables accounts after 45 days of inactivity. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/top-10-it-security-actions-no3-managing-controlling-administrative-privileges-itsm10094check) adds separate administrator accounts, reviewed regularly.
  • Access review: on a fixed schedule, each data owner keeps, reduces or removes every access on the map; the analyst prepares, the custodian (Lucas Martin) applies. Skip it and permissions pile up. INC-04 shows the cost of a missing leaver step: two months after leaving, a former shift supervisor exported 18,500 loyalty member records.
  • Desjardins. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (🔗 https://www.priv.gc.ca/en/opc-news/news-and-announcements/2020/nr-c_201214/check) announced on December 14, 2020 that a Desjardins employee had exfiltrated personal information on nearly 9.7 million Canadians, over at least 26 months. Its investigation findings (🔗 https://www.priv.gc.ca/en/opc-actions-and-decisions/investigations/investigations-into-businesses/2020/pipeda-2020-005/check) say the data had been copied out of data warehouses onto a shared drive that employees could open with no work need for it, and that access controls and data governance fell short.
Finding Meaning Kalmia example Level
EXCESS More than the role matrix allows office has inherited Modify on HR: 7 people can change employee files HIGH (Restricted share)
MISSING Less than the job needs Sales representatives cannot read Production LOW
ORPHAN Active after its owner left lfontaine, gone since August 29 HIGH
SHARED One account, several people admin: three employees and the InfoNord MSP (managed service provider) HIGH (administrator account; MEDIUM otherwise)
DIRECT-ACE Granted to a person, not a group olefebvre on Finance MEDIUM
NO-MFA Privileged or exposed account without MFA (multi-factor authentication) Web shop administrators nroy and egagnon HIGH (administrator roles; MEDIUM for ordinary users)
SOD (separation of duties) One person holds two duties to separate mgauthier changes supplier bank details and releases payments HIGH

🧭 At Kalmia: 14 accounts × 6 shares of NAS-01 = 84 cells and 20 findings, 10 HIGH. Three causes: groups that are too wide (office, Everyone), inheritance nobody checked, and no leaver step. Everyone has Modify on Scans, where PRN-HQ-1 drops every scan, HR forms included.

⚠️ Exam trap: "He is not in hr, so he has no access to HR" is wrong as soon as another of his groups has an entry there. Inherited entries count like explicit ones, and Modify plus Modify is still Modify.

📌 Remember: Grant by role, let the owner decide, let the custodian apply, review on a schedule.

The big idea. Lab 1, Part 1 of the Integrative Project, turns Classes 2 and 3 into one deliverable for Nadia Roy. Labs 2 to 4 sit on top of it, so a sloppy Lab 1 follows you all term.

What you must know

  • The folder Lab1_Lastname_Firstname, zipped: README.txt (your name, student number and date, the sources and tools you used, and the integrity statement "I used fictional lab data only"); workbook/ with six CSV (comma-separated values) exports in workbook/csv/; diagrams/ (both views as .drawio files, each exported as PDF (Portable Document Format) or PNG (Portable Network Graphics)); memo/ (one page for Nadia Roy: the five findings she must hear first, in plain business terms, each with the decision you need from her).
  • Quality rules: one name per device everywhere; ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 8601 (🔗 https://www.iso.orgcheck) dates such as 2026-10-24; durations written as hours (an MTD (maximum tolerable downtime) of 4, never "half a day"); sources cited; fictional data only, never a real SIN (Social Insurance Number) or card number. Lab 1 is confidential (Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice v2.0 (🔗 https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlcheck), sections 7.5, 7.9 and 18).
  • The readiness check (lab1_check.sh, Bash) prints OK, TODO or BLOCKER per check: folder, README, exports and columns, owners, RTO (recovery time objective) shorter than the MTD, diagrams, asset tags, HIGH decisions, memo. A SIN-shaped (three groups of three digits) or card-shaped (four groups of four) number is a BLOCKER. Fix the blocker first, then content, then presentation. The checker confirms every required piece is present; it cannot judge your memo or your diagrams.
Part What it must contain
A. Folder and README Correct name; sources, tools, integrity statement
B. Workbook and exports Six CSV exports with the template's columns
C. Inventories Devices with owner, approval, reconciliation state; software with version, support status
D. Critical data and services Per process: owner, MTD, WRT (work recovery time), RTO shorter than the MTD, RPO (recovery point objective), tier; gaps, single points of failure
E. Infrastructure map Both views with title block, legend, Confidential label, inventory names, zones, trust boundaries, flows
F. Permissions map and access review Effective access per account and share; each finding with level, data owner, decision
G. Memo and privacy A one-page memo to Nadia Roy; no real personal data anywhere

🧭 At Kalmia: On the sample folder of Alex Sample, a fictional student, the checker found 19 OK, 7 TODO and 1 BLOCKER (a SIN-shaped number in access_review.csv). Content fixes came next: P-04 had an RTO of 8 h, equal to its MTD (correct value 8 − 2 = 6 h), and three HIGH findings had no decision.

⚠️ Exam trap: An RTO equal to the MTD is an error, not a tight plan: it leaves no time for work recovery. And deleting an untagged device from the diagram does not remove it from the network.

📌 Remember: The checker finds what is missing; only your judgment decides what is right.

The big idea. Topics 1 and 2 form one chain. Class 1 gave you the vocabulary and the method; Classes 2 and 3 applied its first step to Kalmia: know what you own, what you cannot lose, how it is connected and who can reach it.

What you must know

Part Review these
Topic 1 Asset, threat, vulnerability, risk, impact, control; the risk statement; the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad; the risk analysis steps; NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 (🔗 https://www.nist.gov/cyberframeworkcheck) Functions, Core, Profiles, Tiers; ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27005 (🔗 https://www.iso.org/standard/80585.htmlcheck); Kalmia's people, systems and incidents
Topic 2, Part 1 Hardware inventory fields of CIS (Center for Internet Security) Safeguard 1.1 (🔗 https://www.cisecurity.org/controls/v8-1check), sources, reconciliation states; software support and licences; labels, high-water mark, owner and custodian, tiers; Nmap (Network Mapper) (🔗 https://nmap.org/check) discovery, port states, legal frame
Topic 2, Part 2 BIA (business impact analysis), MTD (maximum tolerable downtime), RTO (recovery time objective), RPO (recovery point objective), gaps; physical and logical views, trust boundaries; permissions map, effective access, findings, access review; Lab 1

🧭 At Kalmia: Nadia Roy, Lucas Martin, NAS-01 and INC-02 follow you into every topic, the mid-term included.

⚠️ Exam trap: Owner and custodian are different roles: the owner decides, the custodian applies.

📌 Remember: You can only protect what you know you have.

Class 4 was the night you switched sides: after two classes spent listing what Kalmia owns, you started looking at it the way an attacker does. Who would harm the company, from outside or inside, with which methods, and what can a real ransomware attack on a Canadian manufacturer teach a 46-person roaster? On the mid-term you will name the actor, the method, the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) property and the evidence, and keep one formula straight: threat + vulnerability + asset = risk.

The big idea. A threat turns into a risk only at the point where it hits a weakness in something that matters to you, so every threat you list must point to a Kalmia asset and to evidence. Calling an attacker "a hacker" is like describing a suspect as "a person". You build a profile instead: four questions, three of them rated from 1 to 5, each rating tied to a fact. The twist of the lesson is that the scariest actor on paper is not the one most likely to reach Kalmia first.

What you must know

  • A threat, in the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) glossary (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/glossarycheck), is any circumstance or event that could harm operations, assets or people through unauthorized access, destruction, disclosure, modification of information or denial of service. The threat source is who or what causes it; a threat actor is a source acting on purpose.
  • NIST SP (Special Publication) 800-30 (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/30/r1/finalcheck) gives four families of sources: adversarial (intend harm), accidental (honest mistakes), structural (failing equipment, software or environmental controls) and environmental (fire, flood, power outage, an outside service failing). An external threat actor has no account, no badge, no contract: whatever it gets, it must take.
  • Four profiling questions. Motivation, from the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/encheck), is written in words: money, ideology, geopolitical advantage, satisfaction, discontent. Capability, intent and targeting come from Appendix D of NIST SP 800-30 and are rated 1–5 on the scale below, each with evidence.
  • Cybercriminals want money. The National Cyber Threat Assessment 2025-2026 (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/national-cyber-threat-assessment-2025-2026check) describes cybercrime-as-a-service: ransomware rented to affiliates (ransomware-as-a-service), initial access brokers selling break-ins, stolen passwords and phishing kits on sale. With every step bought ready-made, attacking a small roaster is cheap. The assessment ranks ransomware first among cybercrime threats to Canada's critical infrastructure, while fraud and scams are what Canadians run into most often. A BEC (business email compromise) fraud needs no malware at all.
  • Hacktivists serve a cause and want visibility: a DDoS (distributed denial of service), a defacement, a leak. They are generally less sophisticated than states or organized crime; the assessment calls them unpredictable and reports pro-Russia DDoS campaigns against federal and private-sector websites in Canada in 2023.
  • State-sponsored groups pursue geopolitical goals (money, for some states) with the highest capability and the patience for an APT (advanced persistent threat). China, Russia and Iran are the greatest strategic threats to Canada, China's program the most sophisticated and active; North Korea steals to fund its regime. They reach small firms through edge devices, including SOHO (small office / home office) routers used as relays, and through supply-chain compromise of an update, a cloud service or an IT (information technology) provider.
  • Opportunistic attackers, thrill-seekers and botnets included, choose nobody: automated scans hit whoever has a known weakness. Textbook case: the 2016 Mirai botnet of cameras and routers on default passwords, in CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) alert TA16-288A (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2016/10/14/heightened-ddos-threat-posed-mirai-and-other-botnetscheck).
  • Attribution is reported only as the official source states it (Legal Notice (🔗 https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlcheck), section 7.3).
Actor type Motivation Capability Targeting Wants at Kalmia
Cybercriminals Money Moderate to high Selective among exposed victims NAS-01 data, supplier payments, checkout page, loyalty records
Hacktivists Ideology, visibility Low to moderate A cause, or collateral Web shop in November–December; reputation
State-sponsored groups Geopolitical; money for some Very high Rarely Kalmia itself Café routers as relays; access through the MSP (managed service provider)
Opportunistic attackers Easy wins Low None: anyone exposed Factory-password cameras, old plugins, remote-access tool
Value Capability Intent Targeting
5 Very high Very sophisticated, resources for continuous attacks Undermine or destroy operations or assets Studies this organization in depth, persistently
4 High Sophisticated, significant resources Disrupt critical operations or seize valuable assets, stay hidden This organization or its key people specifically
3 Moderate Moderate skills and resources Obtain or alter specific information, some risk accepted Organizations of this type or sector
2 Low Limited skills, available tools Easy result, avoids effort and detection Broad selection from public information
1 Very low Very limited skills and resources Little or no interest here No specific selection

🧭 At Kalmia: Cybercriminals (TS-E1): capability 4, intent 5, targeting 4, exposure match 4 of 4, relevance high. Hacktivists (TS-E2): 2, 2, 2, moderate, because of the "direct-trade" claims. State-sponsored (TS-E3): 5, 1, 1, moderate, as the café SOHO routers and InfoNord's admin rights make Kalmia a possible relay, rarely the prize. Opportunistic (TS-E4): 2, 2, 1, yet high: two of seven cameras on factory passwords, four plugins six months out of date, a remote-access tool on ROAST-PC.

⚠️ Exam trap: Highest capability does not mean highest relevance; the opportunistic row outranks the state row. And relevance is only a course convention for choosing which rows to study first. Likelihood is rated in Topic 5, after Topic 4 shows the vulnerabilities.

📌 Remember: You cannot change an attacker's motivation, but you can shrink your exposure, the only thing an opportunistic attacker looks at.

The big idea. An outsider has to break in; an insider already has the keys. A malicious export and a legitimate one look identical in a log, and only the context gives them away. Most insider incidents involve no malice at all. You record facts about accounts and processes. Guilt is for an investigation, never for the analyst.

What you must know

  • An insider, for CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) in Defining Insider Threats (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/defining-insider-threatscheck), is anyone who has, or had, authorized access to or knowledge of the organization's resources. "Had" covers a leaver whose account still works; "knowledge" covers someone who knows how payments are approved. The insider threat is the potential to use that access or knowledge to cause harm, on purpose or by mistake.
  • CISA's types: unintentional (negligence, a rule known and ignored; accident, an honest mistake), intentional (the malicious insider), collusive (an insider working with an outsider) and third-party. The course keeps three families: malicious insiders, negligent users, third parties and suppliers.
  • Malicious insiders steal, defraud, sabotage or take revenge, often out of discontent according to the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/encheck). Judge the context: time, volume, person, need.
  • Negligent users cause harm and are the people outsiders manipulate, so INC-02 takes two rows: an external source (the fraudster) and an internal condition (a payment process one e-mail can change).
  • Third parties and suppliers receive access to do their work: an MSP (managed service provider), a vendor, a freelancer, a cloud service. Compromise them and you inherit that access. The Verizon 2025 DBIR (Data Breach Investigations Report) (🔗 https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/reports/2025-dbir-data-breach-investigations-report.pdfcheck) found third-party involvement in 30% of breaches, double the year before. The National Cyber Threat Assessment 2025-2026 (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/national-cyber-threat-assessment-2025-2026check) recalls October 2023, when ransomware at the IT (information technology) provider of five Southern Ontario hospitals forced them to shut internal systems down for a time. A supplier can also fail with no attacker (INC-03, structural or environmental in NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-30 (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/30/r1/finalcheck) terms) or have its name stolen (INC-02).
  • An indicator is an observable fact that may signal a threat: a leaver's account in use, an unusual bulk export, odd hours, a vendor session outside the window, one person creating bank details and paying. It guides; it proves nothing. Lab 2 records the indicator, asset, CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) property and source; Lab 4 proposes the control; nobody is accused (Legal Notice (🔗 https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlcheck), sections 7.5 and 18).
  • Separation of duties puts two people on the steps of a sensitive task. Offboarding removes accounts, access and equipment on the last day.
  • Under Québec's private-sector privacy act (🔗 https://www.legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca/en/document/cs/P-39.1check), as amended by Law 25, INC-04 is a confidentiality incident. It must be entered in the incident register, and when serious injury is a risk, the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec) (🔗 https://www.cai.gouv.qc.ca/check) and the affected people must be told.
Type (CISA) Intent Kalmia example First control (Lab 4 preview)
Malicious insider Deliberate INC-04 export; 9 refunds in 40 minutes under a shared PIN (personal identification number) Offboarding checklist; export alerts; individual PINs
Negligent user None: rule ignored Shared manager PIN in each café; NAS-01 admin password shared by four Named accounts; password manager
Accidental user None: honest mistake HR (human resources) form scanned into a share everyone can read Restricted share; scan to a personal folder
Collusive threat Deliberate, with an outsider None recorded Separation of duties; access reviews
Third party and supplier Varies RoastTech on ROAST-PC at 02:14, no ticket; plugin from a forum Session approval; end dates; MFA (multi-factor authentication)

🧭 At Kalmia: A supervisor left on July 15; her loyalty-platform admin account stayed active and, on September 18 at 21:47, exported all 18,500 member records (INC-04, found on October 2 after a customer complaint). We know whose account it was, not who typed the password. Lucas Martin's review of 13 accounts and 10 audit entries also found lfontaine signing in after leaving and one Sage 50 user, mgauthier, changing bank details and releasing $6,200 six minutes later. Offboarding, named accounts and MFA alone would have made eight of the thirteen accounts harmless.

⚠️ Exam trap: A former employee with a working account is an insider, not an external actor. And the shared manager PIN is not a threat: it is a weakness any insider can use, and it destroys accountability.

📌 Remember: Write findings as facts about accounts, logs and processes, never as verdicts about people.

The big idea. The first two lessons asked who; this one asks how. Keep three words apart: the threat actor (a person or group), the attack method (what it does: trick, guess, flood) and the tool (what it uses: malware, a phishing kit, a botnet). A method applied to an asset becomes a threat event in your catalogue, as in "ransomware encrypts NAS-01 after a phishing e-mail". Real attacks chain methods, which is good news: break one link and the chain often falls.

What you must know

  • Malware, per NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-83 (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/83/r1/finalcheck), is a program inserted without the owner's consent to compromise the confidentiality, integrity or availability of data or systems. Trojans pose as useful programs, viruses spread with infected files, worms spread over the network by themselves, spyware and keyloggers collect information and keystrokes, information stealers copy saved passwords and session cookies. Malware must be delivered (macro attachment, fake update, USB (Universal Serial Bus) stick, exposed service, tampered update), and delivery is the step you can block.
  • Ransomware encrypts or locks data and demands payment. With double extortion, data is copied out first and publication is threatened, so confidentiality falls along with availability. It takes hours or weeks: initial access → privilege escalation → discovery → reachable backups deleted → data copied → encryption, at night or on a weekend.
  • Social engineering manipulates a person; phishing does it by message: e-mail, smishing (text), vishing (voice), QR (Quick Response) codes, spear phishing aimed at one target. BEC (business email compromise) is simply spear phishing with a payment as its target. Phishing wants the victim to run malware, type a password on a fake page, or act directly (change bank details, read a PIN (personal identification number) aloud). Its levers are urgency, authority, fear or reward, and a familiar context; red flags include an almost-right domain, a different reply-to, a mismatched link, a macro attachment and a request to skip procedure.
  • A DoS (denial of service) makes a service unavailable; a DDoS (distributed denial of service) does it from many machines, usually a botnet, by exhausting bandwidth or sending costly requests such as checkout pages. Availability only: nothing stolen, nothing changed. Hacktivists favour it; criminals sell it and use it for extortion. INC-03 shows that an outage is not always an attack.
  • Credential theft obtains a password, PIN, session cookie or one-time code: password guessing (many passwords, one account), password spraying (one common password, many accounts), credential stuffing (leaked pairs replayed, because people reuse passwords), phishing pages, stealers. With a valid credential the attacker just signs in; advisory AA23-352A (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-352acheck) lists valid accounts among the Play group's usual ways in. MFA (multi-factor authentication) blocks most of this, so attackers try MFA fatigue (push bombing); number matching or phishing-resistant MFA defeats it.
  • The chain: phishing e-mail → fake Microsoft 365 page → mailbox and VPN (virtual private network) → tools installed → backups deleted, HR (human resources) files copied → ransomware on a Saturday night, maybe with a DDoS for pressure. MFA, an offline backup and one employee who reports the first e-mail each break several links.
  • MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) (🔗 https://attack.mitre.org/check) numbers each technique; Class 5 teaches it.
  • The Verizon 2025 DBIR (Data Breach Investigations Report) (🔗 https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/reports/2025-dbir-data-breach-investigations-report.pdfcheck) gives the six numbers below, plus a median ransom payment of $115,000.

Ransomware Availability (plus confidentiality) NAS-01 and its connected backup Tested offline backup; MFA; segmentation T1486

🧭 At Kalmia: Initial access could come through any Microsoft 365 account except the two MFA-protected admins, or through RoastLink; the flat network does the rest, and NAS-01's always-connected backup disk would be encrypted with the data. In the "Monday, 08:30" exercise, E3 (schedule text), E4 (fake InfoNord caller asking for the POS (point of sale) PIN) and E7 (Sophie approving the fifteenth push request) all end in credential theft.

⚠️ Exam trap: Phishing and credential theft are separate rows: obtaining a credential and using it are two events. And watch the mapping: ransomware with double extortion hits availability and confidentiality, a DDoS availability only.

📌 Remember: A stolen password turns a break-in into a log-in.

The big idea. A case study is worth something when the victim looks like you. Ganong Bros., Limited (🔗 https://www.ganong.com/check), founded in 1873 in St. Stephen, New Brunswick, calls itself Canada's original and longest-standing family-owned chocolate company. Like Kalmia it makes food, ships to retailers and lives on a short season. The method matters as much as the chocolate: public sources only, known facts apart from unknowns, attribution as reported, then a comparison with Kalmia's own documents.

What you must know

  • Sources: a first-hand account by the head of IT (information technology) in CSO Online, August 2025 (🔗 https://www.csoonline.com/article/4038381/caught-in-the-cyber-crosshairs-a-candy-manufacturers-2025-ransomware-ordeal.htmlcheck), plus local press reports of company statements. The attack fell between Valentine's Day and Easter production, one of at least 84 known incidents in food and agriculture in the first quarter of 2025.
  • Known: ransomware with double extortion, claimed by the Play group (reported as the sources state it, Legal Notice (🔗 https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlcheck), section 7.3). Unknown: the root cause, how they got in. Do not guess. Cite instead the group's usual methods from advisory AA23-352A (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-352acheck) by CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency), the FBI (Federal Bureau of Investigation) and Australia's ACSC (Australian Cyber Security Centre), updated June 4, 2025: about 900 victims as of May 2025; valid accounts, exposed RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) or VPN (virtual private network) services and known flaws in public-facing products; data stolen before encryption.
  • What saved Ganong: offline backups, in the head of IT's own words. Also isolation in the first hour, responders within hours, a clear ransom decision by the owners, controllers checked before restart. Adopted afterwards: ransomware scenarios, a backup way to communicate, leadership tabletop exercises, stricter vendor requirements, lessons shared with peers.
  • KNP Logistics, a 158-year-old English haulier with about 500 trucks, was hit in 2023. According to the BBC (British Broadcasting Corporation) report of July 21, 2025 (🔗 https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cx2gx28815wocheck), attackers guessed one employee's password, encrypted the data and locked the systems. The company said its IT met industry standards and that it was insured; the demand was estimated at up to £5 million, which it could not pay. No recovery, closure, about 700 jobs lost.
  • Key terms: offline backup (disconnected or immutable copy), isolation (disconnecting while keeping evidence), incident responders, tabletop exercise (managers rehearse decisions), OT (operational technology: Ganong's machinery controllers, Kalmia's ROAST-PC), attribution.
  • Segmentation: on Kalmia's flat network, a single infected PC (personal computer) can get to NAS-01, its backup disk, ROAST-PC and the cameras; rules between office and server or production segments stop that. Segmentation plus an offline backup separates recovery in days from closure.

One to two weeks after Extortion Play claims the attack on its leak site

March, then later Notify, learn Personal-information check; lessons adopted

🧭 At Kalmia: Seven missing, two partial, and Microsoft's Windows 10 end of support (🔗 https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/end-of-supportcheck) on October 14, 2025 left ROAST-PC without free security updates. At about $9,500 of wholesale sales per day, a one-week recovery puts about $47,500 at risk, three weeks of rebuilding about $142,500: discussion figures, not ratings. Kalmia today looks more like KNP than Ganong, a pointer for the labs rather than a conclusion.

⚠️ Exam trap: Do not mix the stories: the guessed password is KNP's, by the BBC's account. Ganong's entry point was never published, so any sentence naming one invents a root cause.

📌 Remember: Ganong restored and KNP closed; the difference was preparation, not the attacker.

Class 5 covered where the profession reads about threats each week, how to read those documents without being fooled, and how the reading becomes Kalmia's threat catalogue for Lab 2. Carry one fact into the mid-term: severity describes the flaw, relevance describes your organization, evidence links them, and every catalogue row needs all three.

One detail before you start: the asset identifiers in this chapter (A-01, A-02, and so on) follow the Class 5 hand-out, which numbers Kalmia's assets differently from the Class 1 starter list. NAS-01, for example, is A-03 here and A-08 in Chapter 1. Always quote the identifier of the inventory you are working from.

The big idea. A public information source is anything an organization can read freely, with no contract and no confidentiality agreement: alerts, vendor bulletins, vulnerability databases, newsletters, annual reports. Competency EZ02 (criterion 2.3) asks you to analyze them methodically, and the Verizon 2026 DBIR (Data Breach Investigations Report) (🔗 https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/reports/dbir/check) shows why. For the first time in nineteen editions, exploiting a software vulnerability was the most frequent way in (31 % of breaches); ransomware appeared in 48 % of breaches, and a third party in 48 %. Exploited flaws are announced within days: whoever reads first acts first.

What you must know

  • Primary vs secondary. The vendor or agency that observed a fact is primary; a newsletter or news article that reports it is secondary. Only the vendor can say which versions are vulnerable and which release cures them.
  • Four words, four meanings at the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/encheck). An alert (AL26-nnn) flags an active threat or a critical vulnerability with detection and mitigation advice, and is updated (AL26-026 (🔗 https://cyber.gc.ca/en/alerts-advisories/al26-026-critical-vulnerabilities-impacting-php-cve-2026-109618-cve-2026-109619check) reached Update 2 within a week). An advisory (AV26-nnn, several a day) reports that a vendor has shipped a security update and lists the affected and fixed versions. A security bulletin is the vendor's own notice. These three are primary; a newsletter is a secondary digest.
  • IOC (indicator of compromise): an artefact you can search for in logs (address, domain, file hash). TTP (tactics, techniques and procedures): the behaviour behind it. Indicators change daily, behaviours slowly.
  • Source register: one row per source with publisher, address, type, cadence, delivery channel (e-mail, feed, web page) and asset types covered. Eight to twelve sources suffice for Kalmia's 46 people.
  • Weekly watch routine, twenty minutes a day and one hour on Friday: collect from the register; filter against the Lab 1 inventory (product and version) or a Class 4 exposure fact; record each kept item on the watch list (date, source, item, asset, severity as published, action, owner, deadline); decide.
  • Decisions: act now (critical or exploited flaw on an exposed asset, or an active campaign), add to the threat catalogue, or watch (a supplier's product, an announced release, an informational notice). Items that match nothing are discarded with one line (title, reason, rating), so nobody re-reads them.
  • Course rule: read, never interact. Opening an address from an alert or downloading a sample is prohibited (Legal Notice (🔗 https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlcheck), section 7.3).
Family Examples used in the course · status
National authorities Cyber Centre; CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/check) and its KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) catalogue (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalogcheck); partner agencies · primary
Software and hardware vendors Microsoft Security Update Guide (🔗 https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guidecheck), monthly on the second Tuesday; WordPress security releases (🔗 https://wordpress.org/news/category/security/check); PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) advisories; Kalmia's device vendors · primary
Vulnerability and technique databases CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) (🔗 https://www.cve.org/check), NVD (National Vulnerability Database) (🔗 https://nvd.nist.gov/check), EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) (🔗 https://www.first.org/epss/check), KEV, MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) (🔗 https://attack.mitre.org/check) · primary records, derived scores
Response teams and sharing centres MS-ISAC (Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center) advisories (🔗 https://www.cisecurity.org/advisorycheck); FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams) (🔗 https://www.first.org/cvss/check) standards · primary or relayed
Newsletters and digests SANS (SysAdmin, Audit, Network and Security Institute) NewsBites (🔗 https://www.sans.org/newsletters/newsbites/check), agency e-mail subscriptions · secondary
Research and industry reports Verizon DBIR; Mandiant M-Trends 2026 (🔗 https://cloud.google.com/security/resources/m-trendscheck); ENISA (European Union Agency for Cybersecurity) Threat Landscape (🔗 https://www.enisa.europa.eu/topics/cyber-threats/threat-landscapecheck) · secondary, feeds likelihood in Lab 3

🧭 At Kalmia: Lucas Martin used to forward every bulletin to Nadia Roy, who read none of them. In the week of November 2, 2026, eight items became eight decisions: four act now + catalogue (AL26-026; AL26-027 (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/alerts-advisoriescheck) on the Brotli library; AL26-028 (🔗 https://cyber.gc.ca/en/alerts-advisories/al26-028-ongoing-help-desk-voice-phishing-campaign-targeting-canadian-organizationscheck) on help-desk vishing; the Wordfence (🔗 https://www.wordfence.com/threat-intel/check) UpdraftPlus advisory, if installed), three watch (AL26-025 (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/alerts-advisoriescheck) on a supplier's remote-support tool, Microsoft's November 10 release, a POS (point of sale) maintenance notice) and one discard (an unsourced "all WooCommerce stores hacked" post).

⚠️ Exam trap: "Critical" in a title keeps nothing; a match with the inventory does. A Critical flaw in software Kalmia does not run is discarded in one line.

📌 Remember: The inventory is the filter; the vendor is the authority on versions.

The big idea. The industry shares two identifier systems: a CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) (🔗 https://www.cve.org/check) number names one vulnerability, an identifier in MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) (🔗 https://attack.mitre.org/check) names one attacker behaviour, and three scores say how urgent a vulnerability is. A CVE names a weakness, not a threat; the catalogue only borrows it as evidence.

What you must know

  • Identifier: CVE-YYYY-NNNNN, the year the identifier was reserved, then four or more digits. It never changes; the rest of the record can.
  • Publishers. The CVE Program (🔗 https://www.cve.org/check), since 1999, run by MITRE and sponsored by CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/check), finds no flaws itself. Records are written by CNAs (CVE Numbering Authorities), 502 on March 31, 2026, such as the PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) project and Wordfence (🔗 https://www.wordfence.com/threat-intel/check). With 48,185 records in 2025, nobody reads them all.
  • Record anatomy: metadata (identifier, CNA, state Reserved, Published or Rejected, dates); the CNA container (affected and fixed versions, CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration), CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) (🔗 https://www.first.org/cvss/check), references); an optional ADP (Authorized Data Publisher) container from CISA (a decision-tree rating and the KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalogcheck) date). CVE-2026-109618 (🔗 https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-109618check), condensed:
CVE-2026-109618   State: Published   CNA: php   Published 2026-10-21, updated 2026-11-05
Affected   PHP 8.2 to 8.5; fixed in 8.2.35 / 8.3.36 / 8.4.27 / 8.5.12
Problem    CWE-416 Use after free
Metrics    CVSS v4.0 base score 9.2 (Critical)
Refs       vendor advisory, KEV catalogue (added 2026-10-26)
  • NVD (National Vulnerability Database) (🔗 https://nvd.nist.gov/check), run by NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) (🔗 https://www.nist.govcheck), republishes every record. Since April 15, 2026 it enriches by risk (KEV entries and critical software first, the rest Not Scheduled), so the CNA's score is often the only one.
  • CVSS bands: None 0.0, Low 0.1–3.9, Medium 4.0–6.9, High 7.0–8.9, Critical 9.0–10.0, computed from a vector string; v4.0 is current, v3.1 still common. CVSS and EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) (🔗 https://www.first.org/epss/check) belong to FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams) (🔗 https://www.first.org/cvss/check), the KEV catalogue to CISA.
  • BOD (Binding Operational Directive) 26-04 (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directivescheck), June 10, 2026, replaced BOD 22-01 (which created the KEV in November 2021) with four questions (publicly exposed? in the KEV? automatable? full control?) and five tiers. Course reading: KEV + full control, or exposed + automatable + full control → 3 days, with a compromise check when in the KEV; any other KEV combination, or exposed with automatable exploitation or full control → 14 days; any other "yes" → 60 days; no "yes" → next scheduled upgrade.
  • ATT&CK is a free knowledge base of observed attacker behaviour, maintained by MITRE in three matrices and updated twice a year. v20 (October 13, 2026): Enterprise has 15 tactics, 227 techniques, 479 sub-techniques and 178 groups.
  • Levels: a tactic is the why (Initial Access, TA0001); a technique is the how (Phishing, T1566); a sub-technique is a more specific how (Spearphishing Voice, T1566.004); a procedure is what a named group actually did. Prefixes: TA tactic, T technique, G group (G0046 FIN7), S software (S0154 Cobalt Strike), C campaign, M mitigation (M1032 Multi-factor Authentication).
  • Tactics in matrix order: Reconnaissance (TA0043), Resource Development (TA0042), Initial Access (TA0001), Execution (TA0002), Persistence (TA0003), Privilege Escalation (TA0004), Stealth (TA0005), Defense Impairment (TA0112), Credential Access (TA0006), Discovery (TA0007), Lateral Movement (TA0008), Collection (TA0009), Command and Control (TA0011), Exfiltration (TA0010), Impact (TA0040). Stealth and Defense Impairment replaced Defense Evasion in v20.
  • Both identifiers in a row make it verifiable: the CVE leads to the fixed version, the technique to mitigations (Lab 4) and known groups. The ATT&CK Navigator (🔗 https://mitre-attack.github.io/attack-navigator/check) maps them for Lab 2.
Score Owner Question it answers Scale Use in Lab 3
CVSS v4.0 / v3.1 FIRST, published by the CNA How severe is the flaw? 0.0–10.0, five bands Impact
EPSS FIRST How likely is exploitation in the next 30 days? Daily probability 0–1, plus percentile Likelihood
KEV CISA Is it exploited in the wild now? Listed or not; about 1,700 entries in 2026 Likelihood (strongest evidence)

🧭 At Kalmia: Five CVE records, five decisions, none made by the score alone. CVE-2026-109618 (PHP, 9.2, KEV) on the exposed web shop A-16: 3 days, host asked today. CVE-2026-10795 (UpdraftPlus, 8.1, no KEV): 3 days once installation is confirmed. CVE-2026-56155 (AD FS (Active Directory Federation Services), 7.8, KEV): no match, discarded. Kalmia's facts map too: INC-02 → T1657 Financial Theft, INC-04 → T1078 Valid Accounts, INC-05 → T1566.002 Spearphishing Link, RoastLink → T1133 External Remote Services, the always-connected backup → T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact.

⚠️ Exam trap: A KEV entry proves exploitation somewhere, not on your network. And TA0001 (a tactic, the why) is not T1566 (a technique, the how).

📌 Remember: CVSS is severity, EPSS is probability, KEV is evidence; only the inventory says relevance.

The big idea. A threat report is any document describing a threat, a vulnerability, a campaign or an incident. Read without a method, it yields conclusions nobody can explain. The method asks seven questions in a fixed order and writes the answers down for others to check, the discipline NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-150 (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/150/finalcheck) expects: know the source, judge its quality, decide its use.

What you must know

  • Structure (first table): questions 1 to 3 concern the document, 4 and 5 the organization, 6 and 7 the decision. No date or no identifiable publisher fails question 1 and earns F6.
  • Observed vs assessed (question 3): a released patch, seen exploitation, identified infrastructure are observations; "probably responsible" and "likely to follow" are assessments.
  • Estimative language of the Cyber Centre (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/encheck): almost no chance 1–9 %, very unlikely 10–24 %, unlikely 25–39 %, roughly even chance 40–59 %, likely 60–74 %, very likely 75–89 %, almost certainly 90–99 %, never 100 %. Confidence (low, moderate, high) grades the sources and reasoning, not the probability (ODNI (Office of the Director of National Intelligence) Intelligence Community Directive 203 (🔗 https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD%20203%20Analytic%20Standards.pdfcheck)).
  • Attribution is always an assessment: "the Cyber Centre assesses…", never a fact (Legal Notice (🔗 https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlcheck), section 7.3).
  • Relevance (question 4): High when an exposed asset or exposure fact matches directly, Moderate when indirect or through a supplier, Low or none otherwise. Indicators (question 5) are copied for the log search, never visited.
  • Two scales (second table), independent and written together: the Admiralty or NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organization) system, reproduced in United States Army FM (Field Manual) 2-22.3, Appendix B (🔗 https://irp.fas.org/doddir/army/fm2-22-3.pdfcheck). A good source with an unconfirmed item is B3; an unknown source that others confirm is F1. OpenCTI (🔗 https://filigran.io/solutions/open-cti/check) stores both; Lab 2 puts them in the Source rating column.
  • TLP (Traffic Light Protocol) 2.0 of FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams) (🔗 https://www.first.org/tlp/check), since August 2022: CLEAR, no limit (alerts, CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) (🔗 https://www.cve.org/check) records); GREEN, the community, not the Internet; AMBER, the organization and its clients, need-to-know; AMBER+STRICT, the organization only; RED, named recipients only. Your Lab 2 catalogue stays confidential (section 7.5).
  • Six errors prevented: severity read as risk; CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) (🔗 https://www.first.org/cvss/check) used as likelihood; acting on a secondary source; attribution repeated as fact; ignoring update numbers (AL26-026 (🔗 https://cyber.gc.ca/en/alerts-advisories/al26-026-critical-vulnerabilities-impacting-php-cve-2026-109618-cve-2026-109619check) changed twice in six days); visiting an indicator.
# Question What it produces
1 Who publishes it, when, under which marking? Publisher family, date, update, TLP
2 What is it about? One-sentence subject
3 What is the evidence? Observed vs assessed; ratings A–F, 1–6
4 Does it apply to us? Asset identifiers, relevance
5 How does the threat act? ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) (🔗 https://attack.mitre.org/check) identifiers, indicators
6 What is recommended, and can we do it? Actions, fixed versions, owner
7 What is our decision, and where is it recorded? Act now, catalogue, watch or discard
Source reliability (the publisher) Information credibility (the statement)
A Completely reliable: vendor, national agency 1 Confirmed by independent sources
B Usually reliable: recognized research firm, response team 2 Probably true: unconfirmed but logical
C Fairly reliable: mixed or short record 3 Possibly true: partly corroborated
D Not usually reliable: errors, commercial exaggeration 4 Doubtful: illogical or contradicted
E Unreliable: has published false information 5 Improbable: illogical and contradicted
F Cannot be judged: anonymous, new site, forwarded message 6 Cannot be judged: no basis

🧭 At Kalmia: Three documents on the 6 × 6 grid. AL26-026 (October 21; Update 1 added CVE-2026-115560, unfixed by the October 21 releases; Update 2 reported exploitation and the KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalogcheck) listing) is A1, relevance High (A-16, PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) on the hosted VPS (virtual private server)), T1190: act now by November 6, two catalogue rows. AL26-028 (🔗 https://cyber.gc.ca/en/alerts-advisories/al26-028-ongoing-help-desk-voice-phishing-campaign-targeting-canadian-organizationscheck) is A2, consistent with Mandiant M-Trends 2026 (🔗 https://cloud.google.com/security/resources/m-trendscheck) but unconfirmed; relevance High (InfoNord's help desk, MFA (multi-factor authentication) on two admin accounts), T1566.004, T1621, T1556: act now by November 9, two rows. The fictional "All WooCommerce stores hacked" post is F6, discarded in one line.

⚠️ Exam trap: A respected name does not confirm a story (B3, not A1). And "very likely, moderate confidence" is no contradiction: probability and evidence quality are separate judgments.

📌 Remember: The publisher earns a letter; the statement earns a digit.

The big idea. A threat catalogue is the organized list of who or what could act against an organization's assets (threat sources) and what they could do (threat events), every row backed by evidence and a public reference. For every Lab 1 asset it answers three things: who or what could hurt it, by what means, and on what evidence. It is the Lab 2 deliverable, not yet the risk register.

What you must know

  • Method: NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-30 Rev. 1 (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/30/r1/finalcheck): Task 2-1 identifies sources and rates adversarial ones on capability, intent and targeting (Appendix D); Task 2-2 identifies events (Appendix E examples). ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27005:2022 (🔗 https://www.iso.org/standard/80585.htmlcheck), Annex A, groups typical threats by origin. Both are checklists: keep only what evidence supports.
  • A threat event is one sentence with four parts: source + action (an ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) (🔗 https://attack.mitre.org/check) technique if adversarial) + asset (Lab 1 identifier) + means or precondition, one technique per row. "Ransomware" is a tool; "the NAS (network-attached storage) password is shared by four people" is a vulnerability for the evidence column.
  • Six steps: start from the assets and the twelve exposure facts (F01 personal information … F12 backup reachable from the network); list the sources (four external profiles, three internal types, three non-adversarial families), which gives Kalmia twelve named sources, TS-01 to TS-12, because the cybercriminal profile splits by the facts; derive the events; merge and split; rate; check the quality rules.
  • Merge and split: same source, technique, asset and entry point make one row with two pieces of evidence (the two PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) flaws of October 21); a second technique or entry point (an outdated plugin) makes a second row.
  • Relevance formula: computed, never chosen; targeting stays out of it, non-adversarial rows carry 1 · 1 · 1, and it ranks rows without being a likelihood.
High      if (Intent >= 4 and Capability >= 3) or facts >= 3
Moderate  if Intent >= 3 or facts >= 2
Low       otherwise
  • Hand-over to Lab 3: each row gets Topic 4's vulnerabilities, a likelihood (intent, targeting, KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalogcheck) and EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) (🔗 https://www.first.org/epss/check) data, incidents, facts) and an impact (Lab 1 business impact analysis, CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) (🔗 https://www.first.org/cvss/check) impact metrics). Likelihood × impact = risk score; the risk register is the catalogue sorted by it.
  • Confidentiality: fictional data, course folder, professor only (Legal Notice (🔗 https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlcheck), sections 7.5 and 18.2).
  • Six quality rules: complete (every fact, incident and critical asset covered, or the absence explained), specific (source, action, asset identifier), evidenced (Kalmia evidence plus a dated, rated reference), threats, not vulnerabilities (weaknesses only as evidence), factual and ethical (nobody named as guilty), consistent (Lab 1 identifiers, real ATT&CK v20 techniques, fifteen columns in order).
  • Lab 2 (5 %, Léa (🔗 https://dawsoncollege.omnivox.ca/check), Saturday, November 14, 2026, 23:59): at least 25 rows covering every profile, family, incident, fact and critical asset; a source register (8–12 sources); a watch list (eight or more items, seven answers each); an ATT&CK Navigator (🔗 https://mitre-attack.github.io/attack-navigator/check) map with a half-page note; a checker report with zero errors; a one-page memo to Nadia Roy, identifiers in footnotes.
# Columns Content
1–4 Threat ID (identifier), threat source, source family, side T-nn; profile or non-adversarial source; adversarial, accidental, structural or environmental; external, internal or third party
5–7 Threat event, ATT&CK technique, Kalmia asset Four-part sentence; Txxxx or Txxxx.xxx (empty if non-adversarial); A-nn
8–11 Capability, intent, targeting (1–5), exposure facts Appendix D scales (1 if non-adversarial); count of F01–F12
12 Relevance By formula
13–15 Evidence, public source, source rating W-nn, INC-nn, Lab 1 findings; dated reference; A–F and 1–6

🧭 At Kalmia: The fifteen seed rows give six High (T-01 ransomware on NAS-01 and its backup, T-02 the PHP flaw, T-03 the outdated plugin, T-04 supplier bank-detail fraud, T-05 help-desk vishing, T-15 payroll fraud), seven Moderate and two Low (T-08, a state-sponsored group with capability 5 but intent 1; T-12, a power failure). Eleven of twelve facts appear; F11 is absent because Kalmia holds no information of state interest.

⚠️ Exam trap: T-09 (2 · 3 · 5) is Moderate despite a targeting of 5, and T-08 (5 · 1 · 1) is Low despite a capability of 5. Compute; don't guess.

📌 Remember: One row = one source, one technique, one entry point (with every asset it touches), backed by evidence and a rated reference.

B

Part B — Ten case studies

Two situations per chapter. In class, work each one in pairs for about four minutes, then compare with the most possible answers. Often more than one answer can be defended; when that happens, the answer says so.

📍 Based on: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.2 Key vocabulary — asset, threat, vulnerability, risk, impact, control + 1.3 The CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad

The situation

Picture a Monday in early December at the Saint-Laurent roastery. At 07:10 the first batch of the week, 300 kg of beans, comes out of the roaster black and smoking. The operator checks ROAST-PC, the roaster control computer: the "House Espresso" profile, one of Kalmia's 60 roast profiles, now ends 25 °C hotter than the printed copy pinned beside the machine. Karim Haddad stops production and calls Lucas Martin.

Lucas opens the log of the unattended remote-access tool that the roasting-machine vendor uses on ROAST-PC, with a password Kalmia shares with that vendor. The log shows a session on Sunday at 23:40 from an address the vendor does not recognize. Nobody had ever read that log before today. ROAST-PC still runs Windows 10, which has received no free security updates since October 14, 2025, and it sits on the flat roastery network, from which it can reach NAS-01.

NAS-01 keeps a copy of the roast profiles in its Production share. The vendor reloads the correct profiles from that copy, and roasting restarts at 14:00. Three wholesale deliveries leave a day late; Karim puts the delay at about one working day of wholesale preparation, roughly $9,500 of sales, on top of the lost batch. One question stays open: did the visitor also copy the profiles?

Your tasks

  1. Sort the facts into the six terms: primary and supporting assets, threat source and threat event, vulnerabilities (and any predisposing condition), existing controls, and impact.
  2. Name the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) property or properties that were violated, and the one still in doubt. Rate each Low, Moderate or High, and give the roast profiles' category with the high-water mark.
  3. Write the risk statement an analyst could have written before that Monday, using the course template.
  4. Classify the two existing controls by nature and function, then propose two additional controls, each with its nature and function.

Most possible answers

  1. Primary assets: the roast profiles (a trade secret) and the roasting process that depends on them; supporting assets: ROAST-PC and NAS-01, which store the profiles. Threat source: an unknown outsider (adversarial, external); threat event: a remote login through the vendor's tool, then an unauthorized change to a profile. Vulnerabilities: a remote-access password shared with the vendor, a tool left unattended, and Windows 10 without security updates; the flat network is a predisposing condition, since it lets ROAST-PC reach NAS-01. Existing controls: the copy of the profiles on NAS-01 and the remote-access log. Impact: a 300 kg batch destroyed, roasting stopped until 14:00, three deliveries a day late (about $9,500 of wholesale sales delayed) and a possible leak of a trade secret. Also acceptable: someone at the vendor misusing the shared password as the threat source; with a shared password, nobody can tell the difference.
  2. Integrity is violated: a profile was changed without authorization. Rate it High, because a silent change destroyed a batch and could hit any of the 60 profiles. Availability is violated too: roasting stopped for most of a day and deliveries slipped; Moderate, serious but limited to one day. Confidentiality is in doubt: whoever could edit a profile could also copy it, so treat it as at least Moderate until the investigation says otherwise. Category: High, because the highest of the three ratings (integrity) is High, which matches the roast profiles' row in Kalmia's CIA table.
  3. "Because ROAST-PC no longer gets security updates for Windows 10 and leaves a remote-access tool running unattended, with a password shared with the vendor, an outsider could log in remotely and alter Kalmia's roast profiles, which would ruin batches, stop roasting for about a day (roughly $9,500 of wholesale sales per day) and could expose a trade secret." Also acceptable: a statement that stresses the stopped production and the path to NAS-01, close to the register's R5.
  4. The copy on NAS-01 is technical and corrective: it made the restore possible. The remote-access log is technical and detective, but a log nobody reads detects nothing. Additional controls: vendor access disabled by default and opened on request with an individual account and MFA (multi-factor authentication) (technical, preventive); a weekly review of the remote-access log by Lucas (administrative, detective); ROAST-PC isolated in its own network segment (technical, preventive). Also acceptable: comparing each profile file's hash with a reference copy before loading it (technical, detective), or planning ROAST-PC's replacement (technical, preventive).

📍 Based on: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.4 The risk analysis process, step by step + 1.5 Risk analysis frameworks — NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 and ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27005

The situation

A week after the first risk register reached Nadia Roy, two new facts land on the analyst's desk.

The first comes from Café Plateau. Its new manager finally opened the POS (point of sale) refund report that nobody used to read. Since January she has found three evenings with refunds that match no sale, all entered with the manager PIN (personal identification number) that every shift lead shares and that is still written under the cash drawer. Her estimate: about $3,000 gone before anyone noticed, the café's sales records no longer reliable, no customer affected. Nothing has changed at the counter, so the analyst expects it to happen again several times a year.

The second comes from Émile Gagnon, the freelance web developer. One of the four web shop plugins that have gone six months without updates has a publicly known flaw, and criminals are now exploiting it automatically against small WooCommerce shops. The three administrator accounts still have no MFA (multi-factor authentication), and the holiday season has started.

Nadia Roy has about $8,000 for security this year and a half-time IT (information technology) coordinator. By Friday she wants to know where the café problem goes in the register, what Émile's news changes, and what she will be asked to sign.

Your tasks

  1. Rate the refund-fraud risk, call it R8, with Kalmia's scales: likelihood, impact, score, level and required action.
  2. Place R8 in the ranked register (R1 16, R2 15, R4 12, R3 12, R5 8, R6 6, R7 2) and explain its position.
  3. Re-rate R2 after Émile's call: new score, level and required action. Which step of the ten-step process, and which activity of ISO/IEC 27005 (🔗 https://www.iso.org/standard/80585.htmlcheck), send you back to rating?
  4. Choose a treatment option for R8, name its controls with their function, estimate the residual risk and say who accepts it.
  5. Map the R8 controls and the R2 response to the Functions of NIST CSF 2.0 (🔗 https://www.nist.gov/cyberframeworkcheck), and say which gaps in Kalmia's Current Profile they help close.

Most possible answers

  1. Likelihood 4 (Likely): three evenings since January, and nothing has changed, so several times a year. Impact 2 (Minor): about $3,000, between $1,000 and $10,000, one site affected, no customer involved. Score 4 × 2 = 8, Medium: treat within the quarter, or accept with a written justification by the risk owner.
  2. R8 ties with R5 at 8. Kalmia breaks ties with the higher impact: R5 has impact 4 and R8 only 2, so R5 stays ahead. The new order is R1, R2, R4, R3, R5, R8, R6, R7. R8 does not join the 30-day list; it sits in the "within the quarter" group with R5 and R6.
  3. A publicly known flaw that criminals exploit automatically against shops like Kalmia's raises the likelihood to 5 (already happening); 4 is defensible too. The impact stays 5: card data captured at checkout, a declaration under Québec's privacy law (🔗 https://www.legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca/en/document/cs/p-39.1check), PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) (🔗 https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/check) follow-up, a shop closed in peak season. Score 25 (or 20): Critical either way, so immediate action within 7 days, decided personally by Nadia Roy, and R2 now tops the register above R1. The trigger is step 10, communicate and monitor: the analysis is reviewed whenever a new threat appears, which sends you back through steps 5 to 8. In ISO/IEC 27005 terms, monitoring and review opens a new round of risk analysis and evaluation, because the process is iterative.
  4. Reduce. Give every shift lead an individual PIN (technical, preventive: no more anonymous refunds) and have the café manager review the refund report every week (administrative, detective). Both cost next to nothing and do not slow the counter, which respects Nadia Roy's constraints. Residual estimate: about 2 × 2 = 4, Low, accepted in writing by Nadia Roy as risk owner. Also acceptable: accepting R8 as Medium with a written justification, although with controls this cheap that justification would be hard to defend.
  5. Individual PINs belong to PROTECT, in PR.AA (Identity Management, Authentication, and Access Control); the weekly refund review belongs to DETECT. For R2, updating the plugins and adding MFA are PROTECT, and a written procedure for a compromised checkout would be RESPOND. Nadia Roy's decisions and signatures sit in GOVERN. These measures move DETECT toward its target (1 to 2) and PROTECT toward 3, and a written incident procedure starts on the RESPOND gap (1 to 3).

📍 Based on: Chapter 2 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 1 › 2.1 Hardware inventory and associated permissions + 2.2 Software inventory, licences and associated permissions

The situation

Monday, October 26, 9:00. Lucas Martin, Kalmia's half-time IT (information technology) coordinator, lays two printouts on Karim Haddad's desk: Friday's reconciliation of the head-office register and the software check of six computers. Karim, Director of Operations, owns ROAST-PC (KAL-0007, 192.168.10.20), the Windows 10 computer that runs the roaster.

Four items worry Lucas. SALES-LT2 (KAL-0018), the laptop of Nathalie Fortin in wholesale sales, has not appeared in the firewall's DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) log since September 11. The unknown Raspberry Pi at 192.168.10.150 (MAC (Media Access Control) address DC:A6:32:4F:19:C2) proved to be a data logger the roaster vendor plugged in during a maintenance visit and never declared. On ROAST-PC itself, the three roaster operators share the local administrator account roastadmin without MFA (multi-factor authentication), and RoastTech Services keeps unattended remote access through RoastLink Remote 2.1.7, whose RoastLinkSvc service starts automatically as LocalSystem. That program is not in the licence register, and the vendor's contract gives no end date. Finally, Adobe Acrobat Pro, bought as two per-user licences, is installed for Sophie Tremblay, Marc Gauthier and Karim himself.

Karim has a plan within thirty seconds: "Delete SALES-LT2 from the register, unplug the vendor's box, and let the operators keep their password. The roaster has run fine since 2023." Lucas wants a written answer before Friday, because every finding must land in the Hardware, Software and Permissions sheets of the Lab 1 template.

Your tasks

  1. SALES-LT2 is in the "missing" state. Explain what that means, why deleting its line is the wrong reaction, and what Lucas should do instead.
  2. The Raspberry Pi is now identified. What has to happen before it may stay on the network, and what must its inventory line contain?
  3. Rate the two access findings on ROAST-PC with Kalmia's rules, name the principle each one breaks, and propose a fix for each.
  4. Why does an unapproved program running as LocalSystem matter, and what does CIS (Center for Internet Security) Control 2 (🔗 https://www.cisecurity.org/controls/inventory-and-control-of-software-assetscheck) expect Kalmia to do about RoastLink Remote?
  5. Is Kalmia compliant for Adobe Acrobat Pro? Explain with the right metric and give two ways to fix the situation.

Most possible answers

  1. Missing means recorded in the register but not seen on the network for longer than Kalmia's 30-day limit; SALES-LT2 was at 42 days on Friday's reconciliation, 45 by this Monday. That line is Kalmia's only proof that the laptop, and the data on it, exists, so deleting it hides the question instead of answering it. Lucas asks Karim, the recorded owner, and Nathalie: is it on the road, lost, stolen or broken? If it is retired, the line stays with that status and the disk is sanitized before disposal, following NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-88 Rev. 2 (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/88/r2/finalcheck). Also acceptable: noting that the laptop runs unsupported Windows 10, so it should be checked before it reconnects.
  2. Identified does not mean approved. Under CIS Safeguards 1.1 and 1.2, Kalmia either approves the logger formally or removes it, denies it remote connection or quarantines it; pulling the cable in a hurry without talking to the vendor is not the method. If Karim keeps it, it gets an asset tag and a complete line: hardware address DC:A6:32:4F:19:C2, machine name, network address if it is made static, an owner (Karim, since it serves the roaster), a department (Production) and "approved to connect: yes", plus make, model, firmware and last seen. Like every other device, it also needs a password policy, and the vendor's access to it goes on the Permissions sheet.
  3. The shared roastadmin account is HIGH (one administrator account shared by several people). It breaks accountability: when a roast setting changes, the log says "roastadmin", never which operator, and it stretches least privilege as well. Fix: one named account per operator, administrator rights only where the roasting software truly requires them, and MFA where the system allows it. The unattended RoastLink Remote access is HIGH too (an outside company with access and no end date), and it breaks least privilege in time, because rights should last only as long as the job. Fix: an end date in the contract, access opened for scheduled maintenance and closed afterwards, a named vendor account with MFA, all recorded on the Permissions sheet.
  4. LocalSystem has full control of the computer, so whoever controls RoastLink Remote, or the vendor account behind it, controls ROAST-PC and therefore production. That level of rights is normal for an approved updater, not for software nobody approved. Control 2 wants only authorized software installed and running: Kalmia either authorizes RoastLink Remote properly (business purpose, owner Karim, version, licence, register entry, plus the access limits of task 3) or removes it (Safeguard 2.3). Application allowlisting (Safeguard 2.5, App Control for Business or AppLocker) then blocks the next unapproved install. Also acceptable: pointing out that ROAST-PC runs unsupported Windows 10, which makes any extra remote door riskier.
  5. No. Acrobat Pro is licensed per user, so Kalmia counts people, not computers or installations: Sophie, Marc and Karim make three users for two licences, over-deployed by one. Kalmia can buy a third licence, or remove Acrobat Pro from one person who only needs to read files and give that person the free Acrobat Reader. Sophie Tremblay owns the product in the licence register, so she makes the call, and the register is updated either way.

📍 Based on: Chapter 2 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 1 › 2.3 Asset classification, ownership and criticality + 2.4 Hands-on: building an asset inventory with a template and a network scanner (Nmap (Network Mapper))

The situation

Friday, October 23, 19:00, in the lab. Your team sits at the scanning computer (192.168.10.200) with Nmap (Network Mapper) (🔗 https://nmap.org/check) and the signed authorization for 192.168.10.0/24, valid until November 5, which limits 192.168.10.20 (ROAST-PC) to discovery. Before the first command, a teammate suggests two "quick extras": a ping sweep of the college Wi-Fi "to compare", and a version scan of ROAST-PC "since it is only one address".

At 19:05 the authorized scan runs. NAS-01 (192.168.10.10, asset tag KAL-0005) answers with four open ports: 22/tcp ssh (OpenSSH 8.2), 139/tcp and 445/tcp Samba file sharing, and 5000/tcp http (nginx), with an operating-system guess of Linux at 96 %. From Lesson 1 you know that its single administrator account is shared by four people without MFA (multi-factor authentication). From the classification workshop you know what it stores: the HR (human resources) share with the employee files (D-03, Restricted, owner Sophie Tremblay), the Production share with the daily order and delivery plan (D-06, Internal, MTD (maximum tolerable downtime) 4 h) and the roast profiles (D-04, Confidential), the Finance share (D-07, Confidential), the Marketing share (M-01, Public) and the camera recordings (V-01, Confidential). In the hardware register, Lucas Martin is both owner and custodian of the device.

On Monday, Karim Haddad asks your team a simple question: "NAS-01 is just a storage box, right? Why would it be near the top of our list?"

Your tasks

  1. Answer your teammate's two "quick extras" and explain why both are refused.
  2. Read NAS-01's open ports: what does each one tell the inventory, and which one does the converter flag as an exposed service?
  3. Which columns of NAS-01's row can the scan fill, and which must people fill? Give the label, the overall category and the tier that NAS-01 should carry as a system, with your reasoning.
  4. Answer Karim: where does NAS-01 sit on the protection map, and why does it belong near the top of the priority list?
  5. What must your team record after the scan, and how must the scan files be handled?

Most possible answers

  1. Both fall outside the signed authorization, so both are refused. The college Wi-Fi is not in the lab range: scanning it without its owner's written permission may be an offence under section 342.1 of the Criminal Code (🔗 https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/c-46/section-342.1.htmlcheck), and the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice (🔗 https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlcheck) forbids it, ping sweep or not. ROAST-PC is in range but excluded from everything beyond discovery: it is operational technology, and a version scan (-sV) connects to every open port and can crash fragile software, here the computer that drives the roaster. The rule: authorized range, authorized dates, authorization file in hand, exclusions respected.
  2. 22/tcp is SSH (Secure Shell), encrypted administration, so the inventory should note who holds that account (the shared administrator). 139 and 445/tcp are SMB (Server Message Block) file sharing, expected on a file server and therefore not a finding here, although it would be on a workstation. 5000/tcp is the Synology web administration over HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol), without encryption, so the login crosses the network in clear text: this is the exposed service the converter flags (MEDIUM). The Linux guess at 96 % matches DSM (DiskStation Manager, the operating system of Synology storage) 7.2 in the register, but it remains a probability.
  3. The scan fills the tool columns: IP (Internet Protocol) and MAC (Media Access Control) addresses, vendor, status "known" with asset tag KAL-0005, open ports, OS (operating system) guess and accuracy, scan time. People fill owner, custodian, label, C, I, A, category and tier. As a system, NAS-01 takes the highest label of what it holds: the HR share with each employee's SIN (Social Insurance Number) and bank details makes it Restricted. Its category is High by the high-water mark (D-03 alone is rated High, High, Moderate).
