Its tier follows the most urgent information it holds: the daily order plan tolerates 4 hours at most, so NAS-01 is Tier 1. Also acceptable: Tier 2, if the team documents a copy of the order plan that stays usable while NAS-01 is down.
  4. Restricted and Tier 1 put NAS-01 in the "protect and keep running" quadrant: it needs strong access control and fast recovery at the same time. Applied to NAS-01, Nadia Roy's priority rule (category, then tier, then label, then shortest MTD) would even rank it ahead of the web shop: same category and tier, higher label. Add what the scan and Lesson 1 found, an unencrypted administration page and one administrator password shared by four people without MFA, and the answer to Karim is clear. The "storage box" holds the employee files, the roast profiles and the order plan, so it enters the impact column of Lab 3 near the top.
  5. Write the scan in the scan log: date and time (October 23, 19:05), range, authorization file and results folder. Keep both XML (Extensible Markup Language) files, paste the converter's rows into the Scan sheet and update "last seen" on the Hardware sheet; the next scan will be compared with Ndiff. The files list devices, addresses and weaknesses, so they are confidential under section 7.5 of the Legal Notice: course folder only, shared with the professor and the team, never published.

📍 Based on: Chapter 3 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 2 › 3.1 Data and services critical to the organization's operations + 3.2 Physical and logical representation of the infrastructure (network diagrams)

The situation

Thursday, 11:30 a.m. The lunch queue at Kalmia's Plateau café reaches the door when the provider's router at the counter, ISP-RTR-PLA, loses its link to the Internet. The three POS (point of sale) tablets, POS-PLA-1 and POS-PLA-2 at the counter and POS-PLA-3 on the terrace, are still on the staff Wi-Fi, Kalmia-Staff, but they can no longer reach the POS cloud service. The card readers, which reach the payment processor through the tablets over Bluetooth, stop with them. Customers on the guest Wi-Fi, Kalmia-Invite, lose their Internet access at the same moment. The shift lead grabs a notepad and starts writing sales by hand.

Karim Haddad, owner of the café sales process (P-01), calls Lucas Martin. The provider promises a repair by the next business day, which is exactly what the recovery records already say about the café lines: 24 hours to restore, one line per café, no second line.

Lucas opens the critical services register and the two network views of the café. P-01 has a WRT (work recovery time) of 0.5 hour and an RPO (recovery point objective) of 1 hour. When Karim was interviewed, his highest impact rating was 2 for a one-hour outage, and reputation reached 3 (serious) at two hours. On the logical view, Lucas also notices, not for the first time, that the camera CAM-PLA-1 and the menu screen MENU-PLA-1, plugged into the router's LAN (local area network) ports, sit in the same staff zone, 192.168.20.0/24, as the tablets. Karim, meanwhile, wants one answer: "How long do I have?"

Your tasks

  1. Determine the MTD (maximum tolerable downtime) and the RTO (recovery time objective) of P-01, explain how they relate to the WRT and the RPO, and give Karim the two clock times that matter today.
  2. Describe the café Internet line in BIA (business impact analysis) terms (type of dependency, redundancy, findings) and compare it with the POS cloud service.
  3. Lucas wants to show Karim what is physically at the counter and how information moves. Which elements of the situation belong on the physical view, and which on the logical view? Give at least two of each.
  4. Name the finding Lucas sees in the staff zone and its level, explain the risk for the tablets, and say what the guest network demonstrates by contrast.

Most possible answers

  1. The MTD is 2 hours, the shortest outage that Karim rated 3. Since MTD = RTO + WRT, the RTO is 2 − 0.5 = 1.5 hours: the line, or a workaround, must be back by 1:00 p.m., and normal selling, with the paper sales re-entered, by 1:30 p.m. The RPO of 1 hour is a separate limit on data loss (the maximum age of the last good copy of the sales records) and plays no part in the MTD. With an MTD of 4 hours or less, P-01 is Tier 1.
  2. The line is a network dependency with no redundancy, so it is a single point of failure for P-01. Its restore time, 24 hours, is far beyond the 1.5-hour RTO: a recovery gap. It is not shared, since each café line serves only café sales. The POS cloud service, by contrast, is a shared single point of failure (café sales and the loyalty program, P-07) with its own recovery gap: 2.25 hours, as measured during INC-03, against 1.5. Also acceptable: noting that the gap feeds Lab 3 as a risk factor and Lab 4 as a continuity measure, such as a second link from another provider.
  3. Physical view: the router ISP-RTR-PLA at the counter with its WAN (wide area network) cable from the provider and its LAN ports, CAM-PLA-1 and MENU-PLA-1 plugged into those ports, the tablets at the counter and on the terrace, the card readers paired by Bluetooth, the Wi-Fi coverage. Logical view: the staff subnet 192.168.20.0/24 and the guest subnet 192.168.21.0/24 as two zones, the trust boundary towards the Internet, the flow from the tablets to the POS cloud service (F-11, HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) on port 443) and the flow from the card readers to the payment processor through the tablets (F-12). Rule of thumb: what you can touch is physical; addresses, zones and flows are logical.
  4. FLAT-ZONE, rated HIGH: a camera and an IoT (Internet of Things) device, the menu screen, share the staff zone with the POS tablets, so one compromised device could reach the tablets that take every sale. The guest network shows the design that works: customers' phones sit in their own subnet with client isolation and no route to the staff network, a trust boundary with a real control. That separation is simply missing between the cameras or screens and the tablets. Also acceptable: proposing separate zones for cameras and IoT devices, the direction Lab 4 will take.

📍 Based on: Chapter 3 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 2 › 3.3 Documenting who has access to what (permissions map) + 3.4 Lab 1 — Asset inventory and infrastructure map (Integrative Project, Part 1)

The situation

Wednesday, 2 p.m. Sophie Tremblay sits down with Lucas Martin and you, the analyst, for the first access review of the two Restricted shares she owns on NAS-01. The HR (human resources) share holds the employee files: addresses, SIN (Social Insurance Number), bank details. The Scans share receives every document scanned on the office printer PRN-HQ-1, HR forms included.

Your permissions map shows these entries. On HR: hr Modify, office Modify (inherited from the parent folder), administrators Full Control (inherited). On Scans: Everyone Modify, administrators Full Control (inherited). The group office has eight members.

One of them is lfontaine. Léa Fontaine, a marketing intern, left on August 29, yet her account still belongs to the groups marketing and office, and in Microsoft 365 she still holds an active User role, without MFA (multi-factor authentication), licence assigned. Sophie also brings up INC-04, when, two months after leaving, a former shift supervisor exported 18,500 loyalty member records. And Émilie Bélanger's staff PIN (personal identification number), EB-0715, still opens a café cash drawer, although she left on July 15.

Lucas offers to "just fix everything tonight". Sophie hesitates; she is the one who will explain the changes to Nadia Roy. You, meanwhile, still have to complete the Access review sheet of your Lab 1 workbook and the one-page memo.

Your tasks

  1. Work out lfontaine's effective access on HR and on Scans, name the entry that grants each one, and classify the findings attached to her account, with their level.
  2. Which step of the access life cycle failed for Léa Fontaine and Émilie Bélanger? Name the CIS (Center for Internet Security) Safeguard (🔗 https://cas.docs.cisecurity.org/en/latest/source/Controls6/check) that requires it and list what the step should contain.
  3. Should Lucas "just fix everything tonight"? Explain who prepares, who decides and who applies in an access review, and suggest what Sophie should decide for HR and Scans.
  4. Compare the Scans share with the Desjardins case investigated by the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (🔗 https://www.priv.gc.ca/en/opc-news/news-and-announcements/2020/nr-c_201214/check).
  5. What must these findings look like in your Lab 1 folder before you hand it in?

Most possible answers

  1. HR: Modify, through the inherited office entry; she is not in hr, but office applies to her. Scans: Modify, through Everyone. Since she has left, the role matrix expects None everywhere, so her account is an ORPHAN, rated HIGH, on NAS-01 and again in Microsoft 365, where it is also a NO-MFA finding (MEDIUM). She also appears in the EXCESS findings of HR and Scans, both HIGH because the shares are Restricted. Also acceptable: adding that she can still open Production (Read, through office) and Marketing (Modify, through marketing), four shares in all.
  2. The leaver step. CIS Safeguard 6.2 requires a process that revokes access by disabling accounts immediately upon termination. The step should include three actions: human resources informs IT (information technology) on the day of departure; every account is disabled at once, in every system (NAS-01, Microsoft 365, the POS (point of sale) service, the loyalty platform); shared passwords and PINs the person knew are changed. Safeguard 5.3 (45 days of inactivity) and the quarterly account inventory of Safeguard 5.1 are safety nets, not substitutes, and INC-04 shows the price of skipping the step.
  3. Not on his own. In an access review, the analyst only prepares the map and its findings; the data owner chooses to keep, reduce or remove each access; the custodian carries out that choice. Sophie Tremblay owns HR and Scans, so she decides and Lucas Martin applies. A sensible decision: remove the inherited office entry on HR and grant access by role (Modify for her own role, Read for the president, as the role matrix says), replace Everyone on Scans with the roles that need it (her role and the scanner service account), and disable lfontaine today. Also acceptable: any decision that follows the role matrix, as long as Sophie makes it and it is written down.
  4. In December 2020, the OPC (Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada) announced that a Desjardins employee had exfiltrated personal information on nearly 9.7 million Canadians, over a period of at least 26 months. Its investigation findings (🔗 https://www.priv.gc.ca/en/opc-actions-and-decisions/investigations/investigations-into-businesses/2020/pipeda-2020-005/check) explain that the data had been copied out of data warehouses onto a shared drive that employees could open with no work need for it, and that access controls and data governance fell short. Scans has the same shape on a small scale: a share everyone can read and change, holding Restricted documents most people have no reason to see. That is an EXCESS finding against need to know, and section 20 of Québec's Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector (🔗 https://www.legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca/en/document/cs/P-39.1check) lets employees access personal information only when their duties require it.
  5. In the Access review sheet, exported as access_review.csv, every finding carries its level, its data owner and the owner's decision, and every HIGH finding must be decided; the readiness check reports undecided HIGH findings as TODO items. The memo to Nadia Roy presents the most serious findings in plain business terms, each paired with the decision you need from her, for example disabling every account of a departing employee on the day of departure. Only fictional Kalmia data goes in: a pasted number that looks like a SIN is a BLOCKER.

📍 Based on: Chapter 4 — Identifying Threats, Part 1 › 4.1 External threat actors and their motivations + 4.2 Internal threats: malicious insiders, negligent users, third parties and suppliers

The situation

Late October 2026, at the Saint-Laurent office. Lucas Martin, Kalmia's half-time IT (information technology) coordinator, has pulled the account lists from seven systems, along with every audit entry their platforms keep. Four lines bother him, and he forwards them to you, the analyst:

2026-10-19 02:14  RoastLink      vendor session on ROAST-PC, 48 min, ticket: none
2026-10-21        Sage 50        mgauthier changed a supplier's bank details, released $6,200 to it 6 min later
2026-10-26        Microsoft 365  lfontaine signed in from a new device (left Kalmia on 2026-08-28)
2026-10-28        WordPress      egagnon installed a plugin from an unofficial source

Nadia Roy, President and CEO (chief executive officer) and the risk owner, reads the printout and asks two questions. "Is whoever uses mgauthier stealing from us, and should I fire them?" Then, after a pause: "Honestly, who out there would bother attacking a coffee roaster?"

You also have the context from Lab 1 and the incident notes. Two of the seven cameras still use factory passwords. Four web shop plugins have not been updated in six months. The three café routers are SOHO (small office / home office) devices. InfoNord, the MSP (managed service provider), holds global administrator rights in Microsoft 365. RoastTech's remote-access tool runs unattended, with a shared password and no end date. Émile Gagnon (egagnon), the freelance developer, administers WordPress without MFA (multi-factor authentication). In June a look-alike of the importer's domain nearly diverted $18,400 (INC-02), and in September a former supervisor's account exported 18,500 loyalty records (INC-04).

Your tasks

  1. For each of the four lines, say what in its context (the time, the volume, the person, or whether the action was needed) makes it an indicator, and name the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) property at stake.
  2. Answer Nadia's first question the way an analyst must. What do you write about the Sage 50 line, and why is it an indicator rather than proof?
  3. Write the RoastLink line as one Lab 2 row: threat source, threat event, asset, evidence, source.
  4. Answer Nadia's second question. Which two external actor types rank highest in relevance for Kalmia, and why does one of them make the list despite its low capability?
  5. Propose one first control (Lab 4 preview) for each of the four lines.

Most possible answers

  1. RoastLink: the time (02:14, outside the agreed window) and the missing ticket, so nobody approved the need; integrity and availability of the roaster PC (personal computer). Sage 50: the person, since one account performed both steps of a sensitive task six minutes apart; integrity. lfontaine: the person, because a leaver's account should not work at all, let alone from a new device; confidentiality. egagnon: the need, since nothing required software from an unofficial source on the web shop; integrity.
  2. Nadia gets facts, not a name: on 2026-10-21 one Sage 50 account changed a supplier's bank details and released a $6,200 payment to it six minutes later. Several explanations fit: an insider fraud, an honest employee fooled by a BEC (business email compromise) message as in INC-02, or someone else using the account. The investigation decides; the analysis never names a culprit (Legal Notice (🔗 https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlcheck), sections 7.5 and 18). What you can offer her is a control: separation of duties.
  3. Threat source: RoastTech, a third party and supplier, or anyone holding its shared password. Threat event: unapproved remote access to the roaster PC. Asset: ROAST-PC, which runs roasting production. Evidence: RoastLink session on 2026-10-19 at 02:14, 48 minutes, no ticket, through an unattended tool with a shared password and no end date. Source: the RoastLink audit log exported by Lucas Martin.
  4. Cybercriminals rank high (capability 4, intent 5, targeting 4): Kalmia moves money they can divert (INC-02), holds data they can sell or ransom, and keeps a backup disk connected, which makes paying more likely. Opportunistic attackers also rank high with a capability of only 2 and a targeting of 1, because they pick victims by exposure alone, and Kalmia shows three things scanners hunt for: factory-password cameras, outdated plugins and the remote-access tool. Also acceptable: noting that state-sponsored groups stay at moderate, as users of the café SOHO routers or passengers through the MSP, rarely with Kalmia as the final target.
  5. RoastLink: approve each vendor session, set an end date, add MFA. Sage 50: a second approver and a call-back on a known number. lfontaine: disable accounts on the last day (offboarding) and alert on leaver sign-ins. egagnon: official sources only and change approval for plugins. The review also found that three controls (offboarding, named accounts and MFA) would have made eight of the thirteen accounts it examined harmless.

📍 Based on: Chapter 4 — Identifying Threats, Part 1 › 4.3 Common attack methods: malware, ransomware, phishing and social engineering, DoS (Denial of Service), credential theft + 4.4 Case study: a recent ransomware attack on a small manufacturer

The situation

On Saturday morning, February 22, 2025, ransomware shut down the systems of Ganong Bros., Limited (🔗 https://www.ganong.com/check), the family-owned chocolate maker founded in 1873 in St. Stephen, New Brunswick. In the account its head of IT (information technology) published in CSO Online in August 2025 (🔗 https://www.csoonline.com/article/4038381/caught-in-the-cyber-crosshairs-a-candy-manufacturers-2025-ransomware-ordeal.htmlcheck), the plant's networks were cut off from the outside world first. Outside incident responders were on site within hours, reviewing logs and isolated disk images, and the owners, the Ganong family among them, refused to pay. Most systems came back from clean offline backups within about a week; others were rebuilt. Production restarted only after the machinery controllers were checked and found clean, and operations were normal by early March. One to two weeks after the attack, the Play group claimed it publicly. How the attackers first got in has never been published.

KNP Logistics, an English transport company, was not so lucky in 2023. According to the BBC (British Broadcasting Corporation) report of July 21, 2025 (🔗 https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cx2gx28815wocheck), attackers guessed one employee's password, the data could not be recovered, and the firm went under, taking about 700 jobs with it.

On Monday, Nadia Roy asks you: "If that Saturday happened here, how bad would it be?" Kalmia's own documents give you the facts: a flat roastery network; NAS-01 with its only backup disk always connected; MFA (multi-factor authentication) on two Microsoft 365 administrator accounts only; RoastLink reaching ROAST-PC, a Windows 10 machine, with a shared password; no incident response plan; everything, e-mail and Teams included, on Microsoft 365. Class 1 put wholesale sales at about $9,500 per day.

Your tasks

  1. Write the Ganong threat source as it should appear in a Lab 2 catalogue, separating what the public sources state from what they do not.
  2. Walk the typical ransomware chain of Lesson 3 through Kalmia. At which stages do Kalmia's documented weaknesses help the attacker?
  3. Name three measures that helped Ganong recover and are missing at Kalmia today, and one that Kalmia has only in part.
  4. Estimate the wholesale sales at risk with one working week of recovery from a clean backup, and with three working weeks of rebuilding without one. What do these numbers represent, and what do they not?
  5. Explain why segmentation matters on Kalmia's network, and which two controls the KNP contrast points to.

Most possible answers

  1. Stated: ransomware with double extortion, and a public claim by the Play group, reported as the sources state it (Legal Notice (🔗 https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlcheck), section 7.3). Not stated: the initial access, so the root cause stays unknown. The row names a Play-type ransomware group as the source and lists its usual initial access according to CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) advisory AA23-352A (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-352acheck): valid accounts, exposed remote access such as RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) or VPN (virtual private network), and unpatched public-facing services. Any sentence naming Ganong's actual entry point would invent a root cause.
  2. The phishing e-mail and the fake login page work because only the two administrator accounts have MFA, so every staff, loyalty or WordPress account opens with a stolen password; RoastLink's shared password offers another valid way in. The malware stage then meets a flat network, so the attacker reaches NAS-01 freely. Backup deletion is trivial: the only backup disk is connected and gets encrypted with the data. After data is copied out for double extortion, the weekend encryption meets no plan and no backup channel. Also acceptable: adding a DDoS (distributed denial of service) on the checkout page as extra pressure.
  3. Missing: a clean offline backup (the only backup disk stays connected to NAS-01), rapid isolation (flat network, no procedure), and controllers checked before restart (ROAST-PC on Windows 10 with vendor remote access). A backup communication method, tabletop exercises, vendor requirements and strong authentication are missing too. Partial: outside responders within hours (InfoNord's contract covers patching and the helpdesk only), or the ransom decision (Nadia Roy is the risk owner, but there is no written position).
  4. One working week: 5 days × $9,500 ≈ $47,500. Three working weeks: 15 days × $9,500 ≈ $142,500. The numbers show what a usable backup is worth and give Lab 3 a first impact estimate for the ransomware risk. They are not impact ratings, which Lab 3 assigns with the Topic 5 scales, and they leave out the cafés, the web shop and lost recipes.
  5. On today's flat network one infected PC (personal computer) can reach NAS-01, its connected backup disk, ROAST-PC and the cameras, so isolating "the infected part" means unplugging everything. Rules between an office segment and a server and production segment would contain the spread, which is why segmentation is a Lab 4 option. The KNP contrast points to authentication that a guessed password cannot defeat (MFA) and a backup the attacker cannot reach; together with segmentation, they separate recovery in days from closure.

📍 Based on: Chapter 5 — Public Sources, Threat Reports and the Threat Catalogue › 5.1 Public information sources (1/2) — cyberthreat newsletters and security advisories + 5.2 Public information sources (2/2) — CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) and MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge)

The situation

Friday, November 6, 2026, 9:00. Lucas Martin, Kalmia's half-time IT (information technology) coordinator, opens his first one-hour Friday watch slot. No more forwarding everything to Nadia Roy: the Lab 1 inventory is open beside his mailbox, and five items are waiting.

  • Alert AL26-026 (🔗 https://cyber.gc.ca/en/alerts-advisories/al26-026-critical-vulnerabilities-impacting-php-cve-2026-109618-cve-2026-109619check) of the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/encheck), now at Update 2: the PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) flaws CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are exploited in the wild, and CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/check) added them to its KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) catalogue (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalogcheck) on October 26. Fixed in 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12.
  • The hosting provider's reply (fictional), received at 8:40: "Your VPS (virtual private server) runs PHP 8.3.34. Next maintenance window: November 20."
  • The CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) (🔗 https://www.cve.org/check) record of CVE-2026-56155: AD FS (Active Directory Federation Services) and Windows 10 1607/1809 LTSB (Long-Term Servicing Branch) builds, CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) (🔗 https://www.first.org/cvss/check) 3.1 score 7.8 (High), in the KEV catalogue since July 14, 2026.
  • A news article (fictional) forwarded by the Plateau café manager, "Your browser is under attack!", linking to Cyber Centre alert AL26-027 (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/alerts-advisoriescheck) on the Brotli decoder (CVE-2026-111497, in the KEV catalogue since October 27).
  • The record of CVE-2026-10795, published by Wordfence (🔗 https://www.wordfence.com/threat-intel/check): UpdraftPlus 1.26.4 and earlier, fixed in 1.26.5 (free edition), CVSS 3.1 score 8.1. Wordfence's own page later rated it 9.8 and reports mass exploitation attempts; it is not in the KEV catalogue. Émile Gagnon, the freelance web developer, has just confirmed (fictional) that the shop runs UpdraftPlus 1.26.4.

Nadia Roy wants one short list by 10:00: what Kalmia must do, who does it, and by when.

Your tasks

  1. Sort the five items: which are primary public sources, which one is secondary, and which one is not a public source at all? What must Lucas do with the secondary item before deciding anything?
  2. According to the host's reply, is the web shop (A-16) still vulnerable to CVE-2026-109618? Answer the four questions of BOD (Binding Operational Directive) 26-04 (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directivescheck), give the tier in the course's simplified reading, and say whether the November 20 window is acceptable.
  3. CVE-2026-56155 is in the KEV catalogue. Does that make it urgent for Kalmia? Write the decision Lucas records.
  4. CVE-2026-10795 shows two different scores. Give the CVSS band of each, explain why a record and a vendor page can disagree, and say whether the difference changes Kalmia's decision.
  5. Write the threat event for the PHP flaw as one sentence that names the source and the asset and carries both identifiers, the CVE and a technique from MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) (🔗 https://attack.mitre.org/check).

Most possible answers

  1. Primary: alert AL26-026 (a national authority) and the two CVE records, each written by a CNA (CVE Numbering Authority) for its own scope. Secondary: the news article, which reports what others observed. Not a public source: the host's reply, which is Kalmia evidence (a supplier answer) for the evidence column. Before deciding anything on the article, Lucas opens the primary document it links to, AL26-027, reads the product and versions, and matches them against the inventory: the browsers on Kalmia's PCs (personal computers) update themselves, so he confirms their versions, and the server and PHP build of A-16 belong to the host, so he asks the host. Decision for AL26-027: act now, then the catalogue.
  2. Yes. The 8.3 branch is fixed in 8.3.36, and 8.3.34 is older, so A-16 is still vulnerable. The four questions, as the exposure table records them: publicly exposed, yes (Internet-facing web shop); in the KEV, yes (since October 26); automatable, yes; full control, yes. That is the 3-day tier, with a check for an existing compromise because the CVE is in the KEV. November 20 is far too late: Lucas asks the host today, in writing, to move to 8.3.36 or later and to look for signs of compromise. Also acceptable: adding that Update 1 of AL26-026 introduced CVE-2026-115560, which the October 21 releases do not fix, so the host must also apply the interim configuration setting the alert describes.
  3. No. A KEV entry proves that someone, somewhere, exploits the flaw; it says nothing about Kalmia. Kalmia has no AD FS server and no Windows 10 1607/1809 LTSB build, so the record matches nothing in the inventory. Lucas discards it but still writes one line with the date, the title and the reason ("no affected product in the Lab 1 inventory"), so that nobody re-reads it next Friday. The High score and the KEV listing change nothing, because relevance comes from the inventory.
  4. 8.1 is High (7.0–8.9) and 9.8 is Critical (9.0–10.0). The record carries the score the CNA wrote when it published in June; Wordfence's own page later gave 9.8 and reports mass exploitation attempts. Since April 15, 2026 the NVD (National Vulnerability Database) (🔗 https://nvd.nist.gov/check) no longer adds its own analysis to every record, so the CNA's number is often the only one: Lucas notes both numbers and who published each. The decision does not change: exposed, automatable and full control put the flaw in the 3-day tier even without a KEV entry, and the plugin is now confirmed installed. Émile Gagnon updates UpdraftPlus to 1.26.5 or later within three days, and the item goes to the catalogue.
  5. "A cybercriminal doing opportunistic exploitation exploits CVE-2026-109618 in the PHP engine of the web shop (A-16), hosted on a VPS, to run code, through T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application." The CVE ties the row to the vendor's fixed versions (the evidence); the technique ties it to ATT&CK's mitigations and detections for Lab 4. CVE-2026-109619 has the same source, technique, asset and entry point, so it joins the same row as a second piece of evidence instead of creating a new one. Also acceptable: naming the source exactly as in the seed catalogue, TS-02 (cybercriminal, opportunistic exploitation).

📍 Based on: Chapter 5 — Public Sources, Threat Reports and the Threat Catalogue › 5.3 Methodical analysis of public sources — how to read and rate a threat report + 5.4 Building a threat catalogue for an organization

The situation

Tuesday, November 10, 2026, 19:30, the week Lab 2 is due. Lucas Martin forwards you two documents before tomorrow's meeting with Nadia Roy.

Document 1 is a notice (fictional) from InfoNord, Kalmia's MSP (managed service provider), sent to all its client companies and marked AMBER under the TLP (Traffic Light Protocol) (🔗 https://www.first.org/tlp/check). Over the past ten days, staff at three client companies received calls from people posing as "InfoNord technicians" who asked them to approve a Microsoft 365 MFA (multi-factor authentication) prompt "for a security migration". InfoNord saw the calls in its own ticket logs, lists two spoofed caller numbers and recommends a call-back rule: hang up and dial the number in the contract.

Document 2 is a text message (fictional) that a friend sent to Sophie Tremblay, Finance and HR (human resources) Manager. It claims to quote the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/alerts-advisoriescheck): "The Cyber Centre says the ransomware gang behind last month's attacks will almost certainly hit Québec coffee roasters before Christmas. Tell your computer people!" There is no link, no date and no alert number, and Lucas finds nothing matching it among the Cyber Centre's alerts.

Your seed catalogue already holds row T-05. A cybercriminal doing identity theft (TS-04, adversarial, external) phones staff or the help desk, pretending to be IT (information technology), to get a Microsoft 365 account reset or an MFA enrolment. Techniques: T1566.004 Spearphishing Voice and T1621 Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation. Asset: A-17, the Microsoft 365 tenant. Ratings: capability 3, intent 4, targeting 3, facts F06 and F09, relevance High. Evidence: INC-05, W-04 and the help desk run by InfoNord. References: AL26-028 (🔗 https://cyber.gc.ca/en/alerts-advisories/al26-028-ongoing-help-desk-voice-phishing-campaign-targeting-canadian-organizationscheck), rated A2, and Mandiant M-Trends 2026 (🔗 https://cloud.google.com/security/resources/m-trendscheck), rated B1.

Your tasks

  1. Rate Document 1 and Document 2 on the two scales (source reliability A–F, information credibility 1–6) and justify each letter and each digit.
  2. Document 1 is marked TLP:AMBER. What may Lucas do with it, what may he not do, and how are the two phone numbers handled?
  3. Document 2 says "almost certainly" and blames a ransomware gang. Explain how the method treats an estimative word and an attribution, then record the decision for this document.
  4. Does Document 1 create a new catalogue row or strengthen T-05? Justify with the merge-and-split step and say what changes in the row, relevance included.
  5. Tomorrow Nadia Roy will ask why the catalogue does not say how likely each threat is or what it would cost. Prepare a plain-language answer.

Most possible answers

  1. Document 1: InfoNord saw the calls in its own logs, so the account is first-hand, but as a publisher of threat information it is a supplier with a short record: C (fairly reliable). The content is logical and consistent with AL26-028 and M-Trends 2026 on help-desk voice phishing, without independent confirmation of these particular calls: 2 (probably true). Rating C2. Also acceptable: B2, if you argue that InfoNord's help desk works as a response team for its clients. Document 2: an anonymous forwarded message with no record to judge is F; with no date, no reference and no matching agency publication there is nothing to evaluate, so 6. Rating F6.
  2. TLP:AMBER allows sharing inside Kalmia and with Kalmia's clients on a need-to-know basis. Lucas may brief Sophie Tremblay for a staff notice, the café managers and anyone who answers Kalmia's phones. He may not post it on a website or on social media, and he may not pass it to a peer group of roasters, because sharing with a community would need TLP:GREEN. The two spoofed numbers are indicators of compromise: they are copied into the record for whoever checks the call logs, and nobody dials them "to see who answers", which would be interaction with the attackers, prohibited by section 7.3 of the Legal Notice (🔗 https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlcheck).
  3. "Almost certainly" means 90–99 % on the Cyber Centre's estimative scale, never 100 %, and it only means something when an identifiable publisher wrote it. Blaming a named gang is an attribution, which is always an assessment: it is recorded with its author ("publisher X assesses…") and never repeated as a fact. Here question 1 already fails: no publisher, no date, no reference, and the "Cyber Centre says" cannot be found. Nothing matches an asset or a version either. Decision: discard, with one line on the watch list (title, reason, F6) so nobody re-reads it, and a short reply to Sophie: no action; the staff notice on help-desk vishing remains the real priority.
  4. It strengthens T-05. Same source (identity theft by phone, TS-04), same technique (Spearphishing Voice, with the MFA prompt of T1621 already in the row), same asset (A-17) and same entry point (a phone call to staff): the merge rule gives one row with one more piece of evidence, not a new row. The evidence column adds "InfoNord client notice, November 2026: calls posing as InfoNord technicians"; the reference and rating columns add that notice, dated and rated C2, next to AL26-028 (A2). Capability, intent, targeting and the two facts do not change, so relevance stays High (intent ≥ 4 and capability ≥ 3). Also acceptable: a separate row if you argue that impersonating the MSP is a different entry point from impersonating internal IT, provided it fills all fifteen columns and its relevance is computed with the formula.
  5. "For each of our systems, the catalogue says who or what could hurt it, by what means, and on what evidence. For now the rows are ranked by relevance, which tells us where to look first but is not a probability. How likely each threat is and what it would cost come next, in Lab 3. Each row will receive the weaknesses found on the system, a likelihood based on the attacker's intent and targeting, evidence and probability of exploitation (KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalogcheck) and EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) (🔗 https://www.first.org/epss/check) data), our own incidents and exposure facts, and an impact based on the business impact analysis. Likelihood times impact gives a risk score; sorted by that score, the catalogue becomes the risk register, and Lab 4's controls answer the top of it."
C

Part C — 45 multiple-choice questions (MCQs)

Nine questions per chapter. Exactly one option is correct. Decide before you look at the answer, then read the explanation even when you were right: it often contains a second fact worth knowing.

MCQ 1

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.1 Course presentation — objectives, evaluation, tools and the Integrative Project

On the first evening of Lab 1, a classmate wants to leave Kalmia's web shop out of the asset inventory: "It runs on a VPS (virtual private server) at a Montréal hosting company, so it isn't really ours." You apply the three scope questions from Class 1. What should the scope statement say about the web shop?

💡 Hint: Ask who configures and runs the WordPress site day to day, and whether the shop keeps any records about Kalmia's customers.

✅ Answer: B. In scope: Kalmia administers the site, it holds Kalmia's information and its failure would stop sales.

📝 Why this is right: The three questions are control, information and effect on sales. Kalmia administers WordPress and WooCommerce, the shop stores the records of about 2,300 online subscribers, and it brings in about 25% of revenue, so it is in scope and must appear in Lab 1. A is the tempting choice, but "dependency" is for things Kalmia relies on without controlling, such as the payment processor's systems or the providers' data centres. C forgets that subscriber records are Kalmia information even though card numbers are not.

MCQ 2

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.2 Key vocabulary — asset, threat, vulnerability, risk, impact, control

At the roastery, ROAST-PC, NAS-01 and the cameras share one flat network, so any device can reach any other. Nothing is broken inside a single device; the layout of the environment simply makes an attacker's job easier. Which term does NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) (🔗 https://www.nist.govcheck) use for a property like this?

💡 Hint: You want a word that describes the environment itself, not something an attacker does and not a level of risk.

✅ Answer: D. A predisposing condition

📝 Why this is right: NIST calls a property of the environment that makes exploitation easier, without being a defect in itself, a predisposing condition, and the flat network is the classic example. B is tempting because it sounds technical, but an exploit is the use of a vulnerability (or the code that does it): an attacker's action, not a feature of Kalmia's network. A threat event is what happens, such as a phishing e-mail, and an inherent risk is a level of risk before controls.

MCQ 3

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.2 Key vocabulary — asset, threat, vulnerability, risk, impact, control

Four drafts for one row of Kalmia's risk register deal with the cafés' cloud POS (point of sale) service. Which draft is a complete risk statement?

💡 Hint: Hold each draft against the template: Because [ ], [ ] could [ ] [ ], which would [ ]. One draft is a recommendation in disguise.

✅ Answer: A. "Because the café terminals have no offline payment mode, a weekend-rush outage at the cloud POS provider could leave the cafés cash-only, costing about $1,000 in sales per outage."

📝 Why this is right: A names the vulnerability (no offline mode), the threat source and event (a provider outage, a non-adversarial source), the asset (the POS service and café sales) and a business impact in dollars. D is tempting because it is long and sounds professional, but it is a treatment proposal, and solutions belong to the Lab 4 plan, not to the statement. B has no vulnerability and no business impact and announces a level before any rating; C confuses a threat source with a decision about the risk.

MCQ 4

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.3 The CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad

Karim Haddad tells the analyst: "If NAS-01 dies, I can live with re-entering the last four hours of wholesale orders. Not a minute more." Which measure is Karim giving you?

💡 Hint: One time measure says how fast a system must be running again; another says how much recent data the business can afford to lose.

✅ Answer: B. The RPO (recovery point objective) of the order data

📝 Why this is right: The RPO expresses how much recent data the organization can afford to lose, here four hours of orders. C is the trap because the RTO is also counted in hours, but it answers a different question: how quickly NAS-01 must be back in service. Notice what it means for Kalmia: with one nightly backup, up to a full day of orders could be lost, so today's backup does not meet Karim's four-hour RPO.

MCQ 5

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.3 The CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad

An intern filled in this extract of Kalmia's CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) rating table. Which row breaks the high-water mark rule?

Asset Confidentiality Integrity Availability Category
Loyalty member list High Moderate Low High
POS (point of sale) service Moderate Moderate High High
Digital menu boards Low Moderate Low Low
Guest Wi-Fi Low Low Low Low

💡 Hint: The category is not decided by a vote among the three ratings.

✅ Answer: C. Digital menu boards

📝 Why this is right: Under the high-water mark, the category is the highest of the three ratings. The menu boards have integrity at Moderate, so their category must be Moderate, as in Kalmia's real table. B is the trap: two Moderates and one High may look like a "Moderate" asset, but a single High rating makes the POS service High. The guest Wi-Fi is Low everywhere, so Low is right.

MCQ 6

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.4 The risk analysis process, step by step

The analyst adds a new risk to Kalmia's register. The evidence says the event is expected several times a year, and its consequence would be about $80,000 with several days of disruption. With Kalmia's criteria, what are the score, the level and the required action?

💡 Hint: Turn each description into a 1–5 rating with Kalmia's two scales before you compute anything, then look up the band.

✅ Answer: A. 16, High: treatment plan within 30 days, reported to the President

📝 Why this is right: "Several times a year" is likelihood 4 (Likely), and "$50,000 to $250,000 with several days of disruption" is impact 4 (Major), so the score is 4 × 4 = 16, the top of the High band (10–16): a treatment plan within 30 days and a report to the President. B is the trap: 16 feels enormous, but Critical starts at 20. D adds the two ratings instead of multiplying them, and C reads the likelihood as 3.

MCQ 7

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.4 The risk analysis process, step by step

Kalmia's High band ends at 16 and its Critical band starts at 20. A classmate asks: "So what do we do with a risk that scores 18?" What is the best answer?

💡 Hint: List every product you can get by multiplying two whole numbers from 1 to 5.

✅ Answer: D. The case cannot arise: no likelihood × impact product on a 5 × 5 matrix lies between 16 and 20.

📝 Why this is right: A 5 × 5 matrix produces only fourteen scores: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 16, 20 and 25. Nothing gives 17, 18 or 19, so Kalmia's bands leave no real gap. C is tempting because it sounds prudent, but it solves a problem that the arithmetic rules out. For the same reason, you will never see 7, 11 or 13 in a register.

MCQ 8

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.5 Risk analysis frameworks — NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 and ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27005

Kalmia's first look at NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 (🔗 https://www.nist.gov/cyberframeworkcheck) gives the GOVERN Function a score of 1 on the course's 0–4 scale. A student copies this into his report as "Kalmia is at Tier 1 for GOVERN." What is wrong with that sentence?

💡 Hint: Ask who invented the 0–4 scale, and what the Tiers are designed to describe.

✅ Answer: C. The 0–4 score is a course convention; Tiers rate the rigour of the whole program's risk governance.

📝 Why this is right: The 0–4 scale was made up for a first look in class; it is not part of the CSF. Tiers (1 Partial, 2 Risk Informed, 3 Repeatable, 4 Adaptive) describe how rigorous an organization's cybersecurity risk governance and management are, program-wide. B is the trap: it blends the two scales, and Tiers start at 1, not 0. D is wrong because the CSF is voluntary guidance with no certification attached.

MCQ 9

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.6 The case organization of the Integrative Project — Kalmia Coffee Roasters

Lucas Martin collects four proposals for the cafés. Which one clashes with a constraint recorded in Kalmia's context?

💡 Hint: Reread the constraints that frame every recommendation for Kalmia: people, money, season and service.

✅ Answer: C. Make baristas type a long password and approve an MFA (multi-factor authentication) prompt before each card sale.

📝 Why this is right: One of Kalmia's constraints says that no measure may slow down service at the café counter, and a long password plus an MFA approval before every sale would do exactly that during the morning rush. A tempts students who equate "more security" with "slower", but typing an individual PIN takes no longer than typing a shared one, and it restores accountability. B happens away from the counter, and D protects sales during an outage like INC-03.

MCQ 10

📍 Covers: Chapter 2 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 1 › 2.1 Hardware inventory and associated permissions

Lucas Martin's 60-day export of the firewall's DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) sightings contains the row below. When his script looks up the first three bytes of the MAC (Media Access Control) address in the IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) registry (🔗 https://standards.ieee.org/products-programs/regauth/oui/check), it finds no manufacturer. What is the most likely reason?

IP              MAC                HostnameOnNetwork  Source  LastSeen
192.168.10.160  DA:7F:3C:91:05:4E  Galaxy-S23         dhcp    2026-10-22

💡 Hint: Ask who chose these six bytes: the factory that built the network interface, or the phone itself?

✅ Answer: B. The phone joins Wi-Fi with a randomized (private) address that carries no manufacturer prefix

📝 Why this is right: Phones, and many laptops, present a randomized "private" MAC address that changes from one Wi-Fi network to the next. Such an address sets the "locally administered" bit, so its first three bytes are not an OUI (Organizationally Unique Identifier) assigned to a manufacturer, and the device cannot be identified from its address alone. D is the tempting one because DHCP appears in the row, but a lease changes the IP (Internet Protocol) address, never the hardware address; that is exactly why the MAC is normally the best key for matching sources.

MCQ 11

📍 Covers: Chapter 2 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 1 › 2.1 Hardware inventory and associated permissions

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/using-information-technology-asset-management-itam-enhance-cyber-security-itsm10004check) follows every IT (information technology) asset through five life-cycle phases. Which sequence is correct?

💡 Hint: Picture a new laptop for Camille Bouchard: what must happen before the purchase order, and what must happen before IT can patch it?

✅ Answer: D. Planning → procurement and acquisition → deployment → operation and maintenance → retirement and disposal

📝 Why this is right: Planning comes first, then buying, then deployment, when the device gets its asset tag, a named owner and a hardened configuration before its first connection. Operation and maintenance follow, and retirement and disposal close the cycle with storage sanitized according to NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-88 Rev. 2 (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/88/r2/finalcheck). C is tempting because "maintenance" sounds like setup work, but nobody can maintain a device that has not been deployed.

MCQ 12

📍 Covers: Chapter 2 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 1 › 2.2 Software inventory, licences and associated permissions

Microsoft (🔗 https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/end-of-supportcheck) ended support for Windows 10 on October 14, 2025. Suppose Lucas had bought ESU (Extended Security Updates) for Kalmia's three Windows 10 Pro 22H2 computers (ROAST-PC, SALES-LT1 and SALES-LT2) and renewed them every year until the program ends. Using the prices from Lesson 2, what would the three years cost in total, in USD (United States dollars)?

💡 Hint: Work out one computer first, year by year, then multiply by the number of computers.

✅ Answer: A. USD 1,281

📝 Why this is right: ESU costs USD 61 per device in year one and the price doubles every year: 61 + 122 + 244 = 427 per device, and 3 × 427 = 1,281. B (549) is the classic slip, multiplying 61 by three devices and three years as if the price never moved; D (1,098) applies the doubled price of 122 to all three years. In reality Kalmia bought nothing, which is why ROAST-PC and both sales laptops had gone 374 days without a security update on the day of Class 2.

MCQ 13

📍 Covers: Chapter 2 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 1 › 2.2 Software inventory, licences and associated permissions

Kalmia's licence register lists RoastMaster Pro as a per-device licence, with 1 licence bought. It is installed on ROAST-PC, where three roaster operators use it in turn. Karim Haddad now asks Lucas to install it on PC-OPS-01 as well, to plan roasts from his office. If Lucas does this without buying anything, what is the licence status?

💡 Hint: Before you count anything, decide what this metric counts: heads, machines or simultaneous sessions.

✅ Answer: C. Over-deployed by 1, because two computers would run it on one licence

📝 Why this is right: A per-device licence counts distinct computers, whatever the number of people: ROAST-PC plus PC-OPS-01 makes two devices for one licence, so over-deployed by 1. D describes a concurrent licence, a metric Kalmia uses for no product at all, and B counts people, which is the metric of a per-user licence. Lucas should buy a second licence or keep RoastMaster Pro on ROAST-PC only.

MCQ 14

📍 Covers: Chapter 2 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 1 › 2.2 Software inventory, licences and associated permissions

In December 2021, Log4Shell, CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) entry CVE-2021-44228, hit Log4j, a free logging library built into thousands of Java applications. The first step in the guidance of CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/news/apache-log4j-vulnerability-guidancecheck) was to find which programs contained it. Which document lists the components inside one software product and would have answered that question fastest?

💡 Hint: You need a list that goes inside the product, below the level of the name printed on the box.

✅ Answer: D. A software bill of materials for each product

📝 Why this is right: An SBOM (software bill of materials) names every component a product is built from, so it shows at once whether Log4j is in there; CISA describes its elements on its SBOM page (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/topics/information-communications-technology-supply-chain-security/sbomcheck). A is tempting because the register lists products, but it stops at the product name: it says "RoastMaster Pro", not which libraries RoastMaster Pro carries. MCQ 15

📍 Covers: Chapter 2 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 1 › 2.3 Asset classification, ownership and criticality

In Nadia Roy's classification workshop, D-01 (loyalty member records of 18,500 people, owner Nadia Roy) was rated C = High, I = Moderate, A = Low, and its label stayed Confidential. A classmate objects: "That's a contradiction. High confidentiality should mean Restricted." What is the best reply?

💡 Hint: Check what triggers Restricted in Kalmia's minimum rules, then ask why D-01's confidentiality rating is so high.

✅ Answer: A. No contradiction: the type of data sets the label, while the C rating measures how badly a disclosure would hurt

📝 Why this is right: Kalmia's minimum labels depend on what the data is: a SIN (Social Insurance Number), bank details or health data push a file to Restricted, while ordinary customer data such as loyalty records only needs Confidential. The C rating is a FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 199 (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/199/finalcheck) impact level, and 18,500 records make a disclosure severe, hence High. B mixes up the two scales; C is wrong twice, since the high-water mark takes the highest rating (D-01's category is High) and the category never lowers a label.

MCQ 16

📍 Covers: Chapter 2 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 1 › 2.3 Asset classification, ownership and criticality

During the BIA (business impact analysis), Karim Haddad states that the daily order and delivery plan (D-06) cannot be unavailable for more than 4 hours. Lucas proposes a recovery plan: restore it from the nightly backup within 6 hours of an outage. What is wrong with this plan?

💡 Hint: Give each number in the scenario its BIA name, then recall which of the two must always fit inside the other.

✅ Answer: C. The RTO (recovery time objective) exceeds the MTD (maximum tolerable downtime)

📝 Why this is right: Karim's 4 hours is the MTD, the longest interruption the business can accept; Lucas's 6 hours is the RTO, the time to restore. An RTO must never exceed the MTD, so the plan fails on paper before anyone tests it. D is tempting but backwards: the tier comes from the business's tolerance (4 hours or less is Tier 1), not from what the current backup can deliver. B gets the direction wrong: a nightly backup means up to 24 hours of lost data, a long RPO that deserves its own review.

MCQ 17

📍 Covers: Chapter 2 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 1 › 2.4 Hands-on: building an asset inventory with a template and a network scanner (Nmap (Network Mapper))

During the authorized scan of the lab replica with Nmap (Network Mapper) (🔗 https://nmap.org/check), the service scan printed this extract for THERMO-HQ. What does it tell you about the thermostat?

Nmap scan report for 192.168.10.130
Host is up.
All 100 scanned ports on 192.168.10.130 are in ignored states.
Not shown: 100 closed tcp ports (reset)
MAC Address: 18:B4:30:9C:00:25 (Nest Labs)

💡 Hint: A closed port is an answer, not a silence. Who sent the reset?

✅ Answer: B. It is up and reachable, but no service listens on any of the 100 ports scanned

📝 Why this is right: Closed means the host answered, here with a TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) reset, but nothing listens on that port; the inventory records THERMO-HQ as reachable with no service in the top 100. A describes filtered, the result of the six office computers whose firewalls dropped the probes. C is impossible: a switched-off device answers nothing and would not even be listed as up. And "no open port" does not mean "no risk": THERMO-HQ is managed from a personal account in the vendor's cloud application, which was its permission finding.

MCQ 18

📍 Covers: Chapter 2 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 1 › 2.4 Hands-on: building an asset inventory with a template and a network scanner (Nmap (Network Mapper))

A student in the lab replica forgets sudo and runs the discovery step of Lesson 4 as an ordinary user, with Nmap (Network Mapper) (🔗 https://nmap.org/check) writing XML (Extensible Markup Language):

nmap -sn -n -T3 -oX discovery.xml 192.168.10.0/24

The scan completes, but the converter, which matches hosts with Lucas's register by MAC (Media Access Control) address, cannot match a single recorded device. What went wrong?

💡 Hint: Think about what discovery on a local Ethernet network returns when it runs with the right privileges, and what disappears without them.

✅ Answer: D. As an ordinary user, Nmap cannot send ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) requests, so no MAC address is recorded

📝 Why this is right: Only a privileged Nmap sends ARP requests on the local network; without sudo it can only attempt TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) connections on ports 80 and 443, which reveal no MAC address, the very key the converter uses. A confuses discovery with port scanning: -sn performs no port scan at all. B and C do not depend on privileges, since -n and -oX work for any user. Run discovery with sudo, inside the authorization, and the MAC column fills up.

MCQ 19

📍 Covers: Chapter 3 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 2 › 3.1 Data and services critical to the organization's operations

Nadia Roy gave these ratings for the loyalty program (P-07); each figure is the highest of the four impact categories at that outage duration, and Kalmia's threshold is 3 (serious). She needs a WRT (work recovery time) of 4 hours. What are the RTO (recovery time objective) and the tier of P-07?

P-07 Loyalty program - highest rating per outage duration
1h=1  2h=1  4h=1  8h=1  24h=1  72h=2  168h=3

💡 Hint: Find the first duration that reaches the threshold, think about which direction the work recovery time moves the number, then compare with the Class 2 tier limits.

✅ Answer: B. RTO 164 h, Tier 4

📝 Why this is right: The MTD (maximum tolerable downtime) is the shortest duration that reaches 3: 168 hours, one week. The RTO is MTD − WRT = 168 − 4 = 164 hours, and an MTD longer than 72 hours puts the process in Tier 4. D is the tempting trap: it stops at 72 hours because the rating changes there, but a 2 is moderate, below Kalmia's threshold. C has the right RTO with the wrong tier, and A adds the WRT instead of subtracting it.

MCQ 20

📍 Covers: Chapter 3 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 2 › 3.1 Data and services critical to the organization's operations

At 7:30 a.m., Julie Nguyen opens the daily order and delivery plan, stored on NAS-01, in a spreadsheet on the warehouse computer PC-WHS-01 and starts adding today's deliveries. In the critical data inventory, which state describes the plan while it is open in her spreadsheet?

💡 Hint: The inventory records three states for each type of critical data. Ask what is happening to the data at that exact moment.

✅ Answer: C. In use

📝 Why this is right: Data open in an application is in use. The same plan is also at rest on the disks of NAS-01 and briefly in transit while it crosses the network to the computer; the inventory records where the data is found in each of the three states. A is the tempting answer because the file "lives" on NAS-01, but the question asks about the copy open in the spreadsheet. "In backup" is not one of the three states at all.

MCQ 21

📍 Covers: Chapter 3 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 2 › 3.1 Data and services critical to the organization's operations

The dependency test of Kalmia's business impact analysis prints this line for the web shop process. What should the analyst do next?

[DEP] P-02 Payment gateway (supplier service): restore time unknown -> ASK-SUPPLIER

💡 Hint: Ask yourself which figure is missing, and who could actually know it.

✅ Answer: A. Read the service level agreement in the contract, or ask the supplier directly

📝 Why this is right: Without a restore time, nobody can test whether the gateway would come back within the 3-hour RTO (recovery time objective) of the web shop, so the figure must come from the contract or from the supplier. Kalmia had two such cases: the cafés' payment processor and the web shop's payment gateway. C is tempting, yet critical services are precisely the outside services a process depends on. D mixes up the tests: a data gap compares a copy interval with the RPO (recovery point objective), and the missing figure here is a restore time.

MCQ 22

📍 Covers: Chapter 3 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 2 › 3.2 Physical and logical representation of the infrastructure (network diagrams)

The network map check prints this line for the Plateau café, whose staff subnet 192.168.20.0/24 receives its addresses from a DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) server. Why does this finding matter?

[CHECK][MEDIUM] STATIC-IN-DHCP PRN-CAF-PLA 192.168.20.150: fixed address inside the DHCP range 192.168.20.100-192.168.20.199

💡 Hint: Compare the printer's fixed address with the range that the café router hands out on its own.

✅ Answer: B. The DHCP server could lease .150 to another device, causing a conflict

📝 Why this is right: The DHCP server hands out .100 to .199 automatically, so it can give .150 to another device; both then lose connectivity on and off. The fix is to move the printer to a fixed address outside the range and correct the record. A is the tempting one, but the guest network is 192.168.21.0/24 and is isolated; 192.168.20.x is the staff subnet. C fails because 192.168.x.x addresses are private, and D describes a different check, UNTAGGED.

MCQ 23

📍 Covers: Chapter 3 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 2 › 3.2 Physical and logical representation of the infrastructure (network diagrams)

Public addresses in teaching diagrams, Kalmia's included, come from the blocks that RFC (Request for Comments, the numbered documents that define Internet standards) 5737 (🔗 https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc5737/check) reserves for documentation. Which address could NOT be one of Kalmia's public addresses on a course diagram?

💡 Hint: Write down the three documentation blocks, then compare each address with them octet by octet.

✅ Answer: D. 192.168.10.25

📝 Why this is right: RFC 5737 reserves 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24 and 203.0.113.0/24, and A, B and C fall inside them. 192.168.10.25 is a private address in Kalmia's head office subnet, 192.168.10.0/24, so it cannot serve as a public address at all. A is the tempting option: it starts with 192 and looks private, but 192.0.2.0/24 is the first documentation block.

MCQ 24

📍 Covers: Chapter 3 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 2 › 3.3 Documenting who has access to what (permissions map)

Olivier Lefebvre (olefebvre), a sales representative, belongs only to the group sales, and his role needs no access to Finance. Each row below is an ACE (access control entry) of the Finance share, labelled Confidential. What does the permissions map show for him on Finance?

Trustee Right Inherited
group finance Modify No
group management ReadAndExecute No
account olefebvre ReadAndExecute No
group administrators FullControl Yes

💡 Hint: An entry applies when it names Everyone, one of the account's groups, or the account itself.

✅ Answer: C. Read, with two findings: EXCESS and DIRECT-ACE

📝 Why this is right: The third entry names his own account, so it applies, and ReadAndExecute counts as Read. His role needs none, so the map reports EXCESS (MEDIUM, because Finance is Confidential), and since the right was given to a person rather than a group, it also reports DIRECT-ACE (MEDIUM). A is the tempting answer: the group entries indeed do not apply, but an entry naming the account itself does. B is wrong because the administrators entry applies only to members of that group, and D describes the opposite problem, access lower than the job needs.

MCQ 25

📍 Covers: Chapter 3 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 2 › 3.3 Documenting who has access to what (permissions map)

On a lab server, Lucas Martin creates a share for the finance team. The share permissions give Everyone Read; the NTFS (New Technology File System, the Windows file system) permissions of the folder give the group finance Modify. Marc Gauthier, a member of finance, opens the folder over the network from his workstation. What can he do?

💡 Hint: Picture two doors in a row, the share and then the folder. Which one limits him?

✅ Answer: A. Read only: over the network, the more restrictive layer applies

📝 Why this is right: Over the network, Windows checks both the share permissions (read with Get-SmbShareAccess) and the NTFS ACL (access control list) of the folder (read with Get-Acl or icacls), and the more restrictive result applies: Read. B is the classic trap, since NTFS does not override the share; both are checked. C is wrong twice: allowed entries add up within one layer, and even then Read plus Modify gives Modify, never Full Control.

MCQ 26

📍 Covers: Chapter 3 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 2 › 3.3 Documenting who has access to what (permissions map)

Kalmia's first access review of the Scans share involves the four steps below. In which order should they happen?

Step Action
P Lucas Martin removes the Everyone entry on NAS-01
Q The analyst prepares the map of the share and its findings
R Sophie Tremblay chooses, for each line, whether to keep, reduce or remove the access
S The data owners agree the role matrix that says what each job needs

💡 Hint: Ask what the analyst needs before he can call anything an excess, and who has the last word before anything changes on the server.

✅ Answer: D. S → Q → R → P

📝 Why this is right: The role matrix comes first, because an EXCESS or MISSING finding only exists by comparison with it. The analyst then prepares the map, the data owner decides, and the custodian applies the decision. C puts the role matrix after the map, which leaves the analyst nothing to compare with.

Your evidence shows that the actor goes after companies of Kalmia's type and sector, but nothing shows that it has singled out Kalmia or its key people. Which targeting value fits?

✅ Answer: C. 3 (Moderate)

Threat source Capability Intent Targeting Exposure match Relevance
TS-E3 State-sponsored groups 5 1 1 2 of 2 Moderate

Which reading of this row is correct?

💡 Hint: Read capability and intent together, then recall what "relevance" is used for in Lab 2 and when likelihood gets rated.

✅ Answer: A. A highly capable actor with almost no interest in Kalmia itself, kept for the relay and supplier routes

MCQ 30

📍 Covers: Chapter 4 — Identifying Threats, Part 1 › 4.2 Internal threats: malicious insiders, negligent users, third parties and suppliers

INC-04: on September 18 at 21:47, the loyalty-platform administrator account of a supervisor who had left on July 15 exported 18,500 member records. Under Québec's private-sector privacy act (🔗 https://www.legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca/en/document/cs/P-39.1check), as amended by Law 25, what does Kalmia owe?

💡 Hint: The obligation is triggered by what happened to personal information, not by knowing who did it.

✅ Answer: D. An entry in its confidentiality-incident register and, where serious injury is a risk, notice to the regulator and the affected people

📝 Why this is right: Personal information left the company through an account that should have been disabled, which makes INC-04 a confidentiality incident. The act makes Kalmia log it in its incident register and, when serious injury is a risk, inform the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec) (🔗 https://www.cai.gouv.qc.ca/check) and the affected members. B is tempting, but the obligation does not wait for a culprit, and the analyst never names one anyway. A confuses a valid account with authorized use.

MCQ 31

📍 Covers: Chapter 4 — Identifying Threats, Part 1 › 4.2 Internal threats: malicious insiders, negligent users, third parties and suppliers

Each Kalmia café shares one manager PIN (personal identification number) among its shift leads. In Lab 2 you keep threats, vulnerabilities and assets apart. How should this shared PIN be treated?

💡 Hint: Ask whether the PIN does anything on its own, or whether someone has to use it.

✅ Answer: B. As a weakness that insiders can exploit and that removes accountability

📝 Why this is right: A shared PIN does nothing by itself. It is a weakness, a negligent practice, that a malicious or careless insider can use, and it makes it impossible to tie an action such as nine refunds in forty minutes to one person; the control idea is individual PINs. D is tempting, but a collusive threat means an insider deliberately working with an external actor, and colleagues sharing a code is not that.

MCQ 32

📍 Covers: Chapter 4 — Identifying Threats, Part 1 › 4.3 Common attack methods: malware, ransomware, phishing and social engineering, DoS (Denial of Service), credential theft

Lab 2 keeps threat sources and threat events in separate columns. Which entry does NOT belong in the threat event column?

💡 Hint: Recall the three words Lesson 3 keeps apart: the actor, the method and the tool.

✅ Answer: C. A ransomware group that rents its malware to affiliates

📝 Why this is right: A threat event is a method applied to an asset, and A, B and D all do that (NAS-01, the WordPress administrator accounts, the checkout page). C describes a threat source, the actor and its ransomware-as-a-service business model, so it goes in the threat source column. B can look like a tool, but password spraying is a method; the tool would be the script or botnet that runs it.

📍 Covers: Chapter 4 — Identifying Threats, Part 1 › 4.3 Common attack methods: malware, ransomware, phishing and social engineering, DoS (Denial of Service), credential theft

A classmate's notes quote the Verizon 2025 DBIR (Data Breach Investigations Report) (🔗 https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/reports/2025-dbir-data-breach-investigations-report.pdfcheck) as the Class 4 hand-out reports it. Which line is correct?

💡 Hint: Match each percentage to its population before judging it: all breaches, small and medium-sized businesses, large organizations, or ransomware victims.

✅ Answer: D. 64% of ransomware victims did not pay

📝 Why this is right: The report says 64% of ransomware victims did not pay, with a median payment of $115,000. A and C swap populations: 88% is the share at small and medium-sized businesses, 39% at large organizations, and 44% across all breaches analyzed. B borrows the human-element figure (about 60%); third-party involvement was 30%.

MCQ 34

📍 Covers: Chapter 4 — Identifying Threats, Part 1 › 4.3 Common attack methods: malware, ransomware, phishing and social engineering, DoS (Denial of Service), credential theft

Put these steps of a typical ransomware attack on a small company in the order Lesson 3 gives:

1  The attacker deletes the backups it can reach
2  The stolen password opens the mailbox and the VPN
3  A fake Microsoft 365 page collects the password
4  Files are encrypted on a Saturday night
5  The attacker installs tools and finds the file server

💡 Hint: Ask what each step needs from the step before it; encryption is saved for the end for a reason.

✅ Answer: A. 3, 2, 5, 1, 4

📝 Why this is right: The fake page steals the password (credential theft), which then gets the attacker into the mailbox and the VPN (virtual private network); next it sets up its tools and locates the file server (malware), removes the backups within reach, and only then encrypts, at a time when nobody reacts. D is tempting, but the attacker cannot delete backups it has not found yet. Encryption comes last because wiping the backups first is what gives the ransom note its weight.

MCQ 35

📍 Covers: Chapter 4 — Identifying Threats, Part 1 › 4.4 Case study: a recent ransomware attack on a small manufacturer

Class 1 put Kalmia's wholesale sales at about $9,500 per day. Lesson 4 compares two recovery scenarios using working days × daily wholesale sales. How much wholesale revenue is at risk in the scenario with three working weeks of rebuilding and no usable backup?

💡 Hint: Count working days, not calendar days.

✅ Answer: C. About $142,500

📝 Why this is right: Three working weeks are 15 working days, and 15 × $9,500 = $142,500. B (21 × $9,500) and D (7 × $9,500) count calendar days, and A is the one-week scenario with a clean backup (5 × $9,500). Both scenarios are illustrations for discussion, not impact ratings, which Lab 3 assigns with the Topic 5 scales.

MCQ 37

MCQ 38

📍 Covers: Chapter 5 — Public Sources, Threat Reports and the Threat Catalogue › 5.1 Public information sources (1/2) — cyberthreat newsletters and security advisories

Lucas drafted this watch-list line for an alert of the Cyber Centre (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/encheck). Which field required on every kept line is missing?

Date ......... 2026-10-28
Source ....... Cyber Centre alert AL26-028
Item ......... ongoing help-desk voice phishing campaign
Asset ........ A-17 Microsoft 365 tenant (help desk run by InfoNord)
Severity ..... active campaign (no score published)
Action ....... staff notice; call-back rule agreed with InfoNord
Decision ..... act now + catalogue
Deadline ..... 2026-11-09

💡 Hint: List the eight fields of the record step and tick them off, one by one, against the line.

✅ Answer: B. The owner who carries out the action
