A campaign alert carries no CVSS (🔗 https://www.first.org/cvss/check) score and no CVE (🔗 https://www.cve.org/check) identifier, which is why the severity field reads "active campaign". The employee's name adds nothing and breaks the habit of describing accounts and processes rather than people.

MCQ 39

📍 Covers: Chapter 5 — Public Sources, Threat Reports and the Threat Catalogue › 5.2 Public information sources (2/2) — CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) and MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge)

Émile Gagnon reports that Kalmia's web shop (A-16) runs the free edition of UpdraftPlus, version 1.26.4. The CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) (🔗 https://www.cve.org/check) record below was published by Wordfence (🔗 https://www.wordfence.com/threat-intel/check) as a CNA (CVE Numbering Authority).

CVE-2026-10795   CNA: Wordfence   Published: 2026-06-11
Affected   UpdraftPlus WP Backup plugin <= 1.26.4 (free)
Fixed      1.26.5 (free) / 2.26.5 (premium)
Metrics    CVSS 3.1 base score 8.1 (High)
Problem    CWE-347
KEV        not listed

Which conclusion is correct?

💡 Hint: Compare the installed version with the affected range first; then ask what each score or status really measures.

✅ Answer: A. The plugin is affected, and the fix is to move the free edition to 1.26.5 or later

📝 Why this is right: Version 1.26.4 sits inside the affected range (1.26.4 and earlier), and the CNA's record names 1.26.5 as the fixed free version. CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) (🔗 https://www.first.org/cvss/check) measures severity, not relevance: 8.1 is High, and on an Internet-exposed web shop with automatable exploitation and full control the course puts this flaw in the 3-day tier even without a KEV (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalogcheck) entry. A missing KEV listing means CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/check) has no confirmed exploitation on file, not that nobody is trying; Wordfence's own page later reported mass exploitation attempts. And since April 15, 2026 the NVD (🔗 https://nvd.nist.gov/check) enriches records by priority, so the CNA's record is often all there is, and it is enough to act on.

MCQ 40

📍 Covers: Chapter 5 — Public Sources, Threat Reports and the Threat Catalogue › 5.2 Public information sources (2/2) — CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) and MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge)

The course uses a simplified reading of BOD (Binding Operational Directive) 26-04 (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directivescheck), issued by CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/check), to turn four yes/no answers into a deadline. A vulnerability on an internal system gives these answers:

BOD 26-04 question Answer
Is the asset publicly exposed? No
Is the CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) (🔗 https://www.cve.org/check) in the KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalogcheck) catalogue? Yes
Is exploitation automatable? No
Does it give full control of the system? No

Which remediation tier applies?

💡 Hint: Check exactly which combination the shortest tier requires before you settle on it, then read the next line of the rule.

✅ Answer: B. 14 days

📝 Why this is right: In the course's reading, the 3-day tier needs a KEV entry together with full control, or an exposed asset with automatable exploitation and full control. Here the only "yes" is the KEV entry, so the case falls under "any other combination with a KEV entry": 14 days. A is the tempting answer because "a KEV entry is fixed first"; that rule sets the order of the work, while the deadline depends on the other three answers. The 60-day tier only catches combinations with at least one "yes" that none of the earlier lines covers.

MCQ 41

📍 Covers: Chapter 5 — Public Sources, Threat Reports and the Threat Catalogue › 5.2 Public information sources (2/2) — CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) and MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge)

Lab 2 asks you to attach a technique from MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) (🔗 https://attack.mitre.org/check) to each adversarial event in Kalmia's catalogue. Which pairing of a Kalmia fact with its technique is correct?

💡 Hint: For each fact, ask what the attacker is actually doing at that moment, then check whether the technique's name describes that action.

✅ Answer: D. INC-05, the "schedule changed" text messages sent to café staff: T1566.002 Spearphishing Link

📝 Why this is right: INC-05 is a link sent by text message that leads staff to type their Microsoft 365 credentials: T1566.002 Spearphishing Link, under the Initial Access tactic. INC-02 is payment fraud, T1657 Financial Theft; RoastLink is T1133 External Remote Services; and the always-connected backup disk is a weakness that makes T1486 catastrophic, not something attacked through T1190. A tempts because INC-02 and ransomware both cost money, but T1486 describes encryption, and nothing was encrypted in INC-02.

MCQ 42

📍 Covers: Chapter 5 — Public Sources, Threat Reports and the Threat Catalogue › 5.3 Methodical analysis of public sources — how to read and rate a threat report

An analyst applies the seven-question method to a new threat report. In what order must these four questions be answered?

Label Question
P How does the threat act?
Q Who publishes it, when, and under which marking?
R Does it apply to us?
S What is our decision, and where is it recorded?

💡 Hint: The first three questions are about the document, the next two about the organization, the last two about the decision.

✅ Answer: D. Q, R, P, S

📝 Why this is right: The fixed order is 1 publisher, date and marking; 2 subject; 3 evidence and ratings; 4 does it apply to us; 5 how the threat acts, with ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) (🔗 https://attack.mitre.org/check) identifiers and indicators; 6 recommendations and owner; 7 decision and record. Q is question 1, R question 4, P question 5 and S question 7. A swaps 4 and 5; it tempts because behaviour sounds like part of the evidence, but the method checks the match with Kalmia's assets before translating the behaviour into identifiers.

MCQ 43

📍 Covers: Chapter 5 — Public Sources, Threat Reports and the Threat Catalogue › 5.3 Methodical analysis of public sources — how to read and rate a threat report

An assessment from the Cyber Centre (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/encheck) reads: "We assess, with moderate confidence, that exploitation of this vulnerability is very unlikely in the coming months." How should you read this sentence?

💡 Hint: The estimative word and the confidence level answer two different questions. Find the word on the Cyber Centre's scale first.

✅ Answer: A. Roughly a 10–24 % probability, and "moderate" grades how solid the evidence and reasoning behind it are

📝 Why this is right: On the Cyber Centre's estimative scale, "very unlikely" means about 10–24 %. The confidence level (low, moderate, high) is not a second probability: it grades the sources and reasoning, following ODNI (Office of the Director of National Intelligence) Intelligence Community Directive 203 (🔗 https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD%20203%20Analytic%20Standards.pdfcheck). B mixes the two scales, and 1–9 % is "almost no chance". "We assess" marks an assessment, so the sentence is recorded with its author and its words, never as an observation.

MCQ 44

📍 Covers: Chapter 5 — Public Sources, Threat Reports and the Threat Catalogue › 5.4 Building a threat catalogue for an organization

Here is a row from Kalmia's seed catalogue with its relevance hidden.

T-08 | State-sponsored group | Adversarial | External
Compromises the café routers to use them as relay infrastructure | T1584.008 | A-02
Capability 5 · Intent 1 · Targeting 1 | Exposure facts matched: 1 (F10)
Relevance: ?

Using the course formula, what is the relevance of this row?

💡 Hint: Test the High condition first, then the Moderate one, using only intent, capability and the number of facts.

✅ Answer: C. Low, because neither the High nor the Moderate condition is met

📝 Why this is right: High needs intent ≥ 4 with capability ≥ 3, or at least three facts: intent is 1 and only one fact is matched. Moderate needs intent ≥ 3 or at least two facts: neither holds, so the row is Low, as in the seed catalogue. A is the classic trap: capability alone never makes a row High, because a group that could act but has no intent toward Kalmia ranks low. Relevance is computed now from these numbers; likelihood is a separate Lab 3 rating.

D

Part D — 35 multiple-select questions (MSQs)

Seven questions per chapter, each with at least six options. The number in round brackets next to each question tells you how many options are correct. Give yourself the point only when you found all the correct options and none of the wrong ones.

MSQ 1

(3 correct answers)

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.2 Key vocabulary — asset, threat, vulnerability, risk, impact, control

Which of these measures at Kalmia are classified correctly, both by nature and by function? (3 correct answers)

💡 Hint: Nature asks what the measure is made of (a rule, a technology, a physical barrier); function asks when it acts: before the event, by revealing it, or after the damage.

✅ Answers: A, C, E

📝 Why these are right: A: a backup is a technology, and it acts after the damage by restoring data, even if this one sits within reach of ransomware. C: a lock is a physical barrier that stops the event before it happens. E: a procedure is administrative, and removing access on the last day stops a former employee before any misuse. Why the others are wrong: B — training is administrative, not technical; D — alerts reveal events, so the function is detective, and an unread mailbox makes the control weak, not corrective; F — backups restore operations, so they are corrective; G — MFA is a technical, preventive control.

MSQ 2

(3 correct answers)

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.3 The CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad

Kalmia keeps a short incident notebook. Here are its five entries for 2026, in short form.

Entry Date What was written
INC-01 March 14 Web shop down six hours after a failed plugin update; restored from the host's backup
INC-02 June 9 Look-alike e-mail from the "importer"; bank account changed in Sage 50; $18,400 payment stopped by a call-back
INC-03 August 22 Cloud POS (point of sale) service refused cards in all three cafés, 08:05 to 10:20; about $1,000 lost
INC-04 September 18 Former shift supervisor exported the 18,500 loyalty records; found October 2
INC-05 September Texts to baristas: "your schedule changed, log in here"; no compromise known

Which statements about these entries are correct? (3 correct answers)

💡 Hint: Name the property from what happened to the information (disclosed, altered, unusable), not from the way the attacker got in.

✅ Answers: B, D, F

📝 Why these are right: B: the supplier's bank details were changed without authorization, which is unauthorized modification whether or not money moved. D: that is exactly the reasoning behind the Moderate availability rating of the August outage. F: the shop could not be used for six hours, and the failed update damaged site files. Why the others are wrong: A — receiving a phishing text is a threat event; nothing was disclosed, altered or made unusable yet; C — the records were copied, not removed, so Kalmia still had them: this is confidentiality, rated High, and a confidentiality incident under Québec's private-sector privacy law (🔗 https://www.legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca/en/document/cs/p-39.1check); E — INC-02 and INC-05 both began with a deceptive message, yet one is integrity and the other violated nothing.

MSQ 3

(4 correct answers)

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.4 The risk analysis process, step by step

Which statements match the risk criteria that Nadia Roy approved before Kalmia's analysis started? (4 correct answers)

💡 Hint: Picture the two scales and the four bands side by side, and check every dollar figure and every deadline.

✅ Answers: A, D, E, G

📝 Why these are right: A: "Possible, about once a year" is rating 3. D: the Medium rule is to treat within the quarter or accept with the risk owner's written justification. E: Low means accept and monitor, with a yearly review. G: Critical means immediate action within 7 days, decided by the President in person. Why the others are wrong: B — $10,000 to $50,000 is Moderate (3), while Major (4) runs from $50,000 to $250,000; C — "within the quarter" is the Medium rule, and a High risk needs a plan within 30 days and a report to the President; F — the High band starts at 10, so a score of 10 is already High.

MSQ 4

(2 correct answers)

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.4 The risk analysis process, step by step

R7 (guest Wi-Fi abused for illegal downloads, 2 × 1 = 2, Low) comes up at a café managers' meeting. Six responses are on the table, each with a label. Which responses carry the correct treatment option? (2 correct answers)

💡 Hint: For each response ask whether it lowers likelihood or impact, shares the consequences, stops the activity, or keeps the risk knowingly.

✅ Answers: B, F

📝 Why these are right: B: keeping the risk knowingly, with a yearly review, is acceptance, and it is exactly what Kalmia's Low rule expects. F: a terms-of-use notice and filtering lower the likelihood of misuse, so they reduce the risk. Why the others are wrong: A — stopping the activity that creates the risk is avoidance, not transfer; C — insurance shares the financial consequences, which is transfer; D — a warning sign may discourage misuse, which would reduce the risk, but nothing is avoided; E — pushing the consequences onto another party by contract is transfer.

MSQ 5

(2 correct answers)

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.5 Risk analysis frameworks — NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 and ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27005

Which statements about ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27005:2022 (🔗 https://www.iso.org/standard/80585.htmlcheck) are correct? (2 correct answers)

💡 Hint: Sort the statements into three piles: what the document is, what its activities are called, and who has the authority to decide.

✅ Answers: C, F

📝 Why these are right: C: in ISO terms, risk assessment covers identification, analysis and evaluation. F: these two activities run through context establishment, identification, analysis, evaluation and treatment. Why the others are wrong: A — 27005 is guidance; the certifiable standard is ISO/IEC 27001 (🔗 https://www.iso.org/standard/27001check), which 27005 supports; B — the analysis may be qualitative, semi-quantitative or quantitative; D — identification can be event-based or asset-based, or both; E — the risk owners accept residual risk, never the analyst; G — the process is iterative: a treatment changes the context and the analysis starts again.

MSQ 6

(4 correct answers)

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.5 Risk analysis frameworks — NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 and ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27005

Below is Kalmia's first look at the six Functions of NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 (🔗 https://www.nist.gov/cyberframeworkcheck), scored on the course's 0–4 scale.

Function Current Target (end of 2027)
GOVERN 1 3
IDENTIFY 1 3
PROTECT 2 3
DETECT 1 2
RESPOND 1 3
RECOVER 1 3

Which conclusions are correct? (4 correct answers)

💡 Hint: Work out the gap for every row before you read the options.

✅ Answers: B, C, D, G

📝 Why these are right: B: 3 − 1 = 2. C: GOVERN, IDENTIFY, RESPOND and RECOVER all show 2 points, the largest gap. D: DETECT goes from 1 to a target of only 2. G: the IDENTIFY gaps (a list of computers kept only by the MSP (managed service provider), no data inventory, no risk assessment ever done) are the work of Labs 1, 2 and 3. Why the others are wrong: A — PROTECT has the highest current score (2) and one of the smallest gaps (1), and buying products is precisely what Kalmia already did; E — the gap is target minus current; F — every organization chooses and prioritizes its own Target Profile.

MSQ 7

(3 correct answers)

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.3 The CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad + 1.6 The case organization of the Integrative Project — Kalmia Coffee Roasters

Nadia Roy's four priorities are part of Kalmia's context. Which pairings of a priority with the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) property it mainly protects are correct? (3 correct answers)

💡 Hint: For each quote, ask what would hurt the owner most: someone reading the information, someone changing it, or nobody being able to use it.

✅ Answers: A, B, E

📝 Why these are right: A: a missed delivery means planning and ordering were unusable when needed. B: the holiday shop must stay up, and its checkout must not be tampered with, as R2 shows. E: customers' information calls for confidentiality, and Québec's private-sector law (🔗 https://www.legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca/en/document/cs/p-39.1check) adds duties such as the register of confidentiality incidents. Why the others are wrong: C — the worry is who can read members' data, not uptime; D — a recipe book that leaks or gets altered is the real danger, so the profiles call for confidentiality and integrity; F — Kalmia stores no card numbers: the processor and the POS (point of sale) provider hold them, and Kalmia only ever sees tokens.

MSQ 8

(3 correct answers)

📍 Covers: Chapter 2 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 1 › 2.1 Hardware inventory and associated permissions

Lucas Martin is completing the Hardware sheet of the Lab 1 template. Following CIS (Center for Internet Security) Safeguard 1.1 (🔗 https://www.cisecurity.org/controls/inventory-and-control-of-enterprise-assetscheck) and Lesson 1, which items must appear on that sheet? (3 correct answers)

💡 Hint: For each item, ask two questions: is it a device, and does it handle Kalmia's information or connect to its network? Ownership is not one of the questions.

✅ Answers: A, C, E

📝 Why these are right: A: a virtual machine or cloud server is a hardware asset even though nobody at Kalmia can touch it. C: the phone is not Kalmia's property, but it joins Kalmia's network regularly, so the inventory has to show it, at the very least as a known visitor. E: a device without a network interface is still hardware; it is the "not network-visible" case, checked physically. Why the others are wrong: B — a program belongs on the Software sheet; D — information goes to the Classification sheet, with its owner, label and tier; F — licences belong to the Software and Licence check sheets.

MSQ 9

(4 correct answers)

📍 Covers: Chapter 2 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 1 › 2.1 Hardware inventory and associated permissions

For every device, Lesson 1 asks the inventory to document administrator access, the list that Class 3 turns into Kalmia's permissions map. Which pieces of information belong in that record? (4 correct answers)

💡 Hint: Picture the seven HIGH findings of Kalmia's review: what did Lucas need to know about each account to spot them?

📝 Why these are right: B: you cannot judge access you have not listed, and factory accounts such as "admin" on SW-HQ are exactly the ones to find. C: knowing who holds each password exposes shared accounts, like the NAS-01 administrator password known by four people, which destroy accountability. E: an administrator account without a second factor carries the "no MFA" flag. G: the end date separates the MSP (managed service provider) contract on FW-HQ, which ends in June 2027, from the roaster vendor's unattended access, which has no end at all. Why the others are wrong: A — passwords are secrets (administrator passwords carry Kalmia's Restricted label) and never go into an inventory; D — CAM-HQ-3, CAM-HQ-4 and the two printers produced four of the seven HIGH findings; F — vendor and MSP access is precisely what must be recorded.

MSQ 33

(3 correct answers)

📍 Covers: Chapter 5 — Public Sources, Threat Reports and the Threat Catalogue › 5.3 Methodical analysis of public sources — how to read and rate a threat report

Question 3 of the method asks you to separate what a publisher observed from what it assessed. Which of these sentences, of the kind found in an alert of the Cyber Centre (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/encheck), are assessments? (3 correct answers)

💡 Hint: Look for the words that carry a judgment about the future or about who is responsible.

✅ Answers: A, D, F

📝 Why these are right: A and F use estimative words ("likely", 60–74 %; "very likely", 75–89 %) about what may happen next. Why the others are wrong: B — a release of fixed versions is a verifiable fact; C — a dated addition to the KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) catalogue (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalogcheck) is an observation; E — identified infrastructure is something the publisher observed.

💡 Hint: A row can carry several pieces of evidence and several asset identifiers, but only one technique and one entry point.

📝 Why these are right: C: same source and technique, but two entry points (the PHP engine, the plugin) with different evidence, which is why the seed catalogue has T-02 and T-03; E: different techniques and entry points (an exploited firewall flaw, default camera passwords), hence T-14 and T-06. Why the others are wrong: A — same source, technique, asset and entry point: one row with two pieces of evidence; B — two references support one event: one row; D — one action through one entry point can list several assets (T-01 lists A-03 and A-04); F — weaknesses are evidence, and one row can cite several of them.

Part E — 20 short essay questions

Four questions per chapter. Allow about ten minutes per question: two to plan, eight to write. Then compare your text with the model answer and mark it honestly with the marking guide (out of 10).

Short Essay 1

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.2 Key vocabulary — asset, threat, vulnerability, risk, impact, control

In a management meeting, Nadia Roy says: "Our biggest risk is that ransomware gang everybody talks about." Explain to her, in plain words, which two terms she is mixing up. Define threat, vulnerability and risk, say where controls fit, and show how the words connect by writing one risk statement about Kalmia's web shop. (10–14 lines)

0 words

💡 Hint: Start with the gang's role (who could cause harm), then turn to what Kalmia itself can change. Build the statement on the template: Because [ ], [ ] could [ ] [ ], which would [ ].

✅ Model answer:

Ms. Roy is calling a threat a risk. The ransomware gang is a threat source: it is who could cause harm, and it exists whatever Kalmia does. A threat is the potential cause of an unwanted event, made of a source (the gang) and an event (a phishing e-mail, encrypted files). A vulnerability is a weakness in one of our own assets, procedures or controls that the source can exploit, such as an outdated plugin or an administrator account without MFA (multi-factor authentication). A risk exists only when they meet: a threat exploits a vulnerability and harms an asset. We measure it with two separate ratings, likelihood and impact, multiplied on Kalmia's 1-to-5 scales. Controls change the risk by lowering its likelihood, its impact or both. Kalmia cannot switch off a criminal group, but it can remove the weaknesses the group would use.

For the web shop: "Because four of the shop's 23 plugins have gone six months without updates and its three administrator accounts have no MFA, a criminal group running automated attack tools could plant a card-skimming script on the checkout page, which would expose our customers' card data, require a declaration under Québec's privacy law (🔗 https://www.legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca/en/document/cs/p-39.1check) and PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) (🔗 https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/check) follow-up, and could close the shop in November and December, when a third of our online revenue comes in."

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

  • Spots the confusion: the gang is a threat source, not a risk (2 pts)
  • Defines threat (source and event), vulnerability (Kalmia's own weakness) and risk (a threat exploiting a vulnerability, measured by likelihood × impact) correctly (3 pts)
  • Explains that controls act on likelihood, impact or both, and that Kalmia controls its exposure rather than the attackers (1 pt)
  • Writes the statement on the template with a real vulnerability, threat source, threat event and asset from the case (2 pts)
  • States the impact in business terms (money, season, legal duties) and keeps products and solutions out of the statement (2 pts)

Short Essay 2

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.3 The CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) triad + 1.6 The case organization of the Integrative Project — Kalmia Coffee Roasters

Kalmia's CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) table rates the web shop and checkout page Confidentiality = Moderate, Integrity = High and Availability = High. Justify each rating with facts from the case, give the asset's category and the rule that produces it, and explain why integrity matters for the checkout even though Kalmia never stores card numbers. (10–14 lines)

0 words

💡 Hint: Ask the three questions in turn (disclosed? altered? unusable?) and think about what the shop holds, when it earns its money, and what happens at the moment a customer types a card number.

✅ Model answer:

Confidentiality is Moderate. The shop holds the records of about 2,300 online subscribers (name, delivery address, e-mail), so a disclosure would be serious, but card numbers are not kept there: the payment processor handles them and Kalmia sees only tokens, which keeps the rating below High. Integrity is High, because an unauthorized change can cost money directly, as a price changed from $18.99 to $1.89 would, or turn the checkout into a trap. Availability is High: the shop brings in about 25% of revenue, November and December alone bring about one third of the year's online sales, and Nadia Roy insists that it must work during the holidays. The six-hour outage of March (INC-01) shows how quickly that can go wrong. With the high-water mark, the category is the highest of the three ratings, so the web shop is a High asset.

Integrity matters even without stored cards. A card-skimming script slipped into the checkout page through an outdated plugin, which is risk R2, captures the numbers as customers type them, before they reach the processor. Nothing is stored, yet card data leaks. That means a confidentiality incident to assess under Québec's privacy law (🔗 https://www.legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca/en/document/cs/p-39.1check), PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) (🔗 https://www.pcisecuritystandards.org/check) follow-up and a shop closed in peak season, which is why R2 carries an impact of 5.

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

  • Justifies Confidentiality = Moderate with the subscriber records and the absence of stored card numbers (tokens only) (2 pts)
  • Justifies Integrity = High with the direct harm of unauthorized changes to prices or to the checkout (2 pts)
  • Justifies Availability = High with the revenue share, the holiday peak or INC-01, and the owner's priority (2 pts)
  • Gives the category High and states the high-water mark as "the highest of the three", not an average (2 pts)
  • Explains how a skimming script (R2) captures cards at the checkout and names its consequences: Québec law, PCI DSS, closure (2 pts)

Short Essay 3

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.4 The risk analysis process, step by step

Using Kalmia's risk R1 (ransomware encrypting NAS-01 and its attached backup through a phished office account), explain steps 5 to 9 of the risk analysis process. Justify the likelihood and the impact with Kalmia's scales, give the score, the level and what Kalmia's criteria require, then explain the proposed treatment option, how its controls change the ratings, and who accepts the residual risk. (10–14 lines)

0 words

💡 Hint: Quote the evidence behind each rating, then sort the proposed controls by function: which ones make the attack less likely, and which one makes it less damaging?

✅ Model answer:

For R1, the likelihood is 4, Likely (several times a year): phishing e-mails reach the office every week, four people share the NAS-01 administrator password and there is no MFA (multi-factor authentication). The impact is 4, Major, because the consequences match that row of the scale: several days of disruption, with about three days without wholesale preparation (around $28,500 of sales) plus recovery costs, and an HR (human resources) folder that could be exposed, which would force an assessment for a declaration to the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec) (🔗 https://www.cai.gouv.qc.ca/englishcheck). The score is 4 × 4 = 16, the top of the High band (10–16), so Kalmia's criteria require a treatment plan within 30 days and a report to the President.

The proposed option is to reduce the risk. MFA, individual administrator accounts and endpoint protection are preventive: they make a successful attack less likely. An offline backup tested every month is corrective: if an attack still gets through, NAS-01 can be restored quickly and the backup cannot be encrypted along with the data, so the impact drops. The analyst estimates the residual risk at 2 × 2 = 4, which is Low. The analyst does not accept that risk; Nadia Roy, as risk owner, accepts it formally, in writing. The register is then reviewed whenever something changes, and at least once a year.

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

  • Justifies likelihood 4 with the case evidence and the wording of the scale (2 pts)
  • Justifies impact 4 with the scale descriptors: several days of disruption, about $28,500 plus recovery, a possible CAI declaration (2 pts)
  • Computes 16, names the High level and the required action: plan within 30 days, reported to the President (2 pts)
  • Names "reduce" and links the preventive controls to likelihood and the tested offline backup (corrective) to impact (2 pts)
  • Gives the residual risk 2 × 2 = 4 (Low), accepted in writing by the risk owner rather than the analyst, with periodic review (2 pts)

Short Essay 4

📍 Covers: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Threats and Risks › 1.5 Risk analysis frameworks — NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 and ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27005

Compare NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 (🔗 https://www.nist.gov/cyberframeworkcheck) and ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27005:2022 (🔗 https://www.iso.org/standard/80585.htmlcheck): who publishes each one, which question each answers and how each is built. Then explain how this course uses both documents in the labs and in the Integrative Project report. (12–16 lines)

0 words

💡 Hint: One is a method, the other a map of outcomes. Walk through the labs in order, then think about the framework section of the report.

✅ Model answer:

The CSF comes from NIST, a non-regulatory United States federal agency; version 2.0 was published on February 26, 2024. It is voluntary guidance that answers "which outcomes does our cybersecurity program achieve, and which should it achieve?", describing what to achieve rather than how. Its Core has six Functions (GOVERN, IDENTIFY, PROTECT, DETECT, RESPOND, RECOVER), with GOVERN new and in the centre, broken into 22 Categories and 106 Subcategories. An organization describes itself with a Current Profile and a Target Profile, the gap becoming its action plan, and Tiers (Partial, Risk Informed, Repeatable, Adaptive) describe how rigorous its risk governance is.

ISO/IEC 27005 is written jointly by ISO (International Organization for Standardization) and IEC (4th edition, October 2022). It answers "how do we run the risk management process?": context establishment, risk identification (asset-based or event-based), risk analysis, risk evaluation and risk treatment, with communication and consultation, and monitoring and review, running throughout. It supports an ISMS (information security management system) based on ISO/IEC 27001 (🔗 https://www.iso.org/standard/27001check) and repeats as the context changes.

The two complement each other, and NIST even maps CSF outcomes to ISO standards. Our labs follow the ISO/IEC 27005 process: Lab 1 sets the context and identifies the assets, Lab 2 adds the threats, Lab 3 analyzes and evaluates the risks, and Lab 4 treats them. The CSF then reports the result to Nadia Roy as a Current and a Target Profile in the Integrative Project report.

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

  • Gives the publishers and dates correctly: NIST, February 26, 2024; ISO and IEC, October 2022 (2 pts)
  • Describes the CSF: outcomes rather than methods, six Functions with GOVERN in the centre, the Core, Profiles and gap, Tiers (2 pts)
  • Describes ISO/IEC 27005: five activities in order, two continuous activities, iterative, supports an ISO/IEC 27001 ISMS (2 pts)
  • Draws the contrast clearly: method versus map of outcomes and management language, and notes that they are compatible (2 pts)
  • Explains the course use: labs follow 27005 (Labs 1 to 4 mapped), CSF Profiles in the project report (2 pts)

Short Essay 5

📍 Covers: Chapter 2 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 1 › 2.1 Hardware inventory and associated permissions

Lucas Martin's review of administrator access at Kalmia's head office found, among other things: six office employees who work every day in accounts with administrator rights; the standard login "entrepot" shared by the six shipping and warehouse employees on PC-SHIP-01 and PC-WH-01; and CAM-HQ-3 and CAM-HQ-4 still running on their factory passwords. Explain the three rules Lesson 1 uses to judge permissions, apply one rule to each finding with Kalmia's level (HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW), and explain why the Mirai botnet makes the third finding the most urgent. (10–14 lines)

0 words

💡 Hint: One rule per finding, one level per finding, then one or two hard facts about Mirai.

✅ Model answer:

A permission is the right, granted to one identity, to do one particular thing to one particular resource, and Lesson 1 judges every permission with three rules. Least privilege gives each person only the rights the job requires, for as long as it requires them. Accountability means you can always tell which person did what. The third rule says no device goes into service with its factory user name and password.

The six office accounts with administrator rights break least privilege: nobody needs to install software or change system settings to answer e-mail or enter invoices, yet every program they open inherits those rights. Kalmia rates each one MEDIUM and, since none uses MFA (multi-factor authentication), adds the "no MFA" flag. The "entrepot" login breaks accountability: when something goes wrong on PC-SHIP-01, the log shows "entrepot", never which of the six employees acted. Because it is a standard account and not an administrator, it is rated LOW. CAM-HQ-3 and CAM-HQ-4 break the default-credentials rule and are rated HIGH.

Mirai explains why they come first. In 2016 it took over hundreds of thousands of cameras and video recorders simply by trying about sixty factory user names and passwords over Telnet, then used them in some of the largest DDoS (distributed denial of service) attacks of the time. Factory passwords are printed in manuals and built into attack tools, and our scan found Telnet open on both cameras. I would change those passwords this week.

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

  • Defines least privilege, accountability and the default-credentials rule correctly (3 pts)
  • Links the six administrator daily accounts to least privilege and rates them MEDIUM (2 pts)
  • Links the shared "entrepot" login to accountability and rates it LOW, with the reason it is not higher (2 pts)
  • Rates the factory-password cameras HIGH and supports it with Mirai facts: 2016, about sixty factory logins, Telnet, hundreds of thousands of devices, DDoS attacks (2 pts)
  • Ends with a clear priority or next action (1 pt)

Short Essay 6

📍 Covers: Chapter 2 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 1 › 2.2 Software inventory, licences and associated permissions

Three Kalmia computers still run Windows 10 Pro 22H2: ROAST-PC, which controls the roaster, and the two wholesale sales laptops, SALES-LT1 and SALES-LT2, which travel to clients. Explain what end of support means and what CIS (Center for Internet Security) Safeguard 2.2 (🔗 https://www.cisecurity.org/controls/inventory-and-control-of-software-assetscheck) requires. Then compare Kalmia's three options (upgrade or replace, ESU (Extended Security Updates), documented exception) and recommend one for ROAST-PC and one for the laptops. (10–14 lines)

0 words

💡 Hint: Start from the date and the rule. Then remember that one computer is tied to a physical process and its vendor, while the other two leave the building.

✅ Model answer:

End of support is the date after which the publisher stops releasing security updates; for Windows 10 it was October 14, 2025. Every flaw discovered since then stays open, and on the day of Class 2 Kalmia's Windows 10 computers had gone 374 days without a patch. Safeguard 2.2 lets only supported software be authorized. If the business truly needs unsupported software, it needs a documented exception that describes the mitigating controls and the residual risk management accepts, reviewed every month.

Kalmia has three options. Upgrading or replacing restores support for good. ESU buys time: up to three years, one year at a time, on version 22H2, at USD (United States dollars) 61 per device in year one, doubling every year. An exception keeps the computer as it is, but only with written controls and Nadia Roy's acceptance of the residual risk.

For the sales laptops I recommend upgrading them to Windows 11 or replacing them. They travel and connect to outside networks, which makes them the most exposed, and twelve other Kalmia computers already run Windows 11. ROAST-PC is harder: it is operational technology, and its roasting software and vendor must support any change, so the upgrade has to be planned with them. Until then, I would buy ESU or write a documented exception whose mitigating controls include isolating ROAST-PC from the office network and removing the unauthorized remote-access tool.

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

  • Defines end of support correctly, gives the Windows 10 date and a consequence (2 pts)
  • States the Safeguard 2.2 rule with the documented exception, mitigating controls, accepted residual risk and monthly review (2 pts)
  • Describes the three options, with correct ESU details: up to three years, version 22H2, USD 61 in year one, doubling (2 pts)
  • Gives a recommendation for the laptops justified by their exposure (2 pts)
  • Gives a recommendation for ROAST-PC that respects its operational-technology constraints and names at least one mitigating control (2 pts)

Short Essay 7

📍 Covers: Chapter 2 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 1 › 2.3 Asset classification, ownership and criticality

Nadia Roy asks why eight of the ten assets rated in the classification workshop came out "High", and yet the priority list still puts them in a clear order. Explain the FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standard) 199 (🔗 https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/199/finalcheck) ratings and the high-water mark, the difference between classification and criticality, and how Kalmia's protection map and priority rule separate assets that share the same category. Use at least three Kalmia assets. (10–14 lines)

0 words

💡 Hint: One High rating decides the category. After that, look at two other measures: how sensitive the information is, and how long the business can live without it.

✅ Model answer:

FIPS 199 rates the impact of a loss of confidentiality, integrity and availability as low (limited), moderate (serious) or high (severe or catastrophic). The overall level of an asset is the highest of its three ratings, the high-water mark, so a single High is enough. That is why eight of the ten workshop assets landed in the High category: the category says severe damage is possible somewhere, not what kind.

Two other measures do the sorting. Classification measures sensitivity, the harm if information leaks or is altered, with Kalmia's four labels from Public to Restricted. Criticality measures dependence, how long the business survives without the asset, expressed as a tier derived from its MTD (maximum tolerable downtime). Crossing the two gives the protection map: the daily order plan (Internal, Tier 1) mainly needs to keep running, the employee files (Restricted, Tier 3) mainly need confidentiality controls, and the web shop (Confidential, Tier 1) needs both.

Nadia Roy's priority rule then sorts by category, then tier, then label, then the shortest downtime. Among the three Tier 1 assets, all rated High, the web shop ranks first because its label beats Internal, and the POS (point of sale) service ranks second because its 2 hours beat the order plan's 4. The ranked list becomes the impact column of Lab 3 and the order of controls in Lab 4.

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

  • Explains the FIPS 199 levels and the high-water mark as a maximum, not an average (2 pts)
  • Distinguishes classification (sensitivity, label) from criticality (dependence, tier from the MTD) (2 pts)
  • Places at least three Kalmia assets correctly on the protection map (2 pts)
  • States the priority rule in the right order (2 pts)
  • Applies the rule to break a tie with Kalmia data and links the result to Labs 3 and 4 (2 pts)

📍 Covers: Chapter 2 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 1 › 2.4 Hands-on: building an asset inventory with a template and a network scanner (Nmap (Network Mapper))

Describe, in order, how your team turns the lab replica of Kalmia's head office into rows of the Lab 1 template with Nmap (Network Mapper) (🔗 https://nmap.org/check), from the written authorization required by Annex D of the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice (🔗 https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlcheck) to the scan log. Then name three things a scan can never tell you, and explain why the scan is only one of the four sources of the inventory. (10–14 lines)

0 words

💡 Hint: Start before the first packet and finish after the last file is saved. For the limits, think of what is switched off, out of range, hidden, or not technical at all.

✅ Model answer:

Nothing starts without the written authorization: the owner and authority, the range 192.168.10.0/24, the exclusions (ROAST-PC at .20, the scanner at .200), the permitted activities, the dates and an emergency contact. We scan nothing else, not even with a ping sweep.

Step one is host discovery with sudo nmap -sn. On the local network Nmap uses ARP (Address Resolution Protocol), so it finds the addresses that are up and records their MAC (Media Access Control) addresses and manufacturers; 25 hosts answered. Step two runs -sV and -O on the 100 most common ports of the live hosts, minus the exclusions, to list open ports, services, versions and an OS (operating system) guess. Both steps write XML (Extensible Markup Language), the format for programs. Step three converts the XML: each host is matched with the register by MAC address and becomes a row marked known, new or scanner, with ROAST-PC as "discovery only". Step four is human work: people add owner, label and tier, review the exposed services, write the scan log, keep the files and repeat later with Ndiff.

A scan cannot tell who owns a device or how critical it is, it cannot see what is switched off, travelling or out of range (the cafés, the cloud services), and its OS guess is only a probability. That is why it joins the records, the physical check and the network logs instead of replacing them.

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

  • Puts the authorization first, with the Annex D content, tonight's scope and exclusions, and refuses anything outside it (2 pts)
  • Describes discovery correctly: -sn, ARP, sudo and the MAC addresses it returns (2 pts)
  • Describes the service and OS step, the XML output and the conversion by MAC with the three statuses (2 pts)
  • Separates the people columns from the tool columns and includes the review, scan log and repeat with Ndiff (2 pts)
  • Names three real limits and explains why the scan is one of four sources (2 pts)

Short Essay 9

📍 Covers: Chapter 3 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 2 › 3.1 Data and services critical to the organization's operations

Define the MTD (maximum tolerable downtime), the WRT (work recovery time), the RTO (recovery time objective) and the RPO (recovery point objective), and explain how they relate. Then apply them to P-03, Kalmia's wholesale order preparation and delivery: MTD 4 hours, WRT 1 hour, RPO 4 hours. Its key data sits on the Production share of NAS-01, which takes about 12 hours to restore and is copied once a night, at 01:00, to the USB (Universal Serial Bus) disk BKP-USB-01 that stays plugged into NAS-01. (10–14 lines)

0 words

💡 Hint: Start with the relation between the three time values, keep the RPO apart, then run the two gap tests and look at where the copy lives.

✅ Model answer:

The MTD is the longest total outage a process can take before its owner judges the harm unacceptable; at Kalmia, it is the shortest outage duration that any impact category rates 3 (serious) or more. The RTO is the time budget for bringing the systems and data back, and the WRT is what people need afterwards to check the data, catch up and restart. They are linked by MTD = RTO + WRT, so the RTO must always be shorter than the MTD. The RPO is a different kind of number: it is the maximum age of the last good copy, so it limits data loss, not downtime, and it is not part of the MTD.

For P-03, the RTO is 4 − 1 = 3 hours, and an MTD of 4 hours makes it a Tier 1 process. The BIA (business impact analysis) then shows two problems. Restoring the Production share takes about 12 hours, far beyond the 3-hour RTO: a recovery gap. A nightly copy can be up to 24 hours old, while the owner accepts losing at most 4 hours of data: a data gap. Worse, BKP-USB-01 never leaves NAS-01, so ransomware that encrypts the server can encrypt the backup in the same minute; one copy must be kept offline or off-site, and the restore must be tested. Finally, NAS-01 is a shared single point of failure, since four processes stop with it.

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

  • Correct definitions of the MTD, the RTO and the WRT, with MTD = RTO + WRT and the RTO shorter than the MTD (3 pts)
  • RPO defined as the maximum age of the last good copy and kept separate from the MTD (2 pts)
  • P-03 computed correctly: RTO of 3 hours, Tier 1 (1 pt)
  • Recovery gap (12 h against 3 h) and data gap (24 h against 4 h) identified and explained (2 pts)
  • Backup that stays online flagged, with an offline or off-site copy and a tested restore as the remedy (1 pt)
  • NAS-01 recognized as a shared single point of failure (1 pt)

Short Essay 10

📍 Covers: Chapter 3 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 2 › 3.2 Physical and logical representation of the infrastructure (network diagrams)

Every device at Kalmia's head office sits on a single subnet, 192.168.10.0/24, with no filtering between devices. Explain what a flat network is and why it is a risk, using the idea of a trust boundary and the Target breach of 2013 as reported by the U.S. Senate Committee on Commerce (🔗 https://www.commerce.senate.gov/services/files/24d3c229-4f2f-405d-b8db-a3a67f183883%5Ccheck). Then explain what a logical diagram of the head office reveals that the hardware inventory cannot. (10–14 lines)

0 words

💡 Hint: Name the kinds of devices that share the zone, follow an attacker's path from the weakest one, and recall what the Target report concluded.

✅ Model answer:

A flat network is one zone where any device can talk to any other. Kalmia's head office is exactly that: NAS-01 and the office computers share 192.168.10.0/24 with the cameras, the thermostat, the employees' phones, ROAST-PC and its vendor's data logger, and flow F-10, any device to any device, was never decided. One compromised device, say a camera still using its factory password or an infected phone, can therefore reach NAS-01 and the roaster's control computer.

A trust boundary is the line between zones of different trust, and any flow crossing it has to go through a control such as a firewall rule, an authentication or an approval with an end date. A flat network has no internal boundary, so nothing slows an intruder down once inside. Target learned this in 2013: according to the Senate committee report, attackers used credentials stolen from an HVAC (heating, ventilation and air conditioning) contractor to enter a supplier portal that was not fully isolated, then reached the systems holding customer data. About 40 million payment card accounts were stolen, and the report's verdict was that Target had not properly isolated its most sensitive assets. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/top-10-security-actions-no-5-segment-and-separate-information-itsm10092check) gives the remedy in ITSM.10.092: group systems by sensitivity and function, and control the traffic between groups.

An inventory only lists devices. The logical diagram shows the zones, the 16 flows and every boundary crossing, such as RoastTech's remote control of ROAST-PC.

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

  • Flat network defined and applied to the devices of the head office (2 pts)
  • Risk explained: one compromised device can reach NAS-01 or ROAST-PC because nothing controls internal traffic (2 pts)
  • Trust boundary defined, with examples of the controls a crossing must pass (2 pts)
  • Target case reported accurately: entry path through a contractor's credentials and the report's conclusion (2 pts)
  • What only the logical diagram reveals (zones, flows, crossings, the undecided F-10) (1 pt)
  • Direction of the remedy: segmentation as recommended in ITSM.10.092 (1 pt)

📍 Covers: Chapter 3 — Identifying Information Assets, Part 2 › 3.3 Documenting who has access to what (permissions map)

Compare need to know (with its partner, least privilege) and separation of duties. Illustrate each principle with one finding from Kalmia's permissions map, then explain how role-based access control and the access review help, and who decides the fix. (10–14 lines)

0 words

💡 Hint: One principle limits what a person can see or change; the other limits which combinations of tasks a single person may hold.

✅ Model answer:

Need to know means you get access to a piece of information only if your job calls for it; least privilege adds that the level granted is the lowest one that does the job. CIS (Center for Internet Security) Safeguard 3.3 (🔗 https://cas.docs.cisecurity.org/en/latest/source/Controls3/check) builds access lists on it, and section 20 of Québec's Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector (🔗 https://www.legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca/en/document/cs/P-39.1check) lets an employee see personal information only when his or her duties need it. At Kalmia, the inherited office entry on the HR (human resources) share breaks the principle: seven people, Marc Gauthier and Julie Nguyen among them, can change employee files that hold SIN (Social Insurance Number) and bank details. The share is Restricted, so the EXCESS finding is HIGH.

Separation of duties concerns combinations, not visibility: critical functions are split so that nobody can commit a fraud alone and hide it. In Sage 50, Marc Gauthier can edit a supplier's banking information and also release the payment, the INC-02 scenario, in which only Karim Haddad's call stopped an $18,400 transfer.

RBAC (role-based access control) helps with both, because permissions go to groups built from the role matrix: a mover changes group, and a reviewer reads one line per role. The access review closes the loop. The analyst prepares the map, the data owner decides (Sophie Tremblay for HR and Finance), and the custodian, Lucas Martin, applies the decision.

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

  • Need to know and least privilege defined correctly (2 pts)
  • A Kalmia example where need to know is broken (the office entry on HR or Everyone on Scans), with its level (2 pts)
  • Separation of duties defined and illustrated with the Sage 50 finding and INC-02 (2 pts)
  • Clear contrast between access to information and combinations of duties (1 pt)
  • Role-based access control explained (movers, review by role) (1 pt)
  • Access review roles: the analyst prepares, the data owner decides, the custodian applies (2 pts)

Lab 1 is called "Asset inventory and infrastructure map". Explain what the critical services register, the two network views and the permissions map each add to the hardware and software inventory, why each device must carry the same name everywhere, and what the readiness check can and cannot guarantee before you hand in. The inventories answer one question: what does Kalmia own? Lab 1 adds three products no list can replace. The critical services register, built from the BIA (business impact analysis), says what the company cannot lose and for how long: an MTD (maximum tolerable downtime), RTO (recovery time objective) and RPO (recovery point objective) per process, with the gaps and the single points of failure. The physical view shows where each device sits and how it is cabled, so it can be found and isolated; the logical view shows the zones, the flows and the trust boundaries. The permissions map shows who can really read or change each share, compared with the role matrix.

These pieces only work together if each device carries the same hostname and asset tag in the Hardware sheet, on both diagrams and in the permissions map. A device on the map but missing from the inventory, like the untagged data logger LOG-ROAST-01, is a reconciliation error, and Labs 2 to 4 inherit it, since the threat catalogue and the risk register point back to these names.

The readiness check verifies structure and rules: folder name, README and integrity statement, the six CSV (comma-separated values) exports, an RTO shorter than the MTD, diagrams and exports, asset tags, decisions on HIGH findings, and any number shaped like a SIN (Social Insurance Number), which is a BLOCKER. It makes sure no required piece is absent, but it cannot judge whether my memo is clear or my diagrams accurate.

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

Give capability, intent and targeting a value on the Lab 2 scale, back each value with Kalmia evidence, and explain how the cybercrime-as-a-service model makes a 46-person roaster a realistic target. ✅ Model answer:

Cybercriminal groups act for money, so I write their motivation as financial gain. I rate their capability at 4 (high). Their own skill varies, but under cybercrime-as-a-service they buy what they lack: one group rents ransomware to affiliates, an initial access broker sells a way in, others sell stolen passwords or fake login-page kits. Since every step comes ready-made, attacking a company of 46 people costs very little, which is why small firms are frequent victims.

Intent gets a 5 (very high) because Kalmia offers almost everything they want. Supplier payments go out by bank transfer after an e-mail request, and INC-02 already tried to divert $18,400 that way. The 18,500 loyalty records can be resold or used for extortion, the checkout page could carry card-skimming code, and ransomware would stop operations until someone pays. Targeting gets a 4 (high): these groups choose among exposed victims, and two facts give them reasons to pick Kalmia, a backup disk that stays connected to NAS-01, which makes paying more likely, and a November–December season worth a third of online revenue. With an exposure match of 4 of 4, the row's relevance is high. My evidence: INC-02, the loyalty platform, the Lab 1 inventory and the National Cyber Threat Assessment 2025-2026 (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/national-cyber-threat-assessment-2025-2026check), which names ransomware the top cybercrime threat to Canada's critical infrastructure.

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

  • Capability is rated and justified through cybercrime-as-a-service: rented ransomware, access brokers, stolen passwords or kits (2 pts)

INC-02 and INC-04 both involve people inside Kalmia, yet they are very different stories. Compare them: the category of insider under the definition of CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/defining-insider-threatscheck), the intent, how each one is entered in the Lab 2 catalogue, and the first control you would propose for each. ✅ Model answer:

In INC-04, a shift supervisor left on July 15, but nobody disabled her loyalty-platform administrator account, and on September 18 at 21:47 it exported the 18,500 member records. Under CISA's definition she is still an insider, because she had authorized access and the account still worked. The export is a malicious-insider indicator, but only an indicator: we know a former employee's account did it, not who typed the password or why. In Lab 2 I enter the export of all member records through a leaver's account as the threat event, with the audit-log entry as evidence and confidentiality at stake. Under Québec's privacy act (🔗 https://www.legisquebec.gouv.qc.ca/en/document/cs/P-39.1check), as amended by Law 25, it is also a confidentiality incident: it goes in the incident register and, when serious injury is a risk, must be reported to the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec) (🔗 https://www.cai.gouv.qc.ca/check). First control: an offboarding checklist that disables accounts on the last day, plus export alerts.

INC-02 is the opposite. The employee who updated the importer's banking information in Sage 50 meant no harm: an unintentional insider used as a tool by an outside fraudster through business email compromise. It needs two rows: the fraudster behind the look-alike domain as the external threat source, and, as an internal condition, a payment process that a single e-mail can alter. Karim Haddad's call-back saved the $18,400, so my first control is a mandatory call-back on a known number and a second approver for bank-detail changes.

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

  • INC-02 is classified as an unintentional insider manipulated by an external fraudster, recorded as two rows (2 pts)
  • Lab 2 entries name the evidence and the CIA (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) property; the Law 25 obligation for INC-04 is mentioned (2 pts)
  • Suitable first controls: offboarding and export alerts; a call-back and a second approver, that is, separation of duties (2 pts)

Short Essay 15

📍 Covers: Chapter 4 — Identifying Threats, Part 1 › 4.3 Common attack methods: malware, ransomware, phishing and social engineering, DoS (Denial of Service), credential theft

Explain how several attack methods chain together into one ransomware attack against a small company such as Kalmia, from the first message to the encryption. For each stage, name the method and a Kalmia weakness that would help the attacker, then explain why a single control can break several methods at once. (12–16 lines)

0 words

💡 Hint: Follow the attacker's needs in order: a person to fool, a credential, a foothold, the backups, the data, and finally a moment when nobody is watching.

✅ Model answer:

A ransomware attack is a chain, not a single click. It usually opens with phishing, social engineering by message: a convincing e-mail sends an employee to a fake Microsoft 365 login page. Typing the password there is credential theft, and at Kalmia it would work, because MFA (multi-factor authentication) protects only the two administrator accounts; everyone else, from the nine staff accounts to the loyalty and WordPress administrators, signs in with a password alone. RoastLink's shared password offers a second way in. With a valid password the attacker breaks nothing: it signs in to the mailbox, then the VPN (virtual private network).

Next comes malware. The attacker installs its tools and explores, and the flat roastery network lets it reach NAS-01 freely. Before encrypting, it deletes or encrypts every backup it can reach; NAS-01's only backup disk stays connected, so it would be lost with the data. It copies files out, such as HR (human resources) files, for double extortion, then launches the encryption on a Saturday night. A DDoS (distributed denial of service) on the checkout page could add pressure.

Because each step depends on the one before, one control can cut several. MFA with number matching stops the stolen password at the log-in steps; a tested offline backup removes the pressure that backup deletion and encryption are meant to create; and one employee who reports the first e-mail stops the whole chain.

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

  • The stages come in the right order: phishing, credential theft, log-in with a valid account, malware, backup deletion, data copy, encryption (2 pts)
  • Each stage is labelled with the correct method (2 pts)
  • At least three stages are tied to documented Kalmia weaknesses: MFA gaps, RoastLink, flat network, connected backup (2 pts)
  • Double extortion and the night or weekend timing are explained (1 pt)
  • The answer shows how MFA, an offline backup and a reporting employee each break several steps (2 pts)
  • The answer is clear, organized and within the expected length (1 pt)

📍 Covers: Chapter 4 — Identifying Threats, Part 1 › 4.4 Case study: a recent ransomware attack on a small manufacturer

Lesson 4 used a real incident, the 2025 ransomware attack on Ganong Bros. (🔗 https://www.ganong.com/check), to draw lessons for Kalmia. Explain the rules an analyst follows when using a real incident as a case study, and show how each rule applies to the Ganong case and to the KNP Logistics contrast. (10–14 lines)

0 words

💡 Hint: Think about where the facts come from, what the sources leave out, how you report who did it, and what you compare the lessons with.

✅ Model answer:

First rule: public sources only. For Ganong, that means the first-hand account by the company's head of IT (information technology) in CSO Online (🔗 https://www.csoonline.com/article/4038381/caught-in-the-cyber-crosshairs-a-candy-manufacturers-2025-ransomware-ordeal.htmlcheck) and local press reports; for KNP, the BBC (British Broadcasting Corporation) report of July 21, 2025 (🔗 https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cx2gx28815wocheck). Under the Legal Notice (🔗 https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlcheck), we never visit leak sites or download stolen data.

Second rule: separate the known from the unknown. The sources say the Ganong attack was ransomware with double extortion, discovered on Saturday, February 22, 2025, and that offline backups brought most systems back within about a week. They are silent on how the attackers got in, so I must not guess, and certainly not borrow KNP's guessed password. If the catalogue needs an entry point, I cite the group's usual methods from CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) advisory AA23-352A (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-352acheck) and label them as usual methods.

Third rule: attribution as the source states it. I write that the Play group claimed the attack, not that Play attacked Ganong.

Last rule: compare with the organization's documented state, not with assumptions. Ganong's offline backup, fast isolation and checked controllers become checks against Kalmia's documents: one backup disk always connected, a flat network, ROAST-PC on Windows 10. That comparison shows which lab rows come first; it is not yet a risk rating.

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

  • Public sources only, named (the CSO Online account, local press, the BBC report), with no leak sites or breach data (2 pts)
  • What is known is separated from what is not; the root cause was never published (2 pts)
  • No entry point is invented or borrowed from KNP; the usual methods from AA23-352A are cited with careful wording (2 pts)
  • Attribution is reported as the source states it (Legal Notice, section 7.3) (2 pts)
  • The lessons are compared with Kalmia's documented state, using at least two concrete gaps, and the answer says this is not yet a risk rating (2 pts)

📍 Covers: Chapter 5 — Public Sources, Threat Reports and the Threat Catalogue › 5.1 Public information sources (1/2) — cyberthreat newsletters and security advisories

Suppose that on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, the day after Microsoft's monthly security release, Lucas Martin finds three items about it: an advisory of the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/alerts-advisoriescheck), the entry in the Microsoft Security Update Guide (🔗 https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guidecheck) and a newsletter that sums up the release. Compare an alert, an advisory, a vendor security bulletin and a newsletter, say which of the three items are primary sources, and explain how Lucas runs them through the weekly routine. (8–12 lines)

0 words

💡 Hint: Ask who observed the fact and who only reports it. Then walk through collect, filter, record and decide with Kalmia's Windows machines in mind.

✅ Model answer:

An alert (AL26-nnn at the Cyber Centre) warns about a newly identified threat or a critical flaw and tells defenders how to detect and mitigate it; it is updated as the situation changes. An advisory (AV26-nnn) tells you that a vendor has shipped a security update and lists the affected and fixed versions. A security bulletin is the vendor's own statement of those facts, and only the vendor can confirm which versions are affected and which one fixes the problem. A newsletter summarizes several items for a general audience; it only reports, so it is secondary. Here the Cyber Centre advisory and Microsoft's guide are primary, and the newsletter is just a pointer to them.

Lucas collects all three but works from the primary ones. He filters them against the Lab 1 inventory: the release covers the twelve Windows 11 PCs (personal computers), while the two Windows 10 sales laptops and ROAST-PC no longer get free updates and already have their own rows in the threat catalogue. He records one watch-list line with the date, the source, the item, the assets (A-08, A-09, A-12), the severity as published for each CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) (🔗 https://www.cve.org/check), the action, the owner and the deadline. His decision is watch: InfoNord, the MSP (managed service provider), applies the release within its monthly window by November 20, and Lucas checks that it did.

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

  • Defines the alert and the advisory correctly, with their AL/AV numbering and content (2 pts)
  • Names the vendor as the authority on affected and fixed versions, classes the advisory and the vendor guide as primary and the newsletter as secondary (2 pts)
  • Works from the primary documents rather than from the newsletter (2 pts)
  • Filters against the Lab 1 inventory with the right Kalmia assets: Windows 11 PCs covered, Windows 10 laptops and ROAST-PC already catalogued (2 pts)
  • Records a watch-list line with an owner and a deadline and decides "watch", with InfoNord's November 20 window (2 pts)

Short Essay 18

📍 Covers: Chapter 5 — Public Sources, Threat Reports and the Threat Catalogue › 5.2 Public information sources (2/2) — CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) and MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge)

Nadia Roy has heard that two CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) (🔗 https://www.cve.org/check) records on this week's list, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-56155, both appear in the KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) catalogue (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalogcheck). She asks why one gets three days and the other is thrown away. Explain what CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) (🔗 https://www.first.org/cvss/check), EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) (🔗 https://www.first.org/epss/check) and KEV each measure and who publishes them, then use these two records to show why none of the three, on its own, decides the order of work at Kalmia. (10–14 lines)

0 words

💡 Hint: Severity, probability, evidence: then add the one Kalmia document that says whether the product is actually there.

✅ Model answer:

CVSS, maintained by FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams) (🔗 https://www.first.org/cvss/check) and usually published by the CNA (CVE Numbering Authority) in the CVE record, measures the technical severity of a flaw from 0.0 to 10.0 (Low 0.1–3.9, Medium 4.0–6.9, High 7.0–8.9, Critical 9.0–10.0). EPSS, also from FIRST, is a daily probability between 0 and 1 that the CVE will be exploited in the next 30 days. The KEV catalogue of CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/check) is evidence: it lists CVEs with reliable proof of exploitation in the wild and a clear fix, about 1,700 entries in 2026. Severity, probability, evidence: three different questions, and none of them says whether Kalmia runs the product. Only the Lab 1 inventory says that.

CVE-2026-109618 is Critical (9.2), in the KEV, and it affects PHP (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) on the web shop A-16, which faces the Internet. The four questions of BOD (Binding Operational Directive) 26-04 (🔗 https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/directivescheck) (exposed? in the KEV? automatable? full control?) are all answered "yes", so it falls in the 3-day tier with a compromise check: Lucas asks the host today. CVE-2026-56155 is also in the KEV, rated High (7.8), but it affects AD FS (Active Directory Federation Services) and Windows 10 1607/1809 LTSB (Long-Term Servicing Branch) builds, and Kalmia has none. It is discarded in one line, with the reason written down. Same catalogue, opposite decisions: the inventory makes the difference.

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

  • Defines CVSS as technical severity on 0–10 with its bands, published by the CNA under the FIRST standard (2 pts)
  • Defines EPSS as the daily probability of exploitation in the next 30 days (2 pts)
  • Defines KEV as evidence of exploitation in the wild, kept by CISA, a short list (2 pts)
  • Applies the four BOD 26-04 questions to CVE-2026-109618 and reaches the 3-day tier with a compromise check (2 pts)
  • Explains the discard of CVE-2026-56155 by the inventory, with the reason recorded (2 pts)

Short Essay 19

📍 Covers: Chapter 5 — Public Sources, Threat Reports and the Threat Catalogue › 5.3 Methodical analysis of public sources — how to read and rate a threat report

Question 3 of the reading method, "What is the evidence?", is where most beginners slip. Explain the difference between what a publisher observes and what it assesses, how the estimative words and confidence levels of the Cyber Centre (🔗 https://www.cyber.gc.ca/encheck) are read, and how an attribution must be recorded. Illustrate with alert AL26-028 (🔗 https://cyber.gc.ca/en/alerts-advisories/al26-028-ongoing-help-desk-voice-phishing-campaign-targeting-canadian-organizationscheck) and with this invented sentence: "We assess with high confidence that a criminal group is likely behind these calls." (10–14 lines)

0 words

💡 Hint: One scale gives a probability, another grades the evidence, and a name in a report is never a fact by itself.

✅ Model answer:

An observation is something the publisher saw and can show: a patch was released, exploitation was seen, infrastructure was identified. An assessment is a judgment: who is probably responsible, what is likely to happen next. In AL26-028, the Cyber Centre observed the campaign's infrastructure and described how the callers work (posing as IT (information technology) or help-desk staff and asking for an urgent passkey migration, MFA (multi-factor authentication) enrolment or password change); the sectors it says are targeted are its assessment. Each statement goes into the record labelled as what it is.

The Cyber Centre's estimative words carry defined ranges: almost no chance 1–9 %, very unlikely 10–24 %, unlikely 25–39 %, roughly even chance 40–59 %, likely 60–74 %, very likely 75–89 %, almost certainly 90–99 %. A confidence level (low, moderate, high) is a separate judgment about the quality of the sources and reasoning, as in ODNI (Office of the Director of National Intelligence) Intelligence Community Directive 203 (🔗 https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD%20203%20Analytic%20Standards.pdfcheck). In the invented sentence, "likely" means roughly 60–74 %, and "high confidence" says the analysts trust their evidence; it does not raise the probability.

Naming a responsible group is always an assessment. I would write "publisher X assesses, with high confidence, that a criminal group is likely (60–74 %) behind the calls", with the date and the source rating, and never "a criminal group made the calls" (section 7.3 of the Legal Notice (🔗 https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.htmlcheck)).

📝 Why this answer works (marking guide):

  • Defines observation and assessment correctly (2 pts)
  • Applies the distinction to AL26-028 (2 pts)
  • Gives the estimative scale correctly, with "likely" at 60–74 % (2 pts)
  • Explains that confidence grades the sources and reasoning, not the probability (2 pts)
  • Records the attribution with its author and its words, never as a fact, and cites the rule (2 pts)

Applying these tools or techniques to any other system, network or data without the owner's express written authorization may be a criminal offence (Criminal Code, ss. 342.1, 342.2, 430(1.1) and 184) and is strictly prohibited. You alone are responsible for your actions and your equipment. Full terms: Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, Terms of Use and Acceptable Use Policy, v2.0, section 7.

The rule of this course (section 7.3 and Annex E). Study threat information; never interact with live malicious infrastructure or its operators. In practice, you never open a phishing or command-and-control address from your own computer, you never download a leaked database, and you scan only the lab targets you are given (section 7.6).

The case organization. Torréfaction Kalmia inc. (Kalmia Coffee Roasters Inc.) and every person, system, incident and number about it in this review are fictional. Never search for, contact or test a real company with a similar name. Never put real data from an employer or a relative into a submission without written permission and de-identification. Testing any real organization requires the written authorization of Annex D (sections 7.6 and 7.9). The real organizations named in this review are discussed only from public, official reporting.

Course notice. Unauthorized access to, or interference with, computer systems is a criminal offence, regardless of intent. For example: Criminal Code of Canada, s. 342.1 — Unauthorized use of computer (🔗 https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/c-46/section-342.1.htmlcheck); 18 U.S.C. § 1030 — CFAA (Computer Fraud and Abuse Act) (🔗 https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/1030check); EU (European Union) Directive 2013/40/EU on attacks against information systems (🔗 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32013L0040check); Ley Orgánica 10/1995 (Spain) — Código Penal (🔗 https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-1995-25444check). Never test a system you do not own or do not have written permission to test.
